title: The pod is in the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
body:
We found that after the kubelet process restarts, some pods dependent on device plugins may enter the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
The reason is that when the kubelet restarts, it retrieves the pod list from the apiserver and begins processing the pods. At this point, the device plugin has not yet had the chance to register, which can cause the pods to enter an UnexpectedAdmissionError state. As a result, the containers are killed, and the workload then pulls up a new replica.
Assuming the service has only two replicas, the aforementioned reasons may lead to the pod being rebuilt, during which the service will be interrupted.

Containers should not exit due to kubelet restarts.

Configure the pod to depend on the device plugin and restart kubelet.

title: Pod crashloop backoff isn't entered until after the first restart
body:
While working on a crashloop backoff fix, I noticed that containers are often restarted immediately when they first crash, rather than being delayed by the appropriate backoff time. Essentially, containers have to crash twice before a backoff is applied.

When a pod first runs, [doBackOff](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b4b973c23757b28d1753c0803f85dfb655d905f1/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1607) is called but exits early because the container status is not “exited”. The container then starts and crashes, with the restart count at 0.

In the next sync loop, `doBackOff` is called again and returns false because no entry exists from the previous crash (because of the early exit). The backoff tracker adds an entry due to the call to `backOff.Next()` before returning. The container is restarted with a restart count of 1 and crashes a second time.

In the third loop, `doBackOff` properly reports the backoff duration and the pod is enqueued.

title: Race condition in kubelet's PodCertsManager might lead to memory leaks
body:
Introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4624cb9bb92186358e001be392e50e5d23b5cdd9, and only observable after enabling the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate.

When https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2825 gets called, it queues PCRs for a given pod to be handled by a `podcertificate.Manager` instance.

However, if the queue keys for these PCRs get async-processed before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2826 is called, the `podcertificate.Manager` will never again attempt to clear its internal state for these PCRs as kept in its `Manager.credStore` map.

Kubelet's state gets cleaned for a given pod when the pod is removed.

Write a unit test that runs https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2822, expose the `podcertificate.Manager{}.credStore` variable, and observe what happens to the `credStore` variable when a cached PCR's state is supposed to get removed. Run a couple hundred times to make sure the race condition appears.

Discussed at https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C05MW3382US/p1754992465556979

title: Debian now deprecates public key file used for K8s APT repo
body:
Hi, the K8s repo at https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/ uses a public key file having a hashing algorithm which Debian APT no longer considers safe.  The message emitted by APT (in response to command `apt update`) is:
```
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
```
The command `apt update --audit` outputs:
```
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
Audit: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Sub-process /usr/bin/sqv returned an error code (1), error message is:
   Error: Policy rejected packet type
   Caused by:
       Signature Packet v3 is not considered secure since 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
```
As I understand it, this would be because the public key is hashed using SHA1, rather than SHA256 or SHA512.  

I can suppress this warning (presumably until 1 February 2026) by copying file `/usr/share/apt/default-sequoia.config` to new file (in new parent directories) `/etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/apt-sequoia.config`, and changing the date in the last line from `2026-02-01` to `2027-02-01`.

title: kubelet: Refactor ComputePodQOS by extracting resource-collection logic (no behavior change)
body:
@ndixita Hi! I know you’re very busy. if you have a moment, I’d really appreciate your quick thoughts on this small refactor 🙏 

While reading the kubelet code, I came across the TODO comment you left in ComputePodQOS, which prompted me to think about this. If this looks reasonable, I can open a PR with the extraction and tests

### Summary
`ComputePodQOS` currently does two things:
1. collect resources from the Pod/containers, and
2. decide the QoS class.
Per the existing TODO, I propose extracting the resource-collection into a helper to improve readability and testability (behavior remains the same).

### Proposal
Introduce a helper like:
```go
func collectPodResources(pod *v1.Pod) (v1.ResourceList, v1.ResourceList, bool)
```

and simplify `ComputePodQOS`:
```go
func ComputePodQOS(pod *v1.Pod) v1.PodQOSClass {
    reqs, lims, isGuaranteed := collectPodResources(pod)

    if len(reqs) == 0 && len(lims) == 0 {
        return v1.PodQOSBestEffort
    }
    if isGuaranteed && resourceListsEqual(reqs, lims) {
        return v1.PodQOSGuaranteed
    }
    return v1.PodQOSBurstable
}
```

### Why
- Clear separation of concerns (“collect inputs” vs “decide QoS”)
- Easier unit testing for edge cases (pod-level vs container-level, initContainers, missing cpu/memory)
- Pure refactor, no semantic changes

### Tests
- Add focused unit tests for the helper covering

title: Pods rejected by kubelet admission control enter 'ContainerStatusUnknown' state after kubelet restart
body:
In scenarios where kubelet [rejects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8a28b17c3adab3f0c9ffb8107554b2ed5021fd14/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2273-L2279) a pod via its own admission control (`canAdmitPod`), for instance-

- When the NodeResourcesFit filter is disabled in kube-scheduler, or when a pod is directly created with a spec.nodeName (ensuring the scheduler does not validate pod resource requests against a node's capacity) AND the pod's requests exceed the node's available capacity. In this case, kubelet will reject the pod, eg. with the reason 'OutOfCpu'.

- When pods are stuck pending due to taints on a node, and the taint is removed, there appears to be a race between kube-scheduler placing the pod on the node and kubelet detecting the updated taints on the node (which makes sense, they are both presumably backed by independent watches). In this case, kubelet will reject the pod with the 'TaintToleration' reason. This is a lot harder to reproduce though, because it's racey.

This leaves the pod with a status that has an overall failed phase but no containerStatuses.
```yaml
...
status:
  message: 'Pod was rejected: Node didn''t have enough resource: cpu, requested: 8000,
    used: 950, capacity: 4000'
  phase: Failed
  qosClass: Guaranteed
  reason: OutOfcpu
  startTime: "2025-08-27T15:47:53Z"

```

After a kubelet restart (Which can be done for a few reasons, eg. handling in-place node resize, or a node reboot.), these pods transition into a ContainerStatusUnknown state.

```bash
$ kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS     RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     OutOfcpu   0          2s

$ docker exec -it $(docker ps | grep kindest | awk '{print $1}') systemctl restart kubelet

$ kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS                   RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     ContainerStatusUnknown   0          17s

```

where the overall status now has additional conditions for last probe time, container statuses showing container status unknown, etc.
```
status:
  conditions:
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    status: "False"
    type: PodReadyToStartContainers
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    status: "True"
    type: Initialized
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    reason: PodFailed
    status: "False"
    type: Ready
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    reason: PodFailed
    status: "False"
    type: ContainersReady
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    status: "True"
    type: PodScheduled
  containerStatuses:
  - image: busybox:1.37.0-glibc
    imageID: ""
    lastState: {}
    name: busybox
    ready: false
    restartCount: 0
    started: false
    state:
      terminated:
        exitCode: 137
        finishedAt: null
        message: The container could not be located when the pod was terminated
        reason: ContainerStatusUnknown
        startedAt: null
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
      name: kube-api-access-79svn
      readOnly: true
      recursiveReadOnly: Disabled
  hostIP: 172.18.0.2
  hostIPs:
  - ip: 172.18.0.2
  message: 'Pod was rejected: Node didn''t have enough resource: cpu, requested: 8000,
    used: 950, capacity: 4000'
  phase: Failed
  qosClass: Guaranteed
  reason: OutOfcpu
  startTime: "2025-08-27T15:47:53Z"
```

A similar issue can also be reproduced when using init containers
```bash
kubectl get po -A
NAMESPACE            NAME                                         READY   STATUS                        RESTARTS   AGE
default              busybox                                      0/1     Init:ContainerStatusUnknown   0          11s
```

I'm not sure if this is by design, but I would expect such rejected pods to remain in an OutOfCpu/TaintsToleration failure state. No containers were ever started as the pod was rejected in admission control. The error _sounds_ like something went missing from the container runtime, but that did not happen, of course.

We could work around this by GCing such pods, but I wonder if this could be handled more gracefully at the Kubernetes layer (and I would also hate to mask genuine container runtime issues by clubbing multiple such ContainerStatusUnknown issues together)

Using 'kind' for ease of cluster LCM, but this can happen in any vanilla K8s cluster.

- Ensure you have kind installed.
```bash
go install sigs.k8s.io/kind@v0.29.0
```

- Create a massive pod (in terms of container requests) that cannot fit on the node based on node selector. eg. pod.yaml

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  ...
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "64000Mi"
        cpu: "8000m"
      limits:
        memory: "64000Mi"
        cpu: "8000m"
```

- Apply the YAML
```bash
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
```
- Verify pod state

```bash
➜  ContainerStatusUnknown-repro kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS     RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     OutOfcpu   0          2s
```

- Docker exec into the kind node and restart kubelet
```bash
docker exec -it $(docker ps | grep kindest | awk '{print $1}') systemctl restart kubelet
```

- Verify pod state

```bash
➜  ContainerStatusUnknown-repro kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS                   RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     ContainerStatusUnknown   0          17s
```

Sifting through the kubelet code, I saw a few sites where we seem to iterate over the containers for a pod and if any are missing statuses (eg. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/850bc09e9b78e49ec2459515379ae042a142e5c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L441-L470) - my guess is post restart there's a full sync being run and kubelet has lost track of the fact that no containers were ever started for that pod. I imagine it's possible to instrument kubelet with targeted logging to see the specific site where this is happening.

Reproduced in multiple k8s versions-

1.31.14 (VMware)
1.33.0 (kind)

N/A, reproduced on VMware and kind.

N/A, does not seem OS specific. reproduced on Photon OS and kind.

title: Kubelet crashes on EKS Windows Node when compiler optimizations enabled
Add Verbose Logging to net/http for Egress Auditing and Rename probe/http/http.go
body:
This proposal includes two related changes to improve egress traffic visibility from core Kubernetes components and to refine logging controls:

Add Verbose Logging to staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go: Introduce new klog V-level logs to provide visibility into outbound HTTP requests and how they are handled by proxy settings.

A V(5) log will be added to record requests that are proxied (i.e., not matching the NO_PROXY environment variable). This helps identify traffic that would be blocked in a restricted environment.

A V(6) log will be added to record requests that are not proxied (i.e., explicitly allowed via NO_PROXY). This helps verify that allowlist rules are functioning as expected.

Rename pkg/probe/http/http.go to pkg/probe/http/http_prober.go: Rename this file to prevent a logging conflict with the file mentioned above, which is the actual target for our enhanced logging.

Downstream distributions of Kubernetes, such as GKE, are implementing security features to strictly control and block all egress traffic originating from the kube-apiserver. A core part of this mechanism involves using HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables to route traffic through a controlled gateway or a "blackhole" proxy, while using a NO_PROXY variable to allowlist essential cluster endpoints.

To safely roll out such a feature, it is critical to have a data-driven way to discover and audit all outbound requests made by the kube-apiserver and other components. This allows operators to build a comprehensive NO_PROXY allowlist and ensure no critical functions are broken. The proposed verbose logging in net/http.go provides this essential visibility.

The second change—renaming pkg/probe/http/http.go—is necessary to avoid unintended log spam. The klog output strips the full file path, so both staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go (our target) and pkg/probe/http/http.go (an unrelated file) show up in logs simply as http.go.

As a result, setting --vmodule=http*=5 to enable our new logs also enables verbose logging in the probe helpers, flooding the logs with messages from liveness and readiness probes. This makes it extremely difficult to isolate the critical egress traffic data needed for validation. Renaming the probe helper file to http_prober.go cleanly resolves this name collision and allows for precise, targeted logging for this important security use case.

title: Incorrect PodMemory usage after container termination
body:
PodMemory metric continued to be available for few minutes after pod was removed from the node. PodMemory metric should have been removed from the old pod instance as soon as new pod was destroyed or new pod was created. From initial understanding, kubelet/cAdvisor housekeepingInterval seems to be the static interval at which housekeeping should occur. If allowDynamicHousekeeping is enabled, cAdvisor determines the actual housekeeping interval based on houseKeepingInterval and maxHousekeepingInterval as shown in [manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2) with some jitter. Need to understand the behaviour of [statsCacheDuration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.4/pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go#L55-L58) and maxHousekeepingInterval when kubelet is restarted. Does kubelet dump the cache data to disk before the package upgrade? Moreover, since these maintenance are happening for kubelet upgrades, does time to upgrade and bootstrap kubelet could lead to additional delay in housekeeping. One more weird observation I could find is, node uuid has changed twice, once while upgrading at 11 AM(which is relevant for this issue) and then again at 2 PM(which is unrelated). This was observed during kubernetes upgrade. Node was drained and kubelet was upgraded. **Context** In case of Kubernetes Upgrade related maintenances, pods are rescheduled or temporarily evicted from the node. It has been observed that the newly formed pod consumes approximately double the memory of the original pod at startup. Multiple alerts are raised due to this as it can violate set alerting thresholds. Below is the original query raising PodMemory alert for workload. We can notice the query is granular at pod level. ``` max_over_time( max by (workload) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="",container!="",image!="",namespace=~"scorpius.*"} * on (namespace, pod) group_left (workload, workload_type) namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",workload_type="statefulset"} ) )[15m:] ) ``` From the graph view, we can see a sudden spike in memory usage before 11 AM when the pod got rescheduled. However, since the above query doesn't show the pod reschedule, we can fix it by adding pod uid into the query. ``` max_over_time( max by (workload, pod, uid) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod, uid) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="",container!="",image!="",namespace=~"scorpius.*"} * on (namespace, pod) group_left (uid) kube_pod_info{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery-2.*"} ) )[15m:] ) ``` Now, the below graph clearly shows data for earlier instance of pod grocery-2-0 is available till 11:10, well into the startup of new instances of pod grocery-2-0. This contributes to the overall memory usage since we are doing a join query with granularity of pod labels. You can also see that once the metrics for older instance stop relaying, the overall memory usage for pod grocery-2-0 drops down. While we have fixed the query to segregate container instances, we can see the cached metrics still getting emitted post 10:55 and before 11:10, after container is terminated. ``` max_over_time( max by (namespace, workload, name, pod) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod, name) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="", namespace=~"scorpius.*", container!="", image!="", pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery.*"} * on(namespace, pod, name) group_left(uid) label_replace( kube_pod_container_info{namespace=~"scorpius.*", container="aerospike-server", pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery.*"}, "name", "$1", "container_id", ".*://(.+)" ) * on (namespace, pod) group_left (workload, workload_type) namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",workload_type="statefulset"} ) ) [15m:]) ```

body:

device1 (allowMultipleAllocations): consume 3 from counterSet0
device2 (allowMultipleAllocations): consume 4 from counterSet0

title: Incorrect pod phase transition after node reboot with init containers
body:
A Pod with multiple init containers does not transition to the correct phase after a Node restart. I came across this issue while investigating the flaky test in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132930. For more information, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132930#issuecomment-3311419471.

The Pod phase is determined based on the ContainerStatus state of regular init containers, restartable init containers, and regular containers. For example, if there are any regular or restartable init containers that haven’t started yet, the Pod phase is considered Pending.

When a Node reboots, all containers in the Pod are restarted. In this case, the previous ContainerStatus state is preserved until the container actually restarts. As a result, if multiple init containers exist, the Pod phase incorrectly transitions to Running right after the first init container completes.

Here’s a rough timeline of what happens after a Node reboot:

1. Node reboots
1. Since all containers are stopped, if restartPolicy=Always, the Pod is considered Running because containers are being restarted
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0aeda7ba3766fe2fce2fa2e04c3fd37b8910efa3/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1831-L1834
1. While a regular init container is running, the Pod phase becomes Pending
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0aeda7ba3766fe2fce2fa2e04c3fd37b8910efa3/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1790-L1800
1. Once the regular init container exits, we fall back to step 2 and the Pod phase becomes Running again1. This flip-flop continues for each regular/restartable init container (Pending while running, Running once exited)

Ideally, the Pod should remain in Pending until the regular containers have started (i.e. `podHasInitialized=true`). But we’ll need to carefully check that fixing this doesn’t break other scenarios outside of Node reboots.

You can reproduce this issue by starting a Pod with multiple init containers similar to this Node E2E test case. And then deleting the PodSandbox to simulate a Node reboot.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0aeda7ba3766fe2fce2fa2e04c3fd37b8910efa3/test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go#L5918-L6054

If you’re able to run the Node E2E tests locally, you can use the following command:

```sh
make test-e2e-node FOCUS="should restart the containers in right order with the proper phase after the node reboot" SKIP="\[Flaky\]|\[Slow\]"
```

title: High-throughput container logs cause kubelet log rotation to hang, leading to unbounded 0.log growth (v1.27+ timestamp-based rotation)
body:
In Kubernetes clusters running v1.27+, the new timestamp-based container log rotation mechanism (0.log.YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS) fails to rotate logs for high-throughput containers (e.g., >50 MB/s). The 0.log file grows indefinitely (observed >12 GiB), even though containerLogMaxSize is set (e.g., 100Mi).

Kubelet’s log shows repeated "Adding new entry to the queue for processing" every containerLogMonitorInterval seconds, but no "rotateLog" or "rotateLog finished" logs for the affected container — indicating the rotation task never gets executed.

[Pasted Graphic 1.tiff](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22593110/Pasted.Graphic.1.tiff)

[Pasted Graphic.tiff](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22593115/Pasted.Graphic.tiff)

log config :  
containerLogMaxSize: 100Mi
containerLogMaxFiles: 5
containerLogMonitorInterval: 1s
containerLogMaxWorkers: 10

The kubelet should properly rotate container logs even under high-throughput logging workloads — specifically, the log rotation mechanism should not hang or fail to trigger when a container generates logs at a high rate. The 0.log file should be rotated once it exceeds containerLogMaxSize, preventing unbounded disk usage.

1. Create a pod that continuously writes logs at high throughput (e.g., ~100 MB/s),my yaml :
```
apiVersion: apps/v1

metadata:

title: preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits
body:
I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. The Pod remains in "Terminating" and the Job remains in "Running" state until the preStop sleep finishes, which delays the completion of the Job.

I expect the preStop sleep to end when PID 1 in the Pod exits. The Job should be marked as complete at that time and the Pod should finish terminating. This is the behavior when a preStop exec is used to run the sleep command in the container's shell.

Define a Job with a preStop sleep lifecycle hook:

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: sleep-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 120
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

Apply the manifest and then delete the resulting Pod. Observe that the Pod is now in "Terminating" state. The preStop sleep will have begun.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f sleep-job.yaml 
job.batch/sleep-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           6s         6s

NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Running   0          6s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods sleep-job-qh2qk
pod "sleep-job-qh2qk" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           24s        24s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          24s
```

After 60 seconds the Pod should complete but instead it remains in Terminating state and the Job shows 0 completions. Only after 2 minutes has elapsed (from the time the `delete` command was issued) does the Pod finish terminating and the Job shows a completion.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           59s        59s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          59s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           69s        69s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          69s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           2m19s      2m19s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          2m19s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Complete   1/1           2m21s      2m22s
```

This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.). The fact that the Job takes longer to complete when the Pod is asked to terminate is problematic when timely completion of the Job is desired. Imagine that the Job takes an hour instead of a minute and so the prestop sleep is set to 3600. Then imagine that the Pod is asked to terminate at minute 59. The duration of the Job will now be 119 minutes instead of 60.

Using a preStop exec to run /bin/sleep produces the expected behavior where the Pod finishes terminating and the Job shows as complete when PID 1 in the container exits. Of course this won't work in a shell-less container which AFAIK is the reason the preStop sleep was introduced.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: exec-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: exec-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sleep", "120"]
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f exec-job.yaml 
job.batch/exec-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           4s         4s

NAME                 READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Running   0          4s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods exec-job-k62r4
pod "exec-job-k62r4" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           23s        23s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          23s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE

title: Static Memory Manager doesn't verify OS reported available huge pages during pod admission
body:
Hi there, 

We have configured the static memory manager to enable numa aware scheduling of our Guaranteed QoS pods. We run various workloads on an m6id.32xlarge 2 numa node system, which accepts both Guaranteed and non Guaranteed QoS pods. These pods run Java based applications which in turn are configured to use huge pages. 

We have noticed an issue that once the pod was scheduled, the JVM was not able to start as it was not able to reserve enough memory (8GB). The pod was configured with the following resource limits:
```
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 6000m
        hugepages-2Mi: 8500Mi
        memory: 4000Mi
      requests:
        cpu: 6000m
        hugepages-2Mi: 8500Mi
        memory: 4000Mi
```

```
and the JVM failed with:

│ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to commit memory (Not enough space)                                                                                                                         ││ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to commit memory (Not enough space)                                                                                                                         │
│ [0.008s][error][gc] Forced to lower max Java heap size from 8192M(100%) to 4094M(50%)                                                                                                  ││ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to allocate initial Java heap (8192M)                                                                                                                       ││ Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.                                                                                                                                      │
│ Error: A fatal exception has occurred. Program will exit.
```

Upon inspection of the node, we noticed that one of the numa nodes are very short on available huge pages:

```
root@ip-10-31-22-160:/var/snap/amazon-ssm-agent/11320# cat /sys/devices/system/node/node*/meminfo | fgrep Huge
Node 0 AnonHugePages:         0 kB
Node 0 ShmemHugePages:        0 kB
Node 0 FileHugePages:         0 kB
Node 0 HugePages_Total: 65536
Node 0 HugePages_Free:  41168
Node 0 HugePages_Surp:      0
Node 1 AnonHugePages:         0 kB
Node 1 ShmemHugePages:        0 kB
Node 1 FileHugePages:         0 kB
Node 1 HugePages_Total: 65536
Node 1 HugePages_Free:   1631
Node 1 HugePages_Surp:      0
```

which happens to be where this pod was assigned to. 

When we looked at what the memory controller thought as free memory is, we found that its much more than what the OS is reporting as free: 

```
    "1": {
      "numberOfAssignments": 12,
      "memoryMap": {
        "hugepages-1Gi": {
          "total": 0,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 0,
          "reserved": 0,
          "free": 0
        },
        "hugepages-2Mi": {
          "total": 137438953472,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 137438953472,
          "reserved": 121110528000,
          "free": 16328425472
        },
        "memory": {
          "total": 266247880704,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 128808927232,
          "reserved": 31457280000,
          "free": 97351647232
        }
      },
```

I am no expert in this space but with a quick inspection of the memory controller code it looks like it assumes all pods on the node are running in Guarnateed QoS, it calculates what the free HP utilisation should be based on those but it doesn't take into account any best effort/burstable pods which can also use up huge pages, resulting in the startup failure we have seen. 

At least the memory controller should look at what the OS is reporting as free memory and reject the pod admission/suggest an alternative numa node if the memory requirements at the time can't be satisfied with the amount of free memory available on the numa node. Also it could consider evicting best effort/burstable pods to free up more memory on a given numa node. 

Given the following kubelet args:
```
--reserved-cpus=0-1,64-65 
--kube-reserved=memory=5Gi 
--system-reserved=memory=5Gi 
--reserved-memory=0:memory=10340Mi 
--memory-manager-policy=Static 
--topology-manager-scope=pod 
--topology-manager-policy=single-numa-node 
--feature-gates CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions=true,CPUManagerPolicyOptions=true,MemoryManager=true 
--cpu-manager-policy static 
--cpu-manager-policy-options full-pcpus-only=true 
--cpu-manager-policy-options strict-cpu-reservation=true 
```

on a 2 numa node system, schedule 2 pods onto said node, one with Burstable and another one with Guaranteed QoS. Both apps should reserve the pod's limits worth of huge pages on start Expect:

/var/lib/kubelet/memory_manager_state.free for numa node 1/2 to take the usage of the burstable pod into an account.

title: PodReadyToStartContainers condition gets flipped  to true after image pull.
body:
According to documentation https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-has-network

> The PodReadyToStartContainers condition is set to True by the kubelet after the successful completion of sandbox creation and network configuration for the Pod by the runtime plugin. The kubelet can start pulling container images and create containers after PodReadyToStartContainers condition has been set to True.

What I am observing is that kubelet is flipping this condition to true after application container image is pulled. 
Also noticed kubelet patched pod with pod ip after image pull.

PodReadyToStartContainers to flip to true as as soon as network ip is assigned and containerd sets up the sand box. To set up the sandbox, AFAIK containerd only needs pause container. It flips condition to ready here https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/7669bb4f04b7a2e88ab6da6c95720a5532c97174/internal/cri/server/podsandbox/sandbox_run.go#L290.

```
FROM public.ecr.aws/amazonlinux/amazonlinux:2023

RUN dnf -y install openssl && dnf clean all && \
    for i in $(seq 1 35); do \
      openssl rand -out /chunk${i}.bin 104857600; \
    done && \
    cat /chunk*.bin > /bigfile.bin && rm /chunk*.bin

CMD ["sleep","3600"]
```

pod yaml

title: No share ID in DRA kubelet plugin's API
body:
kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5104). 

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID. 

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

Without the change to k/k, a driver can have a workaround which wrap the plugin API appending with shareID and use it as a PreparedDevice.

From 
```go
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
to
```go
type DRADevice struct {
	drapbv1.Device
	shareID *types.UID
}
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
implemented code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/939b1fdd3e3efec3a3c7ea758c394c5aabdfa422

However, it looks cleaner when we do that in the provided API.
The change needs at driver is only extending the CDI id with share id if not nil: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/4a625314cb46ed38018d05e17a397420335277eb.

title: (DRA) Requests field not set for config FromClass in ResourceClaim.status.allocation.devices.config
body:
When creating a ResourceClaim with 2 requests with 2 different device class that have a config, the config reported in the allocation devices status is not mentioning from which request the config is coming from. So the DRA-Drivers cannot identify the configuration belonging to the request it is supposed to handle.
```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: my-resource-claim
spec:
...
status:
  allocation:
    devices:
      config:
      - opaque:
          driver: resource-driver.example.com
          parameters:
            test: example-0
        source: FromClass
      - opaque:
          driver: resource-driver.example.com
          parameters:
            test: example-1
        source: FromClass
      results:
      - device: eth0
        driver: resource-driver.example.com
        pool: kind-worker2
        request: request0
      - device: eth1
        driver: resource-driver.example.com
        pool: kind-worker2
        request: request1
```

For each config with the source as `FromClass`, I would expect the requests field to be set with the list of requests that are using the DeviceClass the config is coming from.

```yaml
kubectl apply -n blue -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata:
  name: deviceclass-0
spec:
  selectors:
  - cel:
      expression: device.driver == "resource-driver.example.com"
  config:
  - opaque:
      driver: resource-driver.example.com
      parameters:
        test: "example-0"
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata:
  name: deviceclass-1
spec:
  selectors:
  - cel:
      expression: device.driver == "resource-driver.example.com"
  config:
  - opaque:
      driver: resource-driver.example.com
      parameters:
        test: "example-1"
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: my-resource-claim
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - exactly:
        allocationMode: ExactCount
        count: 1
        deviceClassName: deviceclass-0
      name: request0
    - exactly:
        allocationMode: ExactCount
        count: 1
        deviceClassName: deviceclass-1
      name: request1
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: demo
  labels:
    app: demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine:latest
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    command:
    - sleep
    - infinity
  resourceClaims:
  - name: my-resource-claim
    resourceClaimTemplateName: my-resource-claim
EOF
```

title: A potential goroutine leak in pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_executor_test.go
body:
If the `time.After` case is selected before the `case <-ch:`
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b6e7ee359d0e13f81cd8594820e6ec71bec3c78a/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_executor_test.go#L164-L175
which leads to the ch <- nil below get blocked, results in a goroutine leak.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b6e7ee359d0e13f81cd8594820e6ec71bec3c78a/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_executor_test.go#L188

If the `time.After` case is selected before the `case <-ch:`, the ch <- nil doesn't get blocked either.

1.Set time.After(5 * time.Second) to time.After(time.Millisecond * 100)
2.Add time.Sleep(time.Millisecond * 200) before the `ch <- nil`
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b6e7ee359d0e13f81cd8594820e6ec71bec3c78a/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_executor_test.go#L188
The two steps make the time.After happen before the `case <-ch:`.
3.Using goleak to detect the goroutine leak in the test function
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b6e7ee359d0e13f81cd8594820e6ec71bec3c78a/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_executor_test.go#L50

	defer goleak.VerifyNone(t)
```

title: The pod has been successfully removed, but the volume’s project quota mapping still remains on the node
body:
I enabled the `LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring` feature gate. 
I was able to successfully create a pod using the YAML file, with `hostUsers` set to `false`. However, after the pod was deleted, the project quota information for the pod’s volume still remained in `/etc/project` and `/etc/projid`.

After adding some debug logs to the kubelet, I noticed that `ed.pod.Spec.HostUsers` is `nil` in the code below. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go#L538

As far as I know, since version 1.31, the kubelet checks if a user namespace is in use before assigning or clearing quotas. That means `ed.pod.Spec.HostUsers=nil` would bypass the entire quota teardown process.

The Project ID is an attribute of the directory and is removed when the directory is deleted. However, the tear down process should still be handled properly to avoid side effects such as memory leaks.

Here’s what I actually did:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ephemeral-pod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  hostUsers: false
  containers:
  - name: demo-container
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo Hello World && sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        ephemeral-storage: "5Mi"
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: "5Mi"
    volumeMounts:
    - name: test-storage
      mountPath: /mnt/temp
  volumes:
  - name: test-storage
    emptyDir: {}
```
```console
$ k get pod ephemeral-pod -o yaml | grep uid
  uid: d7b0b7f3-608d-4a30-ae29-60093eb69e9
$ k delete pod ephemeral-pod
pod "ephemeral-pod" deleted from kube-system namespace
$ cat /etc/projects 
1048577:/var/lib/kubelet/pods/d7b0b7f3-608d-4a30-ae29-60093eb69e95/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/test-storage
$ cat /etc/projid 
volume1048577:1048577
```

title: [PodLevelResources] Inconcistency in computing QOSClass
body:
Almost everywhere we check whether a pod has pod level resources (PLRs) we don't differentiate between nil and empty PLRs. For example:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/resource/helpers.go#L73-L82

However, in `ComputePodQOS` we don't make this distinction:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/pkg/apis/core/v1/helper/qos/qos.go#L96-L111

This could lead to some weird situations where you have a best-effort pod running with resources specified. For example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name:      pause-plr
spec:
  resources: {}
  containers:
    - name:    pause
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:latest
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu:    100m
          memory: 50Mi
        limits:
          cpu:    100m
          memory: 50Mi
```

I'm not sure exactly what the implications of this are, but since it breaks some fundamental assumptions, it's probably not good.

What was the reason for ignoring empty pod level resources?

We'll need to be careful about backwards compatibility when fixing this.

title: failing device-plugin health checks causing kubelet SIGABRT by systemd watchdog during initialization.
body:
We have Kubelet, version 1.34, running in a systemd service, configured to expect watchdog updates atleast every 20 seconds. 

If the updateRuntimeUp function does not run to completion within this deadline, it causes the `device-plugin` health check to fail, causing watchdog updates to not be sent to systemd, which causes kubelet to crash-loop. 

In our case, the updateRuntimeUp function was blocked on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L3020

The device-plugin health check is failing because device manager service is initialized, but the device-plugin start is blocked by the delayed updateRuntimeUp. 

device-plugin health check should not be expected to pass until kubelet is fully initialized?

run kubelet with the recommended watchdog timeout of ~15 seconds, and cause updateRuntimeUp to be blocked on first start.

title: Kubelet admission check includes rejected pods in resource accounting, causing subsequent pods to be incorrectly rejected
body:
The kubelet has a race condition in pod admission logic where rejected pods pollute the resource accounting for subsequent pod admissions.

  
  From Openshift CI logs:
  - Pod 1 (pod-out-of-cpu) requested 1000000000000000 millicores (intentionally absurd for testing)
  - Rejected at 03:12:06.086 with used: 759 millicores
  - Pod 2 (resize-test-kngwb) requested 20 millicores
  - Rejected at 03:12:06.220 (134ms later) with used: 1000000000000759 millicores
    - This is exactly: 1000000000000000 + 759

  The rejected Pod 1's CPU request was incorrectly included in the "used" calculation for Pod 2.

From kubelet logs (worker-2):
```
  Nov 06 03:12:06.086726 - Pod admission denied
    pod="e2e-pod-rejection-status-7203/pod-out-of-cpu"
    requested: 1000000000000000, used: 759, capacity: 3500

  Nov 06 03:12:06.220844 - Pod admission denied
    pod="e2e-pod-resize-tests-9859/resize-test-kngwb"
    requested: 20, used: 1000000000000759, capacity: 3500
```
  CI Run: https://prow.ci.openshift.org/view/gs/test-platform-results/logs/periodic-ci-openshift-release-master-nightly-4.21-e2e-metal-ipi-upgrade-ovn-ipv6/1986332510224650240

title: Unsorted list of runtime handlers causes redundant node updates
body:
When you have multiple runtime OCI runtime handlers configured, the list returned by the CRI runtime may not always be in same order, because they might be interesting over a map internally. If the returned order changes, then this causes unnecessary update to the node object even though actual list of runtime handlers is same as earlier (but with different order)  

Unless the actual runtime handlers change, there should not be an update to node CR. 

Have large list of runtime handlers like this, and you would see the order would change everytime you query it, 

```bash
$ kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.metadata.name): \(.status.runtimeHandlers | map(if .name == "" then "(empty)" else .name end) | join(", "))"'

Note that, containerd ensures the [ordering of the runtime handlers](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/4ab5ee32ad3e1b22cc2f33cf1163ba9df23454cb/internal/cri/server/status.go#L68), so this bug doesn't really affect containerd. But CRI-O on the other hand, [iterates over a map](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/6d034a9aaafe86e968559793e55e552a29cd19c3/server/runtime_status.go#L43) causing this issue. 

Initially I considered fixing it in CRI-O, but then IMO it won't be a bad idea to have this defensive code in the kubelet as well, so it doesn't rely on CRI runtimes to do the right thing, especially if CRI API doesn't explicitly mandate that the list of handlers need to be sorted. So this will safeguard kubelet against any future CRI runtimes as well who may not send the sorted list.

title: rewrite command line testing
body:
We have [test/cmd](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/cmd/README.md) with shell scripts which run certain tests, using Kubernetes-specific shell helpers (e.g. `kube::test::if_has_string`) to write assertions.

We could replace all of this with https://github.com/rogpeppe/go-internal?tab=readme-ov-file#testscript, which is roughly the same tooling that the Go team uses to test the go CLI commands. See https://bitfieldconsulting.com/posts/test-scripts for an introduction.

This is a major undertaking and there are good reasons for not doing it ("if it ain't broke, don't fix it"). But it could be a nice summer of code or intern project and might be worth it, so let's at least discuss...

* For newcomers, learning how to write CLI tests is just another "Kubernetes is different" hurdle and knowledge that they cannot reuse elsewhere.
* Integration of running those tests into our CI is awkward. We shuffled it into a separate job ([pull-kubernetes-cmd](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/135395/pull-kubernetes-cmd/1992980878933889024), but it's still a pain:

title: kubelet TopologyManager Stalls on Large NUMA Systems (e.g. Nvidia GB200 Compute Tray with 34 NUMA nodes)
body:
When scheduling a pod (e.g. KubeVirt virt-launcher pod) that requests a PCI device on a very large NUMA system, kubelet’s TopologyManager never finishes computing topology hints and the pod is effectively stuck in admission:

- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call for the requested resource.
- From a higher-level consumer (KubeVirt in our case), the virt-launcher pod stays in Pending and the VM remains in Starting with Ready = False.
- kubelet is responsive, but many goroutines are stuck in topology hint generation.

In our environment this manifests as:

- KubeVirt VM with a hostDevice (GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) never transitions to Running, even though the node has the capacity and the device is free.
- Disabling TopologyManager or constraining the NUMA fan-out immediately lets the VM start

kubelet should compute topology hints in bounded time, even on systems with many NUMA nodes (in a case GB200 with 34 NUMA nodes where only 2 NUMA nodes have CPUs, the rest are for HBM/NVLink), and call device-plugin Allocate so that pods/VMs using PCI host devices can start.

## High-level repro:
1. Use a host with a large NUMA topology  
    Example: Nvidia GB200-class system with 34 NUMA nodes visible to the OS.
 
2. Run Kubernetes with kubelet configured roughly as follows:
```yaml
kubeReserved:
  cpu: "2"
  memory: 4Gi
  ephemeral-storage: 20Gi
systemReserved:
  cpu: "2"
  memory: 8Gi
  ephemeral-storage: 20Gi
topologyManagerPolicy: best-effort
topologyManagerScope: pod
topologyManagerPolicyOptions:
  prefer-closest-numa-nodes: "true"
  max-allowable-numa-nodes: "34"
cpuManagerPolicy: static
reservedSystemCPUs: "0-3,72-75"
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  distribute-cpus-across-numa: "false"
```
3. Deploy a device plugin that:
- Advertises a PCI resource (e.g. GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) as a kubelet device resource.
- Exposes the device with topology information referencing many NUMA nodes (up to 34 in our case).

4. Create a Pod
Requests one unit of that device resource.
Uses Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for CPU/memory) so that TopologyManager participates fully.
 
5. Observe
- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never calls Allocate on the device plugin for that resource.
- The pod stays in Pending indefinitely.
- KubeVirt-specific repro (how we hit it)
- Instead of a raw pod, create a KubeVirt VirtualMachineInstance that uses hostDevices:
```yaml
devices:
   hostDevices:
    - deviceName: nvidia.com/GB100_HGX_GB200
      name: gpu1
```
The pod (if using KubeVirt, it is virt-launcher pod for a VM) is scheduled to the large NUMA node but stays Pending forever. The pod stuck at Pending, (if using KubeVirt, the VM status remains Starting) and never reaches Ready, despite sufficient resources.

## Root cause analysis

- The kubelet TopologyManager asks each hint provider (CPU, memory, device) to compute topology hints over the set of NUMA nodes that the kubelet knows about.
- For the device plugin case, generateDeviceTopologyHints ends up calling bitmask.IterateBitMasks across a bitmask spanning all NUMA IDs known to the machine, not just those relevant to the requested device.
- With 34 NUMA nodes this becomes effectively an exponential search (O(2^n)) over the 34-bit mask.
- On a GB200 host with 34 NUMA nodes and a device plugin that advertises per-node topology across those nodes, generateDeviceTopologyHints spends unbounded time iterating combinations that are not actually schedulable for the requested device.
- While TopologyManager is doing this, kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call, so pods/VMs that need that device are permanently stuck in admission.

## Evidence observed

- Goroutine dumps from kubelet show many workers blocked under TopologyManager/device-manager paths, repeatedly calling IterateBitMasks on a large bitmask.
- No calls to Allocate are observed for the affected device resource while the system is in this hung state.
- If we disable TopologyManager, then virt-launcher pods immediately proceed and the KubeVirt VM starts successfully.

title: Make credential plugin policy/allowlist settable with `kubectl kuberc set`
body:
A new alpha command, `kubectl alpha kuberc set` has been added, which modifies the contents of the `kuberc` file. We should modify the interface to `kubectl alpha kuberc set` to make it possible to set the `credentialPluginPolicy` and `credentialPluginAllowlist` fields (added in 1.35 as an extension to KEP-3104) from the command line.

This is needed in order to further reduce the friction for end-users in securing the `kubectl` client. `credentialPluginPolicy` and `credentialPluginAllowlist` are security knobs, and it would be great to have a simple cli one-liner to turn them on, rather than requiring the user to modify and/or create a new configuration file with which they may not be familiar.  In addition, the appropriate values may depend on provider configurations, but cloud providers can likewise provide CLI one-liners to allow their plugins but no others.

title: kubelet_http_requests_duration_seconds metric records incorrect (near-zero) latency values
body: The `kubelet_http_requests_duration_seconds` histogram metric always records near-zero values (~2 microseconds) regardless of actual request processing time. Below is a screenshot from a downstream CI run showing the average latency of kubetet's /metrics/cadvisor endpoint: The metric should record the actual time taken to handle each HTTP request, from when it's received until the response is sent. 1. Make an HTTP request to the kubelet that takes a measurable amount of time (e.g., `/pods/` endpoint) 2. Query the `kubelet_http_requests_duration_seconds` metric 3. Observe that the recorded duration is always ~2 microseconds instead of the actual processing time **Root cause:** In `pkg/kubelet/server/server.go`, the defer statement evaluates `SinceInSeconds(startTime)` immediately when the defer is declared, not when it executes: ```go defer servermetrics.HTTPRequestsDuration.WithLabelValues(...).Observe(servermetrics.SinceInSeconds(startTime)) ``` In Go, arguments to deferred function calls are evaluated immediately at the defer statement. This means `SinceInSeconds(startTime)` computes the duration at the start of the request (~5µs after `startTime` was set), rather than at the end when the defer actually runs. This affects observability and SLO tracking for kubelet HTTP endpoints since duration data is meaningless. 1.33

title: Kubelet SyncTerminatedPod times out after 30s due to race with cleanupOrphanedPodCgroups
body:
In this [OpenShift CI run](https://prow.ci.openshift.org/view/gs/test-platform-results/logs/periodic-ci-openshift-multiarch-master-nightly-4.21-ocp-e2e-ovn-remote-s2s-libvirt-ppc64le/1999572809340162048), the upstream `[sig-node] Lifecycle sleep action zero value when create a pod with lifecycle hook using sleep action with a duration of zero seconds prestop hook using sleep action with zero duration` test failed because SyncTerminatedPod timed out. The kubelet logs shows:

```
Dec 12 21:19:08.719197 compute-1 kubenswrapper[7200]: E1212 21:19:08.719175    7200 pod_workers.go:1324] "Error syncing pod, skipping" err="failed to delete cgroup paths for [kubepods besteffort poda4418b44-5c5a-4bd5-b7b3-42860ff00483] : unable to destroy cgroup paths for cgroup [kubepods besteffort poda4418b44-5c5a-4bd5-b7b3-42860ff00483] : Timed out while waiting for systemd to remove kubepods-besteffort-poda4418b44_5c5a_4bd5_b7b3_42860ff00483.slice" pod="e2e-pod-lifecycle-sleep-action-allow-zero-761/pod-with-prestop-sleep-hook-zero-duration" podUID="a4418b44-5c5a-4bd5-b7b3-42860ff00483"
```

The systemd journal reveals that the slice was actually removed successfully ~30 seconds before the kubelet timeout:

```
Dec 12 21:18:39.127974 compute-1 systemd[1]: Removed slice libcontainer container kubepods-besteffort-poda4418b44_5c5a_4bd5_b7b3_42860ff00483.slice.
```

This shows that systemd completed the slice removal at 21:18:39, but kubelet still timed out at 21:19:08 (exactly ~30 seconds later). The timeout occurred because the kubelet goroutine that initiated the removal never received the D-Bus completion signal.

Pod deletion should complete promptly after containers terminate, without a 30-second timeout.

### How can we reproduce it? (as minimally and precisely as possible)

1. Create a cluster with cgroupsPerQOS enabled (default)
2. Run a workload that creates and deletes many pods rapidly
3. Observe that some pods take 30+ seconds to fully terminate

The race is more likely to occur when:
- Multiple pods are being terminated simultaneously
- The orphaned pod cgroup cleanup housekeeping runs during pod termination

#### Root Cause

There is a race condition between two code paths that call `pcm.Destroy()` on the same pod cgroup:

1. **`SyncTerminatedPod`** - [pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c34c5a5426aeb48c55c40af5c4b016a71c24d2d1/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2398-L2402):
```go
pcm := kl.containerManager.NewPodContainerManager()
if err := pcm.Destroy(name); err != nil {
    return err
}
```

2. **`cleanupOrphanedPodCgroups`** - [pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c34c5a5426aeb48c55c40af5c4b016a71c24d2d1/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2835-L2836):
```go
go pcm.Destroy(val)
```

Both paths can run concurrently for the same pod cgroup. The `Destroy()` method calls systemd's `StopUnit` via D-Bus using `go-systemd`.

#### Why the 30-second timeout occurs

When `StopUnitContext` is called, the `go-systemd` library:

1. Sends a D-Bus method call to systemd's `StopUnit`
2. Systemd returns a **job path** (e.g., `/org/freedesktop/systemd1/job/12345`)
3. The library registers the caller's `statusChan` in an internal map keyed by that job path
4. When systemd emits a `JobRemoved` D-Bus signal with that job path, the library sends the result to the registered channel

**The problem:** When two goroutines call `StopUnit` on the same unit concurrently, systemd may return the **same job path** for both requests (since it's already processing a stop for that unit). The `go-systemd` library overwrites the first channel registration:

[go-systemd/dbus/methods.go](https://github.com/coreos/go-systemd/blob/f3c9410fa503128ff5a025265768843eb09815ca/dbus/methods.go#L55-L75
)
```go
// In go-systemd's dbus/methods.go (simplified)
func (c *Conn) startJob(ch chan<- string, job dbus.ObjectPath) {
    c.jobListener.Lock()
    c.jobListener.jobs[job] = ch  // OVERWRITES any existing channel for this job path!
    c.jobListener.Unlock()
}
```

**Timeline of the race:**

1. **T=0ms:** Goroutine A calls `StopUnit`, gets job `/job/100`, registers `chanA`
2. **T=1ms:** Goroutine B calls `StopUnit`, gets job `/job/100`, registers `chanB` (overwrites `chanA`!)
3. **T=50ms:** Systemd finishes, emits `JobRemoved` for `/job/100`
4. **T=50ms:** go-systemd sends result to `chanB` (the only one in the map now)
5. **T=50ms:** Goroutine B completes successfully
6. **T=30s:** Goroutine A times out (`chanA` was orphaned, never receives signal)

#### Relevant code

The 30-second timeout is in [opencontainers/cgroups/systemd/common.go](https://github.com/opencontainers/cgroups/blob/main/systemd/common.go#L184-L210):

```go
func stopUnit(cm *dbusConnManager, unitName string) error {
    statusChan := make(chan string, 1)
    err := cm.retryOnDisconnect(func(c *systemdDbus.Conn) error {
        _, err := c.StopUnitContext(context.TODO(), unitName, "replace", statusChan)
        return err
    })
    if err == nil {
        timeout := time.NewTimer(30 * time.Second)
        defer timeout.Stop()

        select {
        case s := <-statusChan:
            // ...
        case <-timeout.C:
            return errors.New("Timed out while waiting for systemd to remove " + unitName)
        }
    }
    // ...
}
```

#### Proposed Fix

Use `singleflight.Group` in `podContainerManagerImpl.Destroy()` to deduplicate concurrent calls for the same cgroup. This ensures only one D-Bus `StopUnit` call proceeds per cgroup while other callers wait and receive the same result, avoiding the channel overwrite race entirely.

### Environment

- Kubernetes version: v1.34+
- CRI: CRI-O (crun/runc)
- cgroup driver: systemd

title: Support cpu.idle (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort QoS to improve isolation and node utilization
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**: 

**Motivation**:
Currently, Kubelet sets `cpu.shares` to `2` for the top-level BestEffort QoS cgroup. The goal is to allow BestEffort tasks to utilize free CPU cycles (improving node utilization) while minimizing the impact on Guaranteed and Burstable workloads.

However, relying solely on `cpu.shares` (even with a minimal value) provides "weight-based" isolation. In high-load scenarios, this can still lead to latency interference for high-priority tasks.

Since Linux Kernel 5.4, significant improvements have been made to `SCHED_IDLE` (Reference Patch: `sched/fair: Improve the scheduling of SCHED_IDLE tasks`).
* **Better Isolation**: `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) ensures that tasks are treated with truly "idle" priority. They only run when there is absolutely no other higher-priority task to run. This offers significantly better isolation for Guaranteed/Burstable pods compared to simply lowering `cpu.shares`（cgroup v2 `cpu.weight`）.
* **Safe Colocation**: It allows safe colocation of BestEffort batch jobs with latency-sensitive services without the risk of performance degradation for the latter.

**Current Barrier (The Conflict)**:
We are currently attempting to utilize `cpu.idle` for BestEffort pods using external agents/extensions on  nodes. However, this conflicts with Kubelet's current initialization logic, causing Kubelet to fail to start.

In Cgroup v1, when `cpu.idle` is set to `1`:
1.  The kernel forces `cpu.shares` to `1` (minimal weight).
2.  The kernel locks `cpu.shares` from being modified.

In Cgroup v2, when `cpu.idle` is set to `1`:
1.  The kernel forces `cpu.weight` to `0` (minimal weight).
2.  The kernel locks `cpu.weight` from being modified.
 
Because Kubelet hardcodes the enforcement of `cpu.shares = 2` or `cpu.weight = 1`   for BestEffort, it crashes during startup if `cpu.idle` is already enabled by an external tool or previous configuration:

For Example in Cgroup v1: 
> "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="failed to initialize top level QOS containers: failed to update top level BestEffort QOS cgroup : failed to write \"2\": write /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpu.shares: invalid argument"

**What you expected to happen:** Kubelet should start successfully even if `cpu.idle` is enabled for the BestEffort cgroup. Kubelet should either detect that `cpu.idle` is enabled and skip setting `cpu.shares` or `cpu.weight`, or handle the write error gracefully.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**

1. On a node with a Kernel supporting `cpu.idle` interface (Linux).

2. Manually (or via an external agent) set `cpu.idle` to `1` for the BestEffort slice:

```
Bash

echo 1 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpu.idle

```
3. Restart Kubelet.
4. Observe the startup failure.

5. Manual verification of the conflict:

```
Bash

# echo 2 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuacct/kubepods.slice/kubepods-besteffort.slice/cpu.shares
-bash: echo: write error: Invalid argument
```

- **Context:** We use `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort tasks to utilize the enhanced scheduling isolation provided by Linux Kernel 5.4+ (Patch: `sched/fair: Improve the scheduling of SCHED_IDLE tasks`). This is often a superior alternative to low `cpu.shares` for maximizing node utilization without interfering with high-priority workloads.

- **Kernel Behavior:** When `cpu.idle` is configured to `1`, the kernel forces `cpu.shares` to `1` and `cpu.weight` to `1` and forbids modification, leading to the Invalid argument error when Kubelet tries to write min shares(or weight)

- **Workaround:** Setting `cpu.idle` back to `0` allows Kubelet to start.

**Proposed Solution:**

1. **Short-term fix (Resilience)**: Modify the Kubelet `qos_container_manager` logic. Before attempting to set `cpu.shares` for the BestEffort cgroup, check if cpu.idle is configured (if the interface exists).

    If `cpu.idle == 1`: Skip setting `cpu.shares` and `cpu.weight` (accept the kernel's forced value).

    If `cpu.idle == 0` or file does not exist: Proceed with setting `cpu.shares` to `2`and `cpu.weight` to `1`.

2. **Long-term feature**: Add native support in Kubelet configuration to support `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort pods, allowing users to opt-in to this scheduling policy directly via Kubelet rather than relying on external agents.

**Benefits:**

**Superior QoS**: Provides strict priority isolation for Guaranteed/Burstable pods, reducing tail latency in colocation scenarios.

**Resilience**: Prevents Kubelet startup failures for users attempting to use SCHED_IDLE via custom tuning agents.

title: Error-level logs incorrectly use verbosity levels
body:
Currently, some components in Kubernetes have been migrated (or partially migrated) to [contextual logging](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/3077-contextual-logging/README.md). However, an incorrect pattern was introduced during the migration: Error-level logs are being called with verbosity methods (e.g., .V()).

The underlying package go-logr/logr, which contextual logging relies on, ignores the verbosity level when printing Error-level logs. For example, in the statement `logger.V(8).Error(nil, "Readiness probe already exists for container", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "containerName", c.Name)`, the error log will be printed regardless of the verbosity level set.

This can lead to error log flooding, which may hinder users' ability to review normal logs for troubleshooting. More critically, according to the [Kubernetes logging policy](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use), logs should only be recorded when the information requires action from an administrator. This directly contradicts the practice of setting verbosity levels for Error logs, as administrators using the default logging level might miss these actionable errors. Therefore, these instances need to be fixed.

title: [kubelet] Unnecessary continuous reconciliation loop for DRA Pods due to non-kubelet-owned fields comparison
body:
new: add test and log for kubelet (Kubernetes v1.35.0).

For Pods using Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), the kubelet status manager continuously logs "Pod status is inconsistent with cached status" and triggers a reconciliation loop (needsReconcile -> syncPod, every ~10s). This loop is unnecessary because no actual status changes are applied, but it adds avoidable load on kubelet, API server, and etcd.
kubelet log -v=4

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster with DRA enabled.
2. Create a Pod that uses DRA resources (with ResourceClaim).
3. Observe the kubelet logs and API server/etcd load.
4. Find the continuous "status inconsistent" logs and repeated reconciliation operations.

title: Container fail to create when env var contains $ followed by non-ASCII character (invalid UTF-8 gRPC error)
body:
After upgrading our Kubernetes cluster from v1.33.5 to v1.34.2 (AWS EKS), pods scheduled on nodes running v1.34.2 fail during container creation with the following error: ```bash grpc: error while marshaling: string field contains invalid UTF-8 ``` The pods are created successfully, but containers fail to create. Important observation: Pods scheduled on nodes still running v1.33.5 continue to work correctly with the same manifests and environment variables. The failure occurs only on nodes upgraded to v1.34.2, strongly indicating a regression. Through isolation and testing, we observed that the failure occurs when an environment variable value contains a $ immediately followed by a non-ASCII character. This behaviour did not occur on v1.33.5 and appears to be a regression introduced in v1.34.x. Pods and containers should start successfully when environment variable values contain valid UTF-8 characters, including non-ASCII characters and literal $ characters. This configuration worked as expected on v1.33.5 nodes, even within the same cluster during a rolling upgrade. 1. Create a pod (or deployment) with an environment variable containing: - a $ - immediately followed by a non-ASCII UTF-8 character 3. Schedule the pod on a v1.34.2 node 4. Observe container creation failure with: - `grpc: error while marshaling: string field contains invalid UTF-8` Minimal reproducible example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: utf8-env-repro spec: containers: - name: test image: busybox command: ["sh", "-c", "echo started && sleep 3600"] env: - name: TEST_ENV value: "$£FOO" ``` Observed result: ❌ Fails on v1.34.2 nodes ✅ Works on v1.33.5 nodes Expected result: Container starts normally on all versions. - We run a custom CRD/operator that propagates env vars from the CR spec into Deployments and multi-container Pods. - The failure occurs after Pod creation, during container creation / runtime interaction. - This reproduces across all containers in the pod that receive the env var. - This is reproducible in a mixed-version cluster: - Pods on v1.33.5 nodes work - Pods on v1.34.2 nodes fail

title: Job validation error message is misleading when updating .status.startTime
body:
I encountered a confusing validation error while trying to update the `.status.startTime` of an existing  
Job.
The error message received was:
```bash
Job.batch "job-c4nbt" is invalid: status.startTime: Required value: startTime cannot be removed for unsuspended job
```
However, I am not trying to remove the `startTime`, but rather update it. I checked the code and found that the validation logic triggers this error for any inequality, not just when the `startTime` is removed (set to nil).

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f4eedc41b8c7aa9a4c66c08d153d8d4ce6c1e6a6/pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go#L740-L746

I expected the error message to reflect the actual validation constraint accurately.

1. create a non-suspended Job
2. update `job.status.startTime` to a different value using:
```go
    kubeClient.BatchV1().Jobs().UpdateStatus()
```

If this is confirmed as an issue, I would be happy to submit a PR to correct the error message and potentially the error type to make it more user-friendly.

title: kubelet saving inconsistent cpu-manager state to checkpoint file
body:
During allocation of CPU resources in CPU manager's static policy and during removal of a container, two modifications to state happen:
* CPU set of the container is changed;
* default CPU set is updated.

CPU manager uses state checkpoint for keeping allocated resources state and after each operation that changes this state, data is saved to checkpoint file.

If the kubelet is interrupted and killed between changing container's CPU set and default CPU set, the state that is saved in checkpoint file is inconsistent.

This can cause:
* **CPU leak** if exclusive CPUs are already removed from default CPU set, but not yet assigned to a container CPU set;
* **CPU leak**, when container and its CPU set is removed from allocated resources, but the CPUs are not returned to default CPU set.

I expect consistent state of cpu sets to be saved to cpu-manager's checkpoint file to properly restore resources after kubelet's restart.

During creation or removal of container using exclusive CPUs:
1) Detect first save operation on filesystem (cpu assignment for container is changed)
2) Restart kubelet before 2nd save operation (or block second save operation and restart kubelet)

I found the issue during review of the cpu-manager's code.
I didn't reproduce it on the cluster.

title: Some crashed or OOMKilled containers fail to restart in v1.35
body:
After upgrading Kubernetes from v1.34.2 to v1.35.0, we observed a scenario where a pod with multiple containers does not restart a crashed application container, leaving the pod in an Error state indefinitely.

This behavior was not observed on v1.34.2. Reverting the kubelet back to v1.34.2 causes the issue to disappear.

**Observed Behavior:**
The main container terminates but never restarts:
```
State:          Terminated
  Reason:       Error
  Exit Code:    2
  Started:      Tue, 27 Jan 2026 16:11:01 +0000
  Finished:     Tue, 10 Feb 2026 11:08:55 +0000
Ready:          False
Restart Count:  0
```

The sidecar container continues to run normally:
```
State:          Running
Started:        Tue, 27 Jan 2026 16:10:54 +0000
Ready:          True
Restart Count:  0
```

Pod conditions show:
```
Conditions:
  Type                        Status
  PodReadyToStartContainers   True
  Initialized                 True
  Ready                       False
  ContainersReady             False
  PodScheduled                True
```

No useful logs or errors appear in `kubectl describe pod` output, events, or `kubelet` logs.

**Notes:**
- This issue seems to only affect pods with more than one container
- We are unsure whether it's just pods with an `initContainer` or does it also apply to `container` sidecars
- Manually killing the process in the sidecar container or deleting the pod helps getting it back to working state
- `RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits` is not enabled

**Possibly related?**
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134345

Containers should reliably restart every time they crash.

The best way we found to reproduce this is by running a pod with 2 containers: an initContainer with `restartPolicy: Always` and an application container that we manually crash with `kill 1` command.
It might not work right first time, but we managed to reproduce this multiple times getting pods stuck in Error state that they never recover from automatically.

title: Cronjob controller try to get existed job without namespace
body:
We're seeing when the senario in [cronjob_controllerv2.go#L615-L637](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L615-L637) happened (Cronjob Controller found an existed job), Cronjob controller will try to get the job without specifying `namespace` value and get HTTP 404:

#### kube-controller-manager log:
```
E0210 18:47:10.835604       1 cronjob_controllerv2.go:179] "Unhandled Error" err="error syncing CronJobController default/sleep-300-job, requeuing: the server could not find the requested resource" logger="UnhandledError"
```

#### API Server log:
```
{
    "kind": "Event",
    "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
    "level": "RequestResponse",
    "auditID": "db48fd5c-6a37-4639-a6f0-2fcfeb0b5e8b",

    =====================
    "requestURI": "/apis/batch/v1/jobs/sleep-300-job-29512485",
    =====================

        ],

            "authentication.kubernetes.io/credential-id": [
                "JTI=b4d33275-b6a9-4266-84ef-6ed222c2414e"
            ]
        }
    },
    "sourceIPs": [
        "192.168.130.2"
    ],
    "userAgent": "kube-controller-manager/v1.35.0 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/6645204/system:serviceaccount:kube-system:cronjob-controller",
    "objectRef": {
        "resource": "jobs",
        "name": "sleep-300-job-29512485",
        "apiGroup": "batch",
        "apiVersion": "v1"
    },
    "responseStatus": {
        "metadata": {},
        "status": "Failure",
        "message": "the server could not find the requested resource",
        "reason": "NotFound",
        "details": {},
        "code": 404
    },
    "responseObject": {
        "kind": "Status",
        "apiVersion": "v1",
        "metadata": {},
        "status": "Failure",
        "message": "the server could not find the requested resource",
        "reason": "NotFound",
        "details": {},
        "code": 404
    },
    "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2026-02-10T18:47:10.834353Z",
    "stageTimestamp": "2026-02-10T18:47:10.835086Z",
    "annotations": {
        "authorization.k8s.io/decision": "allow",
        "authorization.k8s.io/reason": "RBAC: allowed by ClusterRoleBinding \"system:controller:cronjob-controller\" of ClusterRole \"system:controller:cronjob-controller\" to ServiceAccount \"cronjob-controller/kube-system\""
    }
}
```

The issue was the "requestURI": `/apis/batch/v1/jobs/sleep-300-job-29512485` is correct, it should contain `namespace` e.g.:
```
❯ kubectl get job sleep-300-job-29512485 -v 9                                      
...
I0210 18:52:07.314585   31290 round_trippers.go:632] "Response" verb="GET" url="https://192.168.130.2:8443/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/default/jobs/sleep-300-job-29512485" status="200 OK" headers=<
```

And the API Server's 404 indicated there's no `/apis/batch/v1/jobs/` API.

Cronjob controller should query the job `with namespace`:

Incorrect URI (current):
```
/apis/batch/v1/jobs/<JOB_NAME>
```

Correct URI:
```
/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/<NAMESPACE>/jobs/<JOB_NAME>
```

Create a cronjob to create a job every 5 minutes:
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: sleep-300-job
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: echo-sleep
              image: ubuntu
              command:
                - /bin/bash
                - -c
                - echo start && sleep 180 && echo end
          restartPolicy: Never
```

Once the first job was created, create another job manually with the next expected job name (id + 5):
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-300-job-29512465
  namespace: default
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: batch/v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: true
    controller: true
    kind: CronJob
    name: sleep-300-job
    uid: d10ff40f-be9d-47d2-aa67-7a376f054ed2
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - /bin/bash
        - -c
        - echo start && sleep 180 && echo end
        image: ubuntu
        name: echo-sleep
      restartPolicy: Never
```

Check the kube-controller-manager and API Server audit log for the result.

The issue seems to be when Cronjob controller trying to get job, it used the `jobReq` from `getJobFromTemplate2()` function, however, `getJobFromTemplate2()` won't set the job Namespace:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L621
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L604
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/cronjob/utils.go#L256-L263

Seems we're not relying on the `namespace` from `getJobFromTemplate2()`, it seems the correct way to specify `namespace` should be the same as:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65f09e605cb206b2e5fcff4d69a4ae8acf62dbc3/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#L609
