title: Unblock enablement of the ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode by default (to fix scale issues for CRDs)
body:
[ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L1955C18-L1957) is currently Beta, but disabled by default.

**I would like to identify or understand the blockers for graduation (if any) so that this can be moved forward.**

This feature gate looks very promising for handling CRD objects with high cardinality, like Workload objects in [Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/). Without this feature gate migration between versions like `v1beta1` to `v1beta2` is risky at scale.

We would love to have this improved before migrating Kueue v1beta2 -> v1.

In Kueue 0.15 we introduced v1beta2 for serving, while keeping v1beta1 for storage. Which was dictated by the needs of downgrading to 0.14 in case something "goes wrong".

However, this caused issues on high scale clusters (small clusters <10k work fine).

My understanding of the problem:
1. when Kueue is starting up then controller-runtime tries to establish the WATCH on the Workload object in v1beta2
2. If the API server does not have a "warm" cache for the Workloads, then it requests ETCD for the list of Workloads in v1beta1
3. API server receives the workloads list, but before returning to Kueue it tries to convert them sequentially to v1beta2. 

**Issue**: for some larger clusters it was estimated to take around 8min, but this exceeds some timeouts in ETCD to serve the request, and the API server fails with 500 in the meanwhile.

There is a good chance that enabling parallel requests would save the request.

**Mitigation**: we recommend users to move from Kueue 0.15 to 0.16 (which is using v1beta2 for storage and serving) which mitigates the problem, but the situation is not ideal, because 0.15 remains affected.

Related issues in Kueue:
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9094
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9145
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9090

title: image pull credential verification doesn't work
body:
I wanted to use a recently introduced feature called "image pull credential verification". It has been described at:

1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/images/#ensureimagepullcredentialverification
2. https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2535-ensure-secret-pulled-images
3. https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/05/12/kubernetes-v1-33-ensure-secret-pulled-images-alpha/

I execute scenario with following conditions:

1. registry always requires authentication for the image in question
2. two sample pods are created which use the same image
3. pod definition requests to be scheduled to a specific node and it is always started there
4. the node does not have the image locally initially

The scenario:

1. pod A is started in namespace A without specifying service account or image secrets
2. default service account in ns A has a secret attached for the registry in question
3. kubelet pulls the image successfully
4. pod B is started in namespace B, the default service account has no secrets attached
5. pod B is successfully started but it should fail, this is the problem of this issue

This is what I observe. When the second pod is created an event is generated:

> $ k get events | grep 'already present' | tail -n1
> 42m         Normal    Pulled                 pod/sample-pod   Container image "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux:10" already present on machine and can be accessed by the pod

This means the verification passed by it should not.

I have a standard configuration of kubelet with imagePullCredentialsVerificationPolicy set to NeverVerifyPreloadedImages. When this setting is changed to AlwaysVerify the attempt fails properly with message about missing credentials.

i did some digging in the source code to find the cause of it. On the second pod the kubelet thinks the image was not pulled by kubelet so it is treated like a preloaded image. After the first pod is created I see this:

```
$ jq . /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-dd81f502dc5e7f8b60445496abe590916d606411d7c474a2e18e4a42e4e82151
{
  "kind": "ImagePulledRecord",
  "apiVersion": "kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1",
  "lastUpdatedTime": "2026-02-14T09:41:58Z",
  "imageRef": "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux@sha256:b86cb4305db4c29abb1e3a1257fefccc184b5e4a94378e02844b340845ef9460",
  "credentialMapping": {
    "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux": {
      "kubernetesSecrets": [
        {
          "uid": "eeb25318-beff-46d0-bb24-f0c871a11e25",
          "namespace": "kube-system",
          "name": "zot",
          "credentialHash": "0bd56ac49132f1c4ffbf88affd024c6888e40d35fb6c9e10fef0e0b19a09fb06"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The ns A is the kube-system in this case. Note the imageRef as it will be used below. It has a proper sha for rockylinux:10 for linux/amd64 platform at the time this issue is created. zot registry is being used and the /docker-io/** path needs authentication.

The message is generated from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go#L257. The function receives argument of requestedImage with value "zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux:10". In imagePullPrecheck it uses imageService to resolve the image to an imageRef and it receives a value of "812a83d5aec123cbd962ba7cd1e22266db0fe2b3a0b49cb4e9aa521d13ad214f". It matches:
```
$ crictl inspecti zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux:10 | yq .status.id
812a83d5aec123cbd962ba7cd1e22266db0fe2b3a0b49cb4e9aa521d13ad214f
```

The call in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go#L253 uses the requestedImage and imageRef to decide if the image needs to be pulled or not. The MustAttemptImagePull contains a lot of conditionals and yet it doesn't have any debug logging. I had to modify the source code and add print statements everywhere to understand what is going on. The https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/pullmanager/image_pull_manager.go#L211 tries to find by imageRef and returns nil, false, nil. There are no intents at this time so imagePulledByKubelet stays with false value. This in turn is processed by the policy and we have the decision.

Now I wondered why the find failed. The records are stored in memory. The lookup in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/images/pullmanager/mem_pullrecords.go#L197 uses the imageRef into a map. The key isn't there. So I made an investigation when keys are added and the added key was: 

```
zot.kube01.pemlab.net:5001/docker-io/rockylinux/rockylinux@sha256:b86cb4305db4c29abb1e3a1257fefccc184b5e4a94378e02844b340845ef9460
```

and this is what is read from /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled.

I tested this with cri-o and containerd. There is no difference. I wonder how this verification can ever work if there is always mismatch is inserted and lookedup keys ?

I have tested this with the directory clean and a fresh start of kubelet and the directory populated with files and the result is the same. The cache is populated with very long keys yet lookups are done with short imageID as reported by crictl.

I expect the kubelet to verify the credentials again but it doesn't do it.

Scenario in the issue description.

```
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.35.0
Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

On premise.

Linux/amd64.

title: DRA: kubelet: Allow option to skip plugin calls and/or NodeUnprepareResources specifically if noop
body:
Pods with ResourceClaims will be stuck in Terminating for as long as NodeUnprepareResources has not been called (which is WAI per discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129402), as kubelet blocks on a successful NodeUnprepareResourcesResponse. In cases where a given plugin's NodeUnprepareResources would be a no-op, this unnecessarily introduces the potential for a faulty plugin to needlessly block node or driver upgrades when the drain cannot be completed. At an even more extreme end, even NodePrepareResources may be a no-op, unnecessarily introducing delays in pod startup on the node to contact the driver and recieve the response from the no-op prepare call. This issue seeks to make one, or both of these, more forgiving by one of two methods of softening kubelet's expectations regarding plugin prepare/unprepare calls:

1. Allow kubelet to recognize certain devices and/or device classes as no-op for node local preparation

* Kubelet assumes it must contact a DRA driver matching a Pod’s claim’s deviceclass when asked to run a Pod with a claim ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L318)) to perform node local operations
* That DRA driver is implemented as a kubelet plugin ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L49)) of a specific interface (namely, has the NodePrepareResources and NodeUnprepareResources functions) and must return a valid NodePrepareResource response when preparing a claim ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.35/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L397))
* Some device classes do not require any node local operations
* Today, such device classes would still be required to stand up a driver matching the kubelet plugin interface; otherwise scheduled Pods will not run and do not know to be rescheduled
* In these cases, Kubelet should instead allow configured device classes not to require calls to their associated driver’s PrepareResources and UnprepareResources functions

2. Allow kubelet to recognize certain devices and/or device classes as kubeletplugin-less

* Device classes as described above may also implement their ResourceSlice publication off the node (such as in the case of multi-node logical devices), removing the need for any node local driver component at all
* Maintainers for such devices should not need to provide a completely no op driver, nor should cluster operators be forced to deploy and maintain such drivers, just to satisfy Kubelet’s interface requirements
* Kubelet should instead allow configured deviceclasses not to require a handle to a kubeletplugin driver at all

title: ContainerRestartRules: exitCodes.values validation incorrectly reports "bytes" instead of "items"
body:
When a container's `restartPolicyRules[].exitCodes.values` length exceeds 255 elements, the validation error message says:

```bash
containers[0].restartPolicyRules[0].exitCodes.values: Too long: may not be more than 255 bytes
```

The validation uses field.TooLong (byte length checks) instead of field.TooMany (slice length checks).

The field is []int32, and the length limit is at most 255 elements, not 255 bytes.
If I am not wrong, I think the correct error message should be:
```bash

title: StatefulSet pod revisions not updated when MaxUnavailableStatefulSet enabled
body:
I decided to open this issue after investigating https://github.com/stackabletech/trino-operator/issues/854.

The high level description of the problem is that the stateful set controller doesn't update the pods according to the latest STS revision and the pods are left crashlooping **if the first revision is faulty** and can never become available. This doesn't happen if the `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` feature is disabled.

Unfortunately I cannot create a much simpler example, but I attach the relevant controller log messages below.

Based on these logs you can see that:

1. The Stackable Operator for Trino (`trino-op` from now on) creates two `StatefulSet` objects with a single replica. They both expose the same problem, so for simplicity, I will use only one of them from now on (`trino-coordinator-default`).
2. The initial revision of this sts is `trino-coordinator-default-5f5598d4c8`. This first STS  revision has a faulty command args  and can never become available.
3. The `trino-op` updates the sts rapidly to the revision `trino-coordinator-default-787556ff59`. Now the STS command args are correct and the pods should be able to become ready.
4. The pod created initially is never updated so it never becomes ready.

To summarize my understanding, the sts revision is never updated if the pod never becomes ready, and the pod doesn't become ready because it has an old revision.

In the logs you see that `currentRevision` is never the same as `updateRevision`:

```
I0304 15: 25:06.514308       1 stateful_set_control.go: 146]"StatefulSet revisions" statefulSet = "kuttl-test-distinct-turtle/trino-coordinator-default" currentRevision = "trino-coordinator-default-5f5598d4c8" updateRevision = "trino-coordinator-default-787556ff59"
```

The pod should become ready according to the `updateRevision` of the sts.
Again, this was indeed the case until `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` feature gate was enabled.

I can reproduce this bug using the `trino-op` but unfortunately I don't have a minimal example.

Attached are the relevant kube controller logs.

title: [PodLevelResources] CPU Request in PodSpec Status.Resources becomes invalid
body:
Hey! Today I noticed what seems to be strange behavior in a Kind cluster (1.35) when using the Pod level resources feature. When I create the following Pod:

```yaml
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  namespace: default
  name: mypod
spec:
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: "50Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: "100Mi"
    containers:
    - name: pause
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
EOF
```

in the next kubelet loop, the Pod's `status.resources` stanza is updated to: 

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: 28m # here is the issue
  memory: 50Mi
limits:
  cpu: 100m
  memory: 100Mi
```

The CPU request (from `status.resources`) automatically changes from 50m to 28m. Even for other desired cpu requests the field under `status.resources` shows lower value after the next kubelet loop.

 I asked why this was happening on [Slack](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1773193468595889?thread_ts=1773171130.529419&cid=C0BP8PW9G), and I got a pretty detailed write-up explaining it (shoutout to @AutuSnow - thanks again!).

Overall, it seems that when the CPU shares are converted to a weight and saved into cpu.weight, another part of the code later converts the weight back to CPU millicores (the read path). The returned value does not match the millicores I originally set, and this value ends up overwriting `status.resources.requests.cpu`.

Furthermore, I created [this](https://go.dev/play/p/juUY7tDKXKu) small Go program to replicate the issue. For a 50m request, it returns 28.

The Pod's `status.resources` stanza should remain the same, i.e:

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: 50m
  memory: 50Mi
limits:
  cpu: 100m
  memory: 100Mi
```

```bash
KIND_VERSION="kindest/node:v1.35.0@sha256:452d707d4862f52530247495d180205e029056831160e22870e37e3f6c1ac31f"

kind create cluster --image=${KIND_VERSION} --config <(cat <<EOF
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  "InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling": true
  "PodLevelResources": true
  "InPlacePodVerticalScaling": true
  "NodeDeclaredFeatures": true
EOF
)
```

```yaml
kubectl create -f - <<EOF
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  namespace: default
  name: mypod
spec:
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: "50Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: "100Mi"
    containers:
    - name: pause
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.1
EOF
```

wait until the next kubelet loop, and the Pod's `status.resources` stanza will be updated to:

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: 28m
  memory: 50Mi
limits:
  cpu: 100m
  memory: 100Mi
```

title: MemoryQoS does not set memory.high for BestEffort pods on cgroup v2
body:
With `MemoryQoS` enabled on a cgroup v2 node, BestEffort pods do not get a finite memory.high value. Instead, memory.high remains unset and reads as max.

This appears inconsistent with the [MemoryQoS KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos/README.md), which says that for BestEffort pods: _requests.memory = 0 limits.memory should be substituted with node allocatable memory in the memory.high formula:_
`memory.high = floor[ (memoryThrottlingFactor * node allocatable memory) / pageSize ] * pageSize`

In the current kubelet implementation, kubelet skips setting memory.high entirely when both memory requests, limits are 0.

For a BestEffort pod on cgroup v2 with MemoryQoS enabled, memory.high is set to the value calculated as the formula defined in the KEP

Prerequisites
- Linux node with cgroup v2 enabled
- kubelet with MemoryQoS=true

Pod manifests
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: memory-demo-besteffort
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
```

title: performance: prune non-preferred branches early in Topology Manager to avoid combinatorial explosion
body:
`Topology Manager`'s `iterateAllProviderTopologyHints` expands the full Cartesian product of all topology hint providers' hint sets. When a provider returns a large number of hints (e.g. Device Manager (GPU device plugin) calling `bitmask.IterateBitMasks` for all NUMA node power sets), this causes exponential time and memory blowup, making the kubelet unresponsive during pod admission. On an 8-NUMA-node system, a single provider can generate 255 (2^8-1) hints, leading to ~4.2 billion merges with 4 providers.

Measured on Apple M4 Pro (arm64):

**Before optimization:**

```bash
go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
  -run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -benchmem -count=1
```

```
goos: darwin
goarch: arm64
pkg: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager
cpu: Apple M4 Pro
BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists-14    1    257951838000 ns/op    407509652776 B/op    12701401722 allocs/op
PASS
ok      k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager    258.551s
```

A single `Admit()` call took 258 seconds and allocated 407 GB of memory.

`Admit()` completes in bounded time. The hint merging algorithm should not degrade to exponential complexity when providers return large hint sets.

To reproduce, first modify the function:

func (m HintMerger) mergePreferred() *TopologyHint {
}

Force it to return nil directly.

Then run the benchmark:

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
  -run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
  -benchmem -count=1

The benchmark will run for ~4 minutes and consume several hundred GB of memory, reproducing the performance issue.

title: Eviction signal is not hugepages aware
body:
On nodes with hugepages configured, the kubelet's memory.available eviction signal overstates real available regular memory by the total hugepage reservation. This causes eviction to fire later than the configured threshold intends, causing OOM kills.

The root cause is that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where:
- memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM)
- memory.workingSet comes from the memory cgroup controller (does not track hugetlb allocations — those use a separate controller)

This creates "phantom" available bytes equal to the hugepage reservation. The kernel's own MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo does not have this problem because hugepage-reserved pages are removed from the buddy allocator's free pool at boot and never appear in MemFree.

memory.available should reflect memory available for regular (non-hugepage) allocations. 

Configure a node with hugepages.
Query the kubelet summary API: kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/stats/summary".
Observe node.memory.availableBytes — it exceeds what is physically available as regular memory by exactly the hugepage reservation.

The issue can be fixed by subtracting the node's total hugepage capacity from AvailableBytes in the summary stats provider (pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go) before the stats are consumed by the eviction manager. This is a minimal, targeted adjustment at the point where NodeStats.Memory is constructed. It aligns the kubelet's computation with the kernel's own MemAvailable accounting.

This issue is long existing and reproducible on v1.35/master

title: kubelet: SyncPod kills liveness-failed containers sequentially, blocking replacement starts
body:
When multiple containers in a pod fail liveness probes, kubelet's `SyncPod()` kills them sequentially in Step 3 — each `killContainer()` call blocks for up to `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` before moving to the next container. Step 8 (start replacements) only runs after the entire Step 3 kill loop finishes.

A container killed early in the loop cannot get its replacement until all sibling kills in the same cycle complete.

Reproduced with 4 containers, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds=30`, and a `preStop` hook that sleeps 25s. All 4 containers shared one liveness file; removing it caused all 4 to fail simultaneously.

Container restart timestamps from `kubectl logs` and `kubectl logs --previous`:

```
07:08:43  Liveness file removed — all 4 containers fail

Cycle A: kubelet picks up app-a (1 container in this SyncPod cycle)
  07:09:15  app-a STARTED (new container) ← ~30s to restart, expected

Cycle B: kubelet picks up app-b, app-c, app-d (3 containers in one cycle)
  Kill events spaced ~30s apart (= preStop duration), confirming sequential:
    Killing app-b
    Killing app-c  (31s after app-b)
    Killing app-d  (38s after app-c)
  07:10:54  app-b STARTED ← 68 seconds dead, waited for app-c + app-d kills
  07:10:55  app-c STARTED ← 39 seconds dead, waited for app-d kill
  07:10:55  app-d STARTED ← immediate after its own kill
```

app-b was killed at 07:09:46 but could not restart until 07:10:54 because kubelet was still sequentially killing app-c and app-d in the same Step 3 loop. With longer `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (e.g., 300s for connection draining), the first-killed container in a 4-container cycle would wait **15 minutes** instead of 5.

Additional observations:
- The kill order within a cycle is non-deterministic (`ContainersToKill` is a Go map)
- How many containers end up in each cycle is timing-dependent: `computePodActions()` snapshots the liveness cache; only containers that have already crossed `failureThreshold` at that instant are included

A container's replacement should start as soon as its own kill completes, without waiting for sibling container kills to finish.

The whole-pod kill path (`killContainersWithSyncResult` at `kuberuntime_container.go:886-921`) already kills containers in parallel using goroutines + `sync.WaitGroup`. The per-container liveness restart path should either:
1. Parallelize kills using the same pattern, or
2. Start each replacement immediately after its specific kill completes

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: sequential-kill-repro
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: repro
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: repro
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      volumes:
      - name: shared-health
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory
      initContainers:
      - name: init-health
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["touch", "/shared/healthy"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-health
          mountPath: /shared
      containers:
      - name: app-a
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo \"$(date -u +%H:%M:%S) [app-a] STARTED\"; sleep infinity"]
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["cat", "/shared/healthy"]
          periodSeconds: 1
          failureThreshold: 1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-health
          mountPath: /shared
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 25"]
      - name: app-b
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo \"$(date -u +%H:%M:%S) [app-b] STARTED\"; sleep infinity"]
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["cat", "/shared/healthy"]
          periodSeconds: 1
          failureThreshold: 1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-health
          mountPath: /shared
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 25"]
      - name: app-c
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo \"$(date -u +%H:%M:%S) [app-c] STARTED\"; sleep infinity"]
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["cat", "/shared/healthy"]
          periodSeconds: 1
          failureThreshold: 1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-health
          mountPath: /shared
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 25"]
      - name: app-d
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo \"$(date -u +%H:%M:%S) [app-d] STARTED\"; sleep infinity"]
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["cat", "/shared/healthy"]
          periodSeconds: 1
          failureThreshold: 1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-health
          mountPath: /shared
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 25"]
```

Steps:
1. `kubectl apply -f repro.yaml` — wait for 4/4 Running
2. `kubectl exec <pod> -c app-a -- rm /shared/healthy` — all 4 fail at once
3. Wait ~2 minutes, then check start times:
   ```
   for c in app-a app-b app-c app-d; do
     echo "=== $c ==="
     kubectl logs <pod> -c $c
     kubectl logs <pod> -c $c --previous
   done
   ```
4. Observe: containers killed later in the Step 3 loop restart at the same time as the last-killed container. Containers killed early waited much longer than their own preStop duration.
5. Check `kubectl describe pod <pod>` — Killing events are spaced ~30s apart (= preStop duration), confirming sequential blocking.

Source code references (v1.34.0):

| Code | Location |
|------|----------|
| Step 3 sequential kill loop | `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go:1241-1251` |
| `killContainer()` blocks synchronously | `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go:818-882` |
| Step 8 start loop (only after all kills) | `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go:1489-1492` |
| Parallel kill pattern (whole-pod only) | `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go:886-921` |
| Pod worker serialization | `pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go:980-990` |
| `ContainersToKill` is a Go map | `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go:1007-1008` |

`killContainersWithSyncResult()` at `kuberuntime_container.go:886-921` already implements parallel container kills with goroutines + WaitGroup, but is only used for the whole-pod teardown path. The per-container restart path in Step 3 uses a simple sequential `for range` over the map.

Suggested fix directions:
1. Parallelize Step 3 kills for regular container restarts using the same goroutine + `sync.WaitGroup` pattern from `killContainersWithSyncResult()`
2. Or better: a kill-start pipeline where each container's replacement starts immediately after its own kill completes, without waiting for siblings

Either fix should be scoped to regular container restarts in an unchanged sandbox (not init containers, not sandbox recreation, not resize).

Related: #131690 — liveness failure does not mark container not-ready, so during the sequential kill wait, containers in preStop still pass readiness probes and receive traffic. Distinct but compounding issue.

title: Preloaded image pull spec poisoned by a pulled image
body:
This seems to be a corner case in the "Ensure secret pulled images" [feature](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2535).

1. pre-load an image from repo X behind kubelet's back
2. deploy pod A, which references the image from repo X, **without** specifying a pull secret and with `imagePullPolicy: Never`; delete pod A
3. deploy pod B, referencing the same (in terms of identical content digest)  image but from a different repo Y, **using** a pull secret and default `imagePullPolicy`; delete pod B
4. deploy the same pod A again -> get `Container image "X..." is not present with pull policy of Never`

Step (4) should continue working if step (1) did.

Note: @SergeyKanzhelev suggested using agnhost/fakeregistryserver, but I was unable to make the container runtime reach a pod running on the same cluster 🤷🏻 So here is a recipe using my private toy repo on quay. But any non-public repo will do.

# Preparation

1. Prepare an image. You can use any image (does not even need to run properly) that you can get both:
- preloaded on the cluster behind kubelet's back from repository X, and
- present on a private OCI repository Y.

Here is how I did it, after giving up on trying to get the multi-arch `registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10.1` mirrored (`error from registry: manifest invalid` 🙈).

```
$ echo foo >> README.md
$ cat > Dockerfile.foo <<EOF
FROM scratch
COPY ./README.md .
EOF
$ docker build -f Dockerfile.foo . --tag quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo
$ docker tag quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo
$ docker push quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo # X
$ docker push quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo # Y
```

2. Get the image preloaded on a node. I used [image-prefetcher](https://github.com/stackrox/image-prefetcher):

```
$ go run github.com/stackrox/image-prefetcher/deploy@v0.4.3 --version v0.4.3 --namespace t foo > foo-prefetch.yaml
$ echo quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo > image-list.txt
$ kubectl create ns t
$ kubectl create -n t configmap foo --from-file=images.txt=image-list.txt
$ kubectl apply -f foo-prefetch.yaml
```

# Run pod A

```
$ cat > pod-a-never.yaml << EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: testpod-a-never
  namespace: t
spec:
  nodeName: gke-mowsiany-test1-default-pool-1e8c798d-q93d # just to make things deterministic
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: test
    args:
    - foo
    imagePullPolicy: Never
    image: quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo
EOF
$ kubectl apply -f pod-a-never.yaml 
pod/testpod-a-never created
$ kubectl describe -f pod-a-never.yaml
[...]
Events:
  Type     Reason   Age   From     Message
  ----     ------   ----  ----     -------
  Normal   Pulled   6s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Container image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo" already present on machine and can be accessed by the pod
  Normal   Created  6s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Container created
[...]
$ kubectl delete -f pod-a-never.yaml 
pod "testpod-a-never" deleted from t namespace
```

# Run pod B

```
$ cat > pod-b-pull.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: testpod-b-pull
  namespace: t
spec:
  nodeName: gke-mowsiany-test1-default-pool-1e8c798d-q93d
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: test
    args:
    - foo
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    image: quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: mowsiany-robot1-pull-secret
EOF
$ kubectl -n t create -f ~/Downloads/mowsiany-robot1-secret.yml # Attached below
$ kubectl apply -f pod-b-pull.yaml 
pod/testpod-b-pull created
$ kubectl describe -f pod-b-pull.yaml 
[...]
Events:
  Type     Reason   Age   From     Message
  ----     ------   ----  ----     -------
  Normal   Pulling  7s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Pulling image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo"
  Normal   Pulled   7s    kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Successfully pulled image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch-priv:foo" in 285ms (285ms including waiting). Image size: 4601 bytes.
[...]
$ kubectl delete -f pod-b-pull.yaml 
pod "testpod-b-pull" deleted from t namespace
```

# Run pod A again

```
$ kubectl apply -f pod-a-never.yaml 
pod/testpod-a-never created
$ kubectl describe -f pod-a-never.yaml 
[...]
Events:
  Type     Reason             Age              From     Message
  ----     ------             ----             ----     -------
  Warning  ErrImageNeverPull  3s (x3 over 4s)  kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Container image "quay.io/mowsiany/qa-multi-arch:foo" is not present with pull policy of Never
  Warning  Failed             3s (x3 over 4s)  kubelet  spec.containers{test}: Error: ErrImageNeverPull
```

1. [Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1775037474294369)
2. After running pod B, the following file appears in `/var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled` on the node:

```
# # after a again:
gke-mowsiany-test1-default-pool-1e8c798d-q93d /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled # grep -l mowsiany *|xargs jq .

title: Job status shows Running when all pods are Pending
body:
When creating a Job (e.g. `completions: 4`, `parallelism: 1`), the Job's STATUS column in `kubectl get job` shows `Running` even though all of its pods are in `Pending` state.

```console
$ kubectl create -f sleep-job.yaml
job.batch/sleep-job created

$ kubectl get job
NAME        STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
sleep-job   Running   0/1 of 4      3s         3s

$ kubectl get pods
NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
sleep-job-5lp4b              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-b2kvh              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-h7pt4              0/1     Pending   0          9s
sleep-job-rdnlc              0/1     Pending   0          9s
test-nginx-9496d7c6b-2dp67   1/1     Running   0          30h
test-nginx-9496d7c6b-pwfbc   1/1     Running   0          30h
```

The Job status is misleading — it reports `Running` when no pods are actually running (all are `Pending`).

The Job STATUS should reflect that no pods are currently running. When all pods are in `Pending` state, the Job status should not show `Running`. A status like `Pending` or `Suspended` (or a new status that distinguishes "created but not yet scheduled") would be more accurate.

1. Create a Job manifest with `completions: 4` where pods will remain `Pending` (e.g., due to insufficient resources, unschedulable nodes, or a simple sleep Job on a cluster with limited capacity):

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  completions: 4
  parallelism: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: sleep
        image: busybox
        command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```

2. Apply the manifest: `kubectl create -f sleep-job.yaml`
3. Observe Job status: `kubectl get job`
4. Observe pod status: `kubectl get pods`
5. Note that the Job shows `Running` while all pods show `Pending`.

This can be confusing for users debugging scheduling issues, since the Job status suggests work is actively running when it is not.

title: kubepods.slice cgroups (memory and cpu) are reset every minute by kubelet
body: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137719/changes#diff-36d6d25926789aea821105963e22c1fe5fa85bc2a25531a8d295874a4c3a4aedR393-R395 removed the gating behind setting memory QoS, however later on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137889 removed some of this logic due to it resetting the other pod cgroup properties. It seems like this is causing unintended side effects with the same behavior here. Since it was previously gated by an alpha feature gate, I think it makes sense to keep it that way.

title: kubelet: QoS-level memory.min / memory.low is not cleared after MemoryQoS feature gate is disabled (regression from #138430)
body:
After #138430 re-gated the call to `setMemoryQoS` behind `utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.MemoryQoS)`, disabling the `MemoryQoS` alpha feature gate no longer clears stale `memory.min` / `memory.low` values from QoS-level cgroups (`kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice`, `kubepods.slice/kubepods-guaranteed.slice`, etc.) on cgroup v2 unified systems.

Before #138430, `setMemoryQoS` was invoked unconditionally from `UpdateCgroups` on cgroup v2 unified mode. Its zero-out branch at [`pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308) resets `memory.min` / `memory.low` to 0 whenever `memoryReservationPolicy != TieredReservation`, which covers the "feature disabled or policy = None" case. With the gate check added at [L358](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L358), that zero-out branch is unreachable whenever the gate is off.

This is the QoS-level analogue of the pod-level regression that #137674 / #137726 already address. #137726 added `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` on `podContainerManagerImpl` but does not touch QoS-level cgroups, so the stale values at the QoS level remain indefinitely on any node that previously ran with the alpha gate enabled and was later rolled back.

When MemoryQoS is disabled (feature gate off, or `memoryReservationPolicy = None`), QoS-level `memory.min` / `memory.low` should be reset to 0 on the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle. This matches the explicit assumption in #137674 that "QoS-level cgroups are correctly reset via the periodic `setMemoryQoS()` loop."

1. Cgroup v2 unified node.
2. Start kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=true` and `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation`.
3. Create a few Burstable pods so that QoS-level values are populated. Verify:
   `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/memory.low` → non-zero.
4. Disable the gate by restarting kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=false` (or set `memoryReservationPolicy: None`).
5. After the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle, observe that `memory.low` still carries the previous non-zero value. Restart kubelet and repeat — the value persists.

- Closely related: #137674 (pod-level tracking issue), #137726 (pod-level fix), #137889 (earlier removal of `reconcilePodMemoryProtection`), #138431 (motivated #138430).
- The pod-level fix in #137726 does not cover QoS-level cgroups; there is no existing analogue on `qosContainerManagerImpl`.

### Proposed fix options

There are two viable approaches; I would appreciate guidance from sig-node on which shape is preferred:

1. **Keep `setMemoryQoS` unconditional** on cgroup v2 unified mode inside `UpdateCgroups`, and move the feature-gate check *inside* `setMemoryQoS` so it still runs the zero-out branch (L303–L308) but skips the populate branch. Minimal diff; preserves the original cleanup contract.
2. **Add a QoS-level reconcile method** analogous to `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` (#137726) that walks QoS cgroups and zeroes `memory.min` / `memory.low` when the gate is off. Larger diff but symmetric with the pod-level structure.

master at `03779bbd0042` and any release branch that carries the #138430 backports.

title: Kubelet restart triggers UnexpectedAdmissionError for pods using device plugins in both initContainers and containers
body:
Restarting the kubelet causes pods to fail with an UnexpectedAdmissionError when both initContainers and containers use device plugins.

Restart kubelet should not cause running pods to restart

1. Create a pod whose containers and initContainers both use device plugins.
2. Restart kubelet.

pods have initContainers and containers both requesting the same device plugin resources. After kubelet restart, the pod is killed with:

`Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices <resource>`

After kubelet restart, the device manager tries to re-allocate for the completed initContainer and fails.

cherry-picked https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135485 — it does not fix this scenario. This matches the issue reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124345 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118559.

Observed in Kubernetes v1.29.2 and also in v1.34.1

title: Memory Manager static policy rejects TopologyManager best-effort cross-NUMA hints causing UnexpectedAdmissionError
body:
When TopologyManager runs in `best-effort` mode, it may select a cross-NUMA preferred hint (e.g. `{0,1}`) based on CPU/GPU alignment. The static Memory Manager then rejects this hint at allocation time because one of those NUMA nodes already holds a single-node allocation from an earlier container in the same pod.
This surfaces as `UnexpectedAdmissionError` with the message:
```
[memorymanager] preferred hint violates NUMA node allocation
```
even though sufficient memory resources exist on the node.

## Root cause

The static Memory Manager enforces a strict invariant: a NUMA node cannot participate in both single-node and cross-node allocations simultaneously ([upstream docs](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/08/11/kubernetes-1-22-feature-memory-manager-moves-to-beta/#single-vs-cross-numa-node-allocation)). TopologyManager's best-effort policy is unaware of this constraint when scoring hints, so it can choose a cross-NUMA affinity that the Memory Manager will reject as a hard error during `Allocate()`.
The mismatch exists on both allocation paths:
- **Pod-level:** `policy_static.go` → `allocatePod()`
- **Container-level:** `policy_static.go` → `Allocate()`

When TopologyManager is running in `best-effort` mode, a pod with sufficient resources on the node should be admitted successfully. If the preferred cross-NUMA hint conflicts with the Memory Manager's single-vs-cross allocation invariant, the system should either:

1. Avoid selecting that hint in the first place (by incorporating the Memory Manager's constraints into hint preference scoring), or
2. Fall back to a compatible NUMA affinity instead of hard-failing

The pod should not be rejected with `UnexpectedAdmissionError` when allocatable resources exist.

## Reproduction scenario
On a multi-NUMA system (e.g. Grace-family GB200):
1. Configure kubelet with `--topology-manager-policy=best-effort` and `--memory-manager-policy=Static`
2. Submit a Guaranteed pod with multiple containers
3. First container gets a single-NUMA memory allocation on node `{0}`
4. Second container's best-effort preferred hint is `{0,1}` (driven by CPU/device alignment)
5. Memory Manager rejects `{0,1}` because node 0 already has a single-node allocation
6. Pod fails admission with `UnexpectedAdmissionError`

Switching `--topology-manager-scope` from `pod` to `container` does not eliminate the problem , container ordering can still trigger the same conflict.

## Possible directions
- **Memory Manager participates in hint preference scoring:** mark cross-NUMA hints as non-preferred when the target NUMA nodes already have single-node allocations, so TopologyManager avoids them during merging
- **TopologyManager re-evaluates on allocation failure:** if `Allocate()` fails, TopologyManager tries the next-best hint instead of hard-failing
- **Memory Manager falls back gracefully:** instead of returning an error, attempt to find a compatible affinity that satisfies the single-vs-cross invariant
- 
## References
- PR: [#137280 ] (see PR description and review discussion on best-effort-vs-strict admission mismatch)
- TODO breadcrumbs added at both error sites in `pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager/policy_static.go`
- Upstream blog on single-vs-cross NUMA rule: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/08/11/kubernetes-1-22-feature-memory-manager-moves-to-beta/#single-vs-cross-numa-node-allocation

title: Kubelet regression in 1.32, 1.31 and possibly 1.33 and 1.34 where pods get stuck in RunContainerError on OS with cgroupv1
body:
We observed a Kubelet regression in 1.32 and 1.31 (and similar symptoms in 1.33 and 1.34) where pods get stuck in `RunContainerError` on Rocky Linux 8.6 OS which uses cgroup v1. While upgrading Kubernetes from 1.30 to 1.31 and 1.32, we observe the issue once we put the node out of maintenance mode.

The issue is observed with Containerd 1.7 and 1.6 as well.

We initially opened this issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138388 however at the time we didn't know what caused the regression and what versions were affected. We performed a git bisect (using GKE internal builds) and identified the regression was introduced in PR [#131018](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131018). This commit was merged into 1.34 and backported all the way to 1.31. Kubelet works perfectly in the commits immediately preceding this PR.

Following this commit, we observe a massive spike in masked paths. Given our 96-core machines, the `thermal_throttle` paths alone add 96 new entries to the maskedPaths array for every container:

```
crictl inspect 4a44698096076 | jq '.info.config.linux.security_context.masked_paths'
[
  "/proc/asound",
  "/proc/acpi",
  "/proc/interrupts",
  "/proc/kcore",
  "/proc/keys",
  "/proc/latency_stats",
  "/proc/timer_list",
  "/proc/timer_stats",
  "/proc/sched_debug",
  "/proc/scsi",
  "/sys/firmware",
  "/sys/devices/virtual/powercap",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu1/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu2/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu3/thermal_throttle",
[...]
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu94/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu95/thermal_throttle"
]
```

We suspect that this high volume of masked paths is causing kernel-level starvation or resource exhaustion on our cgroup v1 / Rocky 8.6 nodes when scheduling a large number of multi-container pods.

So far we compiled,  we compiled a custom Kubelet that breaks the loop after adding the first `thermal_throttle` path. Under load testing, the system remained completely stable with this patch:

```
v1.32.13-gke.100) ~/gke-internal/kubernetes $ git diff
diff --git a/pkg/securitycontext/util.go b/pkg/securitycontext/util.go
index 5e000f93333..f1889a8cff8 100644
--- a/pkg/securitycontext/util.go
+++ b/pkg/securitycontext/util.go
@@ -213,6 +213,7 @@ var (
                        path := fmt.Sprintf("/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu%d/thermal_throttle", cpu)
                        if _, err := os.Stat(path); err == nil {
                                maskedPaths = append(maskedPaths, path)
+                               break
                        }
                }
 
(v1.32.13-gke.100) ~/gke-internal/kubernetes $ 
``` 

The following kernel settings currently resolve the issue so it is not tracking kernel memory:
  * Set the `cgroup.memory=nokmem` config during the OS upgrade.
  * Reboot the node as part of the OS upgrade process.
  * Upgrade K8s to 1.31

Not tracking kernel memory to mitigate this issue is a big NO for us.

Questions & Asks for the Community: 

The PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131018 that introduced this regression states that it "Mitigates potential Thermal Side-Channel Vulnerability Exploit," linking to a Moby security advisory ([GHSA-6fw5-f8r9-fgfm](https://github.com/moby/moby/security/advisories/GHSA-6fw5-f8r9-fgfm)). However, this link currently returns a 404 error, making it difficult for us to evaluate the exact threat model.

- Could you provide more context on the specific vulnerability (#131018 mitigates) since the advisory link is dead?

- What are the practical security consequences of bypassing or reverting this specific thermal_throttle masking change?

- Is there an appetite to introduce a feature gate or Kubelet flag to bypass this specific path masking for environments where it causes kernel starvation?

Any suggestions, alternative fixes, or guidance from the OSS community would be greatly appreciated.

in 1.31, 1.32, 1.33 and 1.34, cgroupv1 is not yet deprecated https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/13/kubernetes-v1-31-release/#cgroup-v1-enters-the-maintenance-mode  (although it was put in maintenance mode), Kubelet should not yet be unhappy with cgroupv1 until it is fully deprecated. The expectation is that this regression should not happen in Kubelet 1.32, 1.31, 1.33 and 1.34.

title: CPU manager AddContainer does not write cgroup cpuset, reconciler never corrects mismatches
body:
CPU manager's `AddContainer` sets `lastUpdateState` to the desired cpuset without calling `updateContainerCPUSet` to write the cgroup. The reconciler compares `desired` vs `lastUpdateState` — since they always match, it never detects or corrects cpuset mismatches caused by the container runtime.

Additionally, the cpuset is not applied before the container starts. The container inherits the pod-level cgroup cpuset and only gets the correct dedicated cpuset when the reconciler runs (up to 10 seconds later, if the bug above didn't prevent it entirely).

The container should have its dedicated cpuset written to the cgroup before it starts, and the reconciler should detect and correct any subsequent mismatches.

#### How to reproduce it?

1. Create a Guaranteed QoS pod with `cpuManagerPolicy: static` and integer CPU requests
2. Check the container's cgroup `cpuset.cpus.effective` immediately after the container starts
3. Compare with `cpu_manager_state` — they may not match
4. Wait 10+ seconds — the reconciler still does not correct the mismatch because `lastUpdateState` was set without writing

Observed on Dell R760xa with KubeVirt VMs using `dedicatedCpuPlacement` + `guestMappingPassthrough`. The compute container's cgroup showed all odd CPUs (NUMA 1) while `cpu_manager_state` showed CPUs 4,6,68,70 (NUMA 0). The mismatch persisted indefinitely.

KubeVirt's virt-launcher reads `cpuset.cpus.effective` once at startup to build guest NUMA topology. With the wrong cpuset, it generated QEMU memory bindings for NUMA 1, but `cpuset.mems` only allowed NUMA 0, causing `set_mempolicy: Invalid argument`.

The bug is in `pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go` in the `AddContainer` function.

title: HTTP/TCP probes with unresolved named port return Unknown and hide root cause ("port not found")
body:
For HTTP/TCP liveness/readiness/startup probes, port can be `intstr.IntOrString`.

In [ResolveContainerPort](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c3c78e4355ac93436b4c95f39cf1ce576a3f8f41/pkg/probe/util.go#L27) does:
- try `findPortByName` for `intstr.String`
- if not found, fallback to `strconv.Atoi(param.StrVal)`

When probe uses a named port and name is wrong/missing (for example `controller`), kubelet emits:
```
Liveness probe errored and resulted in unknown state: strconv.Atoi: parsing "controller": invalid syntax
```
Then prober returns `probe.Unknown` in [runProbe](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c3c78e4355ac93436b4c95f39cf1ce576a3f8f41/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L165).

Why this is problematic:
- Real reason (`port <name> not found`) is hidden by `strconv.Atoi` parse error.
- Behavior is inconsistent with numeric-port probes:
  - `int` port with unreachable endpoint -> regular probe failure path.
  - bad named port -> repeated `Unknown` events, not failure semantics.
- API validation for port names ([IsValidPortName](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c3c78e4355ac93436b4c95f39cf1ce576a3f8f41/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/validation.go#L332)) requires at least one letter, so pure numeric strings are not valid named ports anyway; `Atoi` fallback in string branch is effectively misleading.

If probe port is `intstr.String` and named port is not found:
- return explicit error like `port "<name>" not found` (no `Atoi` parse noise),
- and consider handling this case as probe `Failure` instead of `Unknown` to match practical liveness behavior.

Suggested direction:
1. Remove `Atoi` fallback from string branch in `ResolveContainerPort`.
2. Optionally add typed `ErrPortNotFound` and map it to `Failure` in prober.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: probe-named-port-typo
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:latest
    ports:
    - name: metrics
      containerPort: 8080
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: metrcis # typo: should be "metrics"
      initialDelaySeconds: 1
      periodSeconds: 2
      timeoutSeconds: 1
      failureThreshold: 1
```

```bash
❯ k describe pod probe-named-port-typo
...
Warning  Unhealthy        48s (x25 over 96s)  kubelet            spec.containers{pause}: Liveness probe errored and resulted in unknown state: strconv.Atoi: parsing "metrcis": invalid syntax
```

title: kubelet eviction manager: 'no observation found' for containerfs.inodesFree on ZFS (no fixed inodes)
body:
On Linux nodes using ZFS as the container filesystem (containerd data directory on ZFS), the kubelet eviction manager logs the following message every ~10 seconds:

```
I0531 17:53:16.101492  192859 helpers.go:949] "Eviction manager: no observation found for eviction signal" signal="containerfs.inodesFree"
```

This is because ZFS does not have fixed inodes — the `F_files` and `F_ffree` fields in `statfs` return 0 for ZFS datasets. As a result, cAdvisor's filesystem stats never report inode information for the container filesystem (containerfs), and `makeSignalObservations()` never creates an observation for `containerfs.inodesFree`.

However, `UpdateContainerFsThresholds()` in `pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers.go` **unconditionally** creates `containerfs.inodesFree` thresholds, even when the source inode thresholds (`nodefs.inodesFree` / `imagefs.inodesFree`) may not have meaningful observations. This causes the eviction manager to log repeatedly every monitoring cycle.

## What you expected to happen

The `containerfs.inodesFree` threshold should not be added when the underlying filesystem does not provide meaningful inode statistics, or the log message should be suppressed to avoid log spam.

## How to reproduce it

1. Set up a Linux node with ZFS as the backing filesystem for the container runtime (e.g., `/var/lib/containerd` on ZFS, or `/var/lib/kubelet` on ZFS).
2. Run kubelet with default eviction settings (which includes `nodefs.inodesFree` and `imagefs.inodesFree` in `DefaultEvictionHard`).
3. Observe kubelet logs — the message appears every eviction-monitoring period (default 10s).

## Environment

- **Kubernetes version**: v1.36.1+k3s1 (also confirmed on older versions)
- **Kubelet version**: v1.36.1
- **Container runtime**: containerd 2.1.5
- **ZFS version**: 2.4.2-2
- **Kernel**: 7.0.9+deb14-amd64 (Debian sid/forky)
- **OS**: Debian GNU/Linux forky/sid

## Additional context

This is the same class of bug as issue #130142 / PR #137318, which fixed the same symptom for **Windows** (where inodes are also not supported). That fix added a guard in `UpdateContainerFsThresholds` to skip creating `containerfs.inodesFree` thresholds when the source inode thresholds (`nodefs.inodesFree` / `imagefs.inodesFree`) don't exist. The same guard is needed for ZFS on Linux.

Prior fix: PR #67709 fixed the equivalent issue for `nodefs.inodesFree` on Windows. The `containerfs.inodesFree` signal was introduced later and did not include the same guard.

The fix should mirror PR #137318: in `UpdateContainerFsThresholds`, check if the hard/soft threshold signals for `nodefs.inodesFree` or `imagefs.inodesFree` are actually set (i.e., `hardNodeINodeDisk.Signal != ""`) before adding `containerfs.inodesFree` thresholds.

title: Job controller manageJob() returns active=0 during backoff, causing "cannot set more ready pods than active" status update rejection
body:
When the Job controller's `manageJob()` function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns `active=0` to the caller. The caller uses this value to set `job.Status.Active=0` in a status update, while `job.Status.Ready` retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` (GA in 1.33 via `JobManagedBy`) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422.

Because the status update fails, the controller cannot:
- Flush `uncountedTerminatedPods`
- Remove `batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking` finalizers from terminated pods

This causes pods to appear stuck in Terminating state and job status to become stale.

**Root cause:** Two locations in `manageJob()` return a hardcoded `0` instead of the real `active` count when backoff is active:

```go
// Location 1: global backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}

// Location 2: per-index backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}
```

The caller sets `job.Status.Active = active` (the returned 0), while `job.Status.Ready` stays at the informer count (e.g., 5). Result: `5 > 0` → 422.

The `0` was likely a "don't care" value from before `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` validation existed. Every other return path in `manageJob` returns the real active count.

The backoff early-return in `manageJob()` should return the real active pod count (unchanged, since no pods were created or deleted), not 0.

Proposed fix:
```diff
     if remainingTime > 0 {
         jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
-        return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
+        return active, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
     }
```

Returning `active` (initialized at top of `manageJob` as `int32(len(jobCtx.activePods))`) means "I didn't create or delete any pods" — the correct semantics for a backoff deferral.

```bash
# 1. Create a Job
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: repro-ready-active
  namespace: default
spec:
  parallelism: 30
  completions: 30
  backoffLimit: 500
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "10m"
            memory: "16Mi"
EOF

# 2. Wait for all pods to be Running+Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active --timeout=120s

# 3. Force-delete 25 pods simultaneously
kubectl get pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active -o name | head -25 | \
  xargs -P25 kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0

# 4. Observe: job status is frozen, KCM logs show error
kubectl get job repro-ready-active -o jsonpath='active={.status.active} ready={.status.ready} failed={.status.failed}'
# Output: active=30 ready=30 failed=   (stale — doesn't reflect reality)

# KCM logs show:
# "Unhandled Error" err="syncing job: tracking status: adding uncounted pods to status:
#   Job.batch \"repro-ready-active\" is invalid: status.ready: Invalid value: 5:
#   cannot set more ready pods than active"

# 5. Bug self-resolves after ~10 min when backoff expires (if no new failures arrive)
```

- The bug fires on any multi-pod Job that experiences a pod failure while other pods are still Ready. For single failures (10s backoff), it produces a few 422 errors that self-resolve. For mass failures (spot reclamation, node failure → backoff capped at 10 min), it causes visible stuck pods and stale status for the full backoff duration.
- No data loss occurs. The job eventually completes. The impact is operational: stuck Terminating pods, stale status, KCM error log spam.
- The `metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated` label on the return is also incorrect (no pods were created), but that's cosmetic.

<details>

Bug present from 1.31 (when `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` was introduced, beta default-on) through latest master. Unconditional from 1.33 (`JobManagedBy` GA).

Tested and reproduced on 1.35.

title: CPUManager shrinks multi-NUMA TopologyManager affinity when distributing exclusive CPUs across NUMA
body:
We observed that CPUManager receives a multi-NUMA affinity selected by TopologyManager, but the final exclusive CPU allocation is still shrunk to fewer NUMA nodes.

  The node topology is:

  - 256 logical CPUs
  - 4 NUMA nodes
  - 8 GPUs distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes
  - NICs also distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes

  Kubelet configuration:

  ```yaml
  cpuManagerPolicy: static
  cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
    distribute-cpus-across-numa: "true"

  topologyManagerPolicy: best-effort
  topologyManagerPolicyOptions:
    prefer-closest-numa-nodes: "true"
  ```

  The pod requests:

  ```yaml
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "176"
      nvidia.com/gpu: "8"
    limits:
      cpu: "176"
      nvidia.com/gpu: "8"
  ```

  TopologyManager selects an all-NUMA affinity because the pod requests 8 GPUs distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes:

  ```text
  Best TopologyHint bestHint={"NUMANodeAffinity":15,"Preferred":false}
  Topology Affinity affinity={"NUMANodeAffinity":15,"Preferred":false}
  ```

  CPUManager receives this affinity:

  ```text
  AllocateCPUs numCPUs=176 socket="1111"
  ```

  However, the final CPU allocation only uses 3 NUMA nodes:

  ```text
  AllocateCPUs result="32-61,64-93,96-124,160-188,192-220,224-252"
  ```

  So CPUManager appears to treat the TopologyManager affinity as an allowed NUMA set, then reselects the minimum number of NUMA nodes needed to satisfy the CPU request.

  On this node, 176 CPUs can fit into 3 NUMA nodes, so the final CPUSet is distributed roughly as:

  ```text
  59 + 59 + 58
  ```

  This is not aligned with the GPU/NIC topology selected by TopologyManager.

  When TopologyManager selects a multi-NUMA affinity and passes it to CPUManager, CPUManager should preserve that topology intent when allocating exclusive CPUs.

  In this case, since the 8 GPUs and NICs span all 4 NUMA nodes, we expected the exclusive CPU allocation to also cover all 4 NUMA nodes, roughly:

  ```text
  44 + 44 + 44 + 44
  ```

  At minimum, there should be an opt-in CPUManager static policy option to distribute exclusive CPUs across all NUMA nodes in the TopologyManager affinity, instead of shrinking the allocation back to the
  minimum number of NUMA nodes required by the CPU request.

 1. Use a node with this topology:

  ```text
  256 logical CPUs
  4 NUMA nodes
  8 GPUs distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes
  ```

  2. Configure kubelet with static CPUManager and NUMA distribution:

  ```yaml
  cpuManagerPolicy: static
  cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
    distribute-cpus-across-numa: "true"

  topologyManagerPolicy: best-effort
  topologyManagerPolicyOptions:
    prefer-closest-numa-nodes: "true"
  ```

  3. Create a Guaranteed pod requesting 8 GPUs and 176 exclusive CPUs:

  ```yaml
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "176"
      nvidia.com/gpu: "8"
    limits:
      cpu: "176"
      nvidia.com/gpu: "8"
  ```

  4. Check kubelet logs for TopologyManager and CPUManager allocation:

  ```console
  journalctl -u kubelet | grep -E "TopologyHints generated|Best TopologyHint|Topology Affinity|AllocateCPUs"
  ```

  5. Observe that TopologyManager selects the all-NUMA affinity, but CPUManager allocates the final CPUSet from only 3 NUMA nodes.

 This looks related to CPU/device NUMA alignment discussed in #122295, but it is different from the `align-by-socket` behavior addressed by #136572.

  In this case:

  - `align-by-socket` is not enabled
  - TopologyManager already passes the all-NUMA affinity to CPUManager
  - the issue happens later, when CPUManager allocates CPUs and shrinks the final CPUSet to fewer NUMA nodes

  A possible direction is to add a new opt-in CPUManager static policy option, for example:

  ```text
  distribute-cpus-across-topology-affinity=true
  ```

  or:

  ```text
  distribute-cpus-across-affinity=true
  ```

  Intended behavior:

  > When TopologyManager provides a multi-NUMA affinity to CPUManager, CPUManager distributes exclusive CPUs across all NUMA nodes in that affinity, instead of shrinking the allocation back to the minimum
  number of NUMA nodes required by the CPU request.

  This should likely be opt-in, not a default behavior change, because existing users may rely on CPUManager minimizing the number of NUMA nodes used.

  Open questions:

  - For `best-effort` TopologyManager policy, should CPUManager strictly fail if it cannot allocate within the selected affinity, or should it fall back to the existing allocation behavior?
  - Should this behavior apply to non-preferred hints selected by `best-effort`, or only to preferred hints?
  - Should this option require `distribute-cpus-across-numa=true`?
  - How should this interact with `align-by-socket`?

title: apiserver: return 4xx instead of 500 when pod runtimeClassName is empty
body:
The Kubernetes API Server returns HTTP 500 Internal Server Error when creating a Pod whose `spec.runtimeClassName` is set to an empty string.

The following request sets `spec.runtimeClassName` to `""`:

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":""}}'
```
Actual response:
```bash
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "resource name may not be empty",
  "code": 500
}
```
The request is invalid or incomplete, but the API Server returns an internal server error.

The API Server should return a client-side error, such as HTTP 400 Bad Request or HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity, instead of HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

Since `spec.runtimeClassName` is invalid when it is an empty string, the error should be reported as a validation error rather than an internal server error.

1. Start a Kubernetes cluster with an affected version.
2. Start a local API proxy:

```bash
kubectl proxy --port=8001
```
3. Send the following request:
```bash
curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":""}}'
```
4. Observe that the API Server returns HTTP 500:
```bash
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "resource name may not be empty",
  "code": 500
}
```

This issue was found during RESTful API fuzzing of the Kubernetes API Server.

The request is invalid because `runtimeClassName` is empty and the Pod body is incomplete. However, this should not be surfaced as HTTP 500. It appears that an empty `runtimeClassName` is propagated to runtime class lookup logic and reported as an internal error.

This behavior is reproducible in my tests on Kubernetes v1.33.1 and v1.36.0.

title: kubelet CleanSubPaths can leave pods stuck Terminating when subPath target stat returns ENOENT but mountinfo still has the mount
body:
A pod using a CSI volume with `volumeMount.subPath` got stuck in `Terminating`.

The workload container had already exited, but kubelet repeatedly failed during volume cleanup before calling CSI `NodeUnpublishVolume`.

Example kubelet logs:

```text
UnmountVolume started for volume "<pvc-name>" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/<driver>^<volume>")
Warning: mount cleanup skipped because path does not exist:
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volume-subpaths/<volume-name>/xxxx/3

Warning: mount cleanup skipped because path does not exist:
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volume-subpaths/<volume-name>/xxxx/5

Operation ... failed. No retries permitted until ...
Error: error cleaning subPath mounts for volume "<pvc-name>" ...
error deleting /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volume-subpaths/<volume-name>/xxxx:
remove .../xxxx: directory not empty
```

If a subPath target path returns ENOENT but the mount is still present in mountinfo, kubelet should not skip cleanup and then fail on the parent directory with directory not empty.

Kubelet should either detect the stale/deleted mountpoint from mountinfo and attempt to unmount it, or re-check/re-walk remaining subPath entries before failing the parent directory removal.

We do not yet have a manifest-only reproducer. The key failure state is:

```text
a kubelet subPath bind target is still present in mountinfo,
but stat(2) on the subPath target returns ENOENT
```

title: [SIG NODE Discussion] Metrics and dashboards for monitoring SIG-Node CI test failures and bug triage health
body:
### Context
In the recent SIG-Node CI subgroup meetings (6/10/2026), we discussed the need to better track our CI stability and test degradation over time. 

Currently, we are manually tracking the status of our Testgrid dashboards in a [Spreadsheet Tracker](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IwONkeXSc2SG_EQMYGRSkfiSWNk8yWLpVhPm-LOTbGM) before every meeting. We document the current status (Passing/Flaky/Failing) of the jobs and link them to tracking GitHub issues, but doing this manually makes it hard to see historic data and trends.

### Goals
We would like to gather community input on what metrics, tooling, and dashboards we should use to automate this monitoring. For starters, we can try to answer questions like:
* How long has a specific test or job been failing?
* Is a recurring failure caused by the same error or a new regression?
* How long do SIG-Node CI bugs remain open?
* How many `important-soon` bugs do we currently have, and what is their average resolution time?
Please recommend any more you think of, open to all suggestions!!

### Existing Efforts & Ideas
* We dug up an [existing dashboard started by dims](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-metrics/failures-latest.html?include=node&sort=days&asc=0), but we need to determine how persistent this data is, how it's generated, and how we can best utilize or adapt it.
* Could we leverage existing Kubernetes `test-infra` tooling (like BigQuery metrics/[Kettle](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/kettle/README.md), `k8s-triage` in the [aggregated failures dashboard](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?sig=node)) to automate the data we currently put in our manual spreadsheet?

### Call to Action
We are opening this issue to invite ideas from the CI/CD community. 
1. What metrics do you think are most important for us to track?
2. Are there existing dashboards or tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem we should be leveraging?
3. Any volunteers interested in helping build out or maintain this reporting?

Please drop your thoughts and suggestions below!

title: Supporting concurrent processing of PLEG events is needed
body:
In kubelet, [GenericPLEG.Relist](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1cd0b215bb5ce2f723cde78660b5524ee3258dcb/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go#L289) periodically retrieves Pods/Containers from the container runtime and compares them with the information in memory to update the cache. When there are a large number of changes to containers on a single node (our production scenario already supports up to 300, although the default is currently 110 Pods), this process can take a significant amount of time, even exceeding 3 minutes. Therefore, we believe that parallel processing should be supported in this area.

In [GenericPLEG.Relist](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1cd0b215bb5ce2f723cde78660b5524ee3258dcb/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go#L289), updates to the cache can be processed concurrently.

This problem is not always reproduced. However, when a large number of pods or containers exist on a node, this problem may be triggered.

title: DRA: allocator clears DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests too aggressively, widening a per-request config to the whole claim
body:
The DRA structured allocator post-processes allocated configs to drop a `DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests` list to `nil` when the config "applies to all requests" (the *empty means all* semantic). It decides this with a length comparison:

```go

for i := range allocationResult.Devices.Config {
    if len(allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests) {
        allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests = nil
    }
}
```

`len(config.Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests)` is **not** equivalent to "this config covers every request in the claim", because `config.Requests` entries may be sub-request references of the form `"<request>/<subRequest>"`  the allocator matches them that way a few lines earlier:

```go
subRequestName := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", request.Name, subRequest.Name)
if slices.Contains(config.Requests, subRequestName) { ... }
```

A config that references **N sub-requests of a single parent request** has `len(config.Requests) == N`. If the claim has **N top-level requests**, the lengths match even though the config covers only one of them  so its `Requests` is cleared and the config is silently re-scoped to **every** request in the claim.

The same defect is present in all three production implementations:
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go` (the cleanup loop)
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/incubating/allocator_incubating.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`

A config that references only sub-requests of one request should remain scoped to that request. `Requests` should be cleared to `nil` (the "applies to all" form) only when the config actually covers **all** top-level requests in the claim.

Add this case to the shared table in `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` (`TestAllocator`) and run `go test ./structured/internal/experimental/ -run 'TestAllocator/repro-config-subrequests-not-all'` (fails identically for `incubating` and `stable`):

```go
"repro-config-subrequests-not-all": {
    features: Features{PrioritizedList: true},
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claim(claim0).withRequests(
            requestWithPrioritizedList(req0,
                subRequest(subReq0, classA, 1),
                subRequest(subReq1, classB, 1),
            ),
            deviceRequest(req1, classA, 1), // second top-level request, unrelated to the config
        ).withConfigs(objects(
            // references BOTH sub-requests of req0 only; must NOT apply to req1
            deviceClaimConfig([]string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo")),
        )),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA), class(classB, driverB)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
        device(device1, nil, nil), device(device2, nil, nil),
    )),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{allocationResultWithConfigs(
        localNodeSelector(node1),
        objects(
            deviceAllocationResult(req0SubReq0, driverA, pool1, device1, false),
            deviceAllocationResult(req1, driverA, pool1, device2, false),
        ),
        []resourceapi.DeviceAllocationConfiguration{{
            Source:              resourceapi.AllocationConfigSourceClaim,
            Requests:            []string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, // expected: stays scoped to req0
            DeviceConfiguration: deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo"),
        }},
    )},
},
```

Device allocation comes out exactly as expected (`req-0/subReq-0` → `device-1`, `req-1` → `device-2`); the **only** difference is the config scope:

```text
expected: Requests: ["req-0/subReq-0", "req-0/subReq-1"]
actual:   Requests: nil      # == applies to ALL requests, including the unrelated req-1
```

`startPodSync` creates a context and stores `status.cancelFn`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ac864492b6076be38e1155bfffe2ddf9005af1e3/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1155
