title: [kubelet] UpdatePod PodPhase race condition
body:
Pod Workers is looking at the status of the pod in updates: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L793

The problem is that in several request paths this is the PodStatus as read from the API server, which might skew from the latest status written to StatusManager. The kubelet's local StatusManager status should be considered the source of truth for pod phase.

xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135296

title: [kubelet] Make AllocationManager the source of truth for pod allocations
body:
This was the intention, but there are some outstanding issues today:

- Not all components that should handle allocated pods do.
    - Proposal: Expose pod getter functions on AllocationManager to get the allocated pod. Audit callers of PodManager to identify components that should be migrated to calling AllocationManager instead. Open to discussing alternative architectures.
- `getAllocatedPods` first calls `getActivePods` and then filters the list. We should make the allocation the source of truth. This requires ensuring that the Allocation is promptly removed for terminated pods.

See also https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139522

title: [kubelet] Calling UpdatePod on an untracked but terminated pod should mark it as terminated, not terminating
body:
The first call to `UpdatePod` for a failed (rejected) pod sets `terminatingAt` but doesn't set `termitatedAt` because we need to run `SyncTerminatingPod` to clean up:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L803-L812

However, the first time we enter the pod worker loop, I'm pretty sure we end up saying the pod can never start, and exit the worker loop:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1234

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1180

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1047-L1049

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1240-L1243

Unless I'm missing something, this looks like a bug with how we handle clean up in this case. But, if that cleanup isn't actually necessary, then maybe we can just set the `terminatedAt` timestamp immediately for the failed pod, which would cause it to be considered inactive.

Note: There is a test case that is suppose to cover this, but since the test uses a fake cache implementation that doesn't match the defaulting logic of the real cache, it skips over the code that generates the terminating sync status.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go#L750-L771

Copied from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136508#issuecomment-4411520959

title: [kubelet] SyncKnownPods should exclude terminated pods from the workers set
body:
`SyncKnownPods` should exclude terminated pods from the workers set, which ensures running runtime pods associated with a terminated pod get cleaned up.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ea231e60e7616f820c544bedc6074f68aa80828c/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1235

xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136508#issuecomment-4411520959

title: [kubelet] Why isn’t DRA prepare failure treated as a pod sync error?
body:
I noticed that DRA `PrepareDynamicResources` / `NodePrepareResources` failures appear not to be propagated as pod sync errors in kubelet. As a result, the retry seems to happen on the regular pod resync interval instead of the pod sync error backoff path.

I would like to understand whether this is intentional, and if so, what the design rationale is.

**code path**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1585-L1597

When PrepareDynamicResources fails,the function returns early, but it does not appear to mark the PodSyncResult as failed, for example via either:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1498-L1522

This matters because if result.Error() == nil, the kubelet will re-process the pod after the default sync interval (60s–90s). Otherwise, the pod is placed into the backoff queue and will be retried sooner. In our experience, the first few PrepareDynamicResources calls sometimes fail, forcing us to wait through several default sync periods, which significantly increases pod startup latency.

title: kubelet allocates hostUsers:false pod UID/GID range ending at UINT32_MAX, causing sandbox creation to fail indefinitely
body:
A pod using:

```yaml

spec:

  hostUsers: false
```
intermittently fails during pod sandbox creation when kubelet allocates the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

This maps container UID/GID 0..65535 to host UID/GID: 4294901760..4294967295
The final mapped value is:
```
4294967295 = 2^32 - 1 = UINT32_MAX
```

The pod then fails sandbox creation indefinitely with:
```
FailedCreatePodSandBox
failed to create network namespace for sandbox:
failed to start noop process for unshare:
fork/exec /proc/self/exe: invalid argument
```

The affected pod never starts its init container or app container. Volume setup succeeds, but sandbox creation fails before container execution.

I have reproduced/observed this again with in same configuration on different cluster:
```
namespace: pim-adapter
pod: pim-adapter-akeneo-attributes-queue-cronjob-29701755-5blmf
```
The kubelet persisted user namespace state for this pod confirms the same terminal range:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```
The persisted kubelet state is from:
```
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/userns
```

Other hostUsers: false pods on the same node with non-terminal UID/GID ranges run successfully.

Either:

1. kubelet should not allocate a pod user namespace range that includes 4294967295 / UINT32_MAX, or
2. the runtime/kernel stack should successfully create the sandbox with this mapping, or
3. the pod should fail with a clear validation/allocation error instead of retrying sandbox creation indefinitely.

In particular, kubelet should probably avoid allocating the final 65,536-ID block:
```
4294901760..4294967295
```
if this range is not valid for pod user namespace mappings.

This appears to reproduce when kubelet assigns the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range to a pod using hostUsers: false.

Minimal pod property:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: userns-terminal-range-repro
  namespace: userns-terminal-range-repro
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/busybox:latest
      command: ["sh", "-c", "id && sleep 3600"]
```

The important condition is that kubelet allocates this persisted user namespace mapping:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

Validation steps on an affected pod:
```
NS=userns-terminal-range-repro
POD=userns-terminal-range-repro

kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='hostUsers={.spec.hostUsers}{"\n"}node={.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}uid={.metadata.uid}{"\n"}phase={.status.phase}{"\n"}'

POD_UID=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
echo "$POD_UID"
```
On the node where the pod is scheduled:
```
sudo cat "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Boundary check:
```
sudo jq -r '
  .uidMappings[0] as $u |
  .gidMappings[0] as $g |
  "uid_hostId=\($u.hostId)",
  "uid_length=\($u.length)",
  "uid_end=\($u.hostId + $u.length - 1)",
  "gid_hostId=\($g.hostId)",
  "gid_length=\($g.length)",
  "gid_end=\($g.hostId + $g.length - 1)",
  "uid_hits_uint32_max=\(($u.hostId + $u.length - 1) == 4294967295)",
  "gid_hits_uint32_max=\(($g.hostId + $g.length - 1) == 4294967295)"
' "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Observed output:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```

Check kubelet events/logs:

```
kubectl describe pod -n "$NS" "$POD" | grep -A8 -B4 'FailedCreatePodSandBox\|CreatePodSandbox\|failed to create network namespace\|noop process\|invalid argument'
```

```
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|CreatePodSandbox|FailedCreatePodSandBox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
```
sudo journalctl -u containerd --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|RunPodSandbox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
The failure occurs before CNI appears to run and before any init/app container starts.

This looks like a boundary bug in the kubelet pod user namespace allocator or in validation of generated mappings.
The node can run other hostUsers: false pods successfully when kubelet assigns non-terminal ranges. Examples of working persisted mappings observed on the same node include:
```
{"hostId":416546816,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":1584726016,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4152492032,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4130734080,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":3823566848,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
```

The affected pod is from a CronJob/Job. In one observed case, the pod stayed stuck for approximately 2 days and accumulated more than 13,000 FailedCreatePodSandBox events. It happened on two different clusters with same CronJob/Job.

Relevant pod spec properties:
```
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
```

The affected workload does not use:
```
hostNetwork: true
hostPID: true
hostIPC: true
volumeDevices:
```
Relevant sysctls on the node:
```
user.max_user_namespaces = 62502
user.max_net_namespaces = 62502
```
Workaround:
```
hostUsers: true
```
or removing:
```
hostUsers: false
```
avoids the kubelet pod user namespace allocation path and prevents this failure for the affected workload.

title: DRA-backed extended resources do not report ResourceHealthStatus in PodStatus
body:
When a Pod uses an extended resource backed by Dynamic Resource Allocation, kubelet prepares the generated special ResourceClaim and injects the CDI devices, but it does not populate `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus` for those resources.
﻿
For DRA-backed extended resources, the container request is in `container.Resources.Requests`, not in `container.Resources.Claims`, so the health status update path never considers `pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.RequestMappings`.
﻿
As a result, DRA-backed extended resources can be prepared and passed into the container, but their health is not reflected in PodStatus.

When `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled and a DRA plugin reports health for a device allocated via a DRA-backed extended resource, kubelet should publish that health in `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus`.
﻿
The reported status should correspond to the generated special ResourceClaim and request from `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus.requestMappings`.

title: Kubelet UID-qualified exec/run routes ignore mismatched pod UID during pod resolution
body:
While investigating kubelet streaming endpoints, I noticed that the UID-qualified `exec` and `run` routes do not appear to enforce the supplied pod UID during pod resolution.

Routes:

```
/exec/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
/run/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
```

parse and forward the UID, but the underlying lookup prefers the pod full name whenever it is available.

As a result, a request using a stale or mismatched UID can still resolve successfully to the currently running pod with the same namespace/name.

I initially treated this as a potential security concern and performed a deeper investigation of the authorization path.

After tracing the complete request flow multiple times, I could not identify any authorization bypass or privilege escalation. Authorization is already enforced before these handlers, so the observed behavior appears to be a correctness/consistency issue rather than a security issue.

I have reproduced and re-verified this behavior twice using the existing runtime tests and local code tracing.

When a UID-qualified kubelet route is used and a non-empty pod UID is supplied, the request should require both:

- pod full name
- pod UID

to match the current pod.

For example:

```
Pod:
namespace: default
name: demo
uid: new-uid

Request:
/exec/default/demo/old-uid/container
```

should be rejected instead of resolving to the recreated pod.

This would also make the behavior consistent with the existing `attach` and `port-forward` implementations, which explicitly reject UID mismatches.

The existing runtime test already documents the lookup precedence.

Run:

```bash
go test ./pkg/kubelet/container \
-run 'TestPodsFindPod/find_by_full_name_takes_precedence' \
-count=1 -v
```

The test demonstrates that:

```
Pods.FindPod("pod1_ns1", "uid2")
```

returns the pod identified by its full name even when the supplied UID belongs to a different pod.

Relevant request flow:

```
HTTP /exec/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
        ↓
getExec()
        ↓
GetExec()
        ↓
findContainer(...)
        ↓
Pods.FindPod(podFullName, podUID)
        ↓
FindPodByFullName(...)
```

I reproduced this behavior twice during investigation and obtained the same result both times.

Additional investigation:

- Traced the complete kubelet exec/run request path.
- Compared behavior with `attach` and `port-forward`.
- Verified that authorization occurs before the streaming handlers.
- Verified that this does **not** appear to introduce RBAC bypass, privilege escalation, or tenant isolation issues.

Behavior comparison:

| Operation | UID validation |
|-----------|---------------|

title: Kubelet emits transient `object "<ns>"/"<name>" not registered` (FailedMount) on cold start
body:
## What happens

On kubelet start/restart (node reboot, kubelet upgrade, cold node join), pods that mount secret
or configMap volumes intermittently fail to mount with a `FailedMount` event:

```
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "sec" : object "bootrace-min"/"s37" not registered
```

It is transient and clears on the volume reconciler's next pass, but delays pod startup and
generates many `FailedMount` events at scale (node reboots, node-pool upgrades).

## Environment

- Kubernetes: reproduced on v1.31.14; symptom reported across 1.22–1.27 (see related issues).
- Node: 2 vCPU Linux, containerd, single-node kubeadm cluster.

## Reproduce

Small node (e.g. **2 vCPU**), kubelet `maxPods` raised to fit the pod count: create N pods each
mounting its **own distinct** secret + configMap, then restart kubelet a few times. A *shared*
object does not reproduce; the objects must be distinct.

```bash
./repro.sh                 # 150 distinct-object pods, 6 kubelet restarts (defaults)
```

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# USAGE: ./repro.sh [NUM_PODS] [RESTARTS] [SETTLE_SECS]   (defaults: 150 6 25)
# ENV:   NS, NODE, RESTART_CMD="sudo systemctl restart kubelet"
# Requires kubectl + ability to restart kubelet on the node. Raise kubelet maxPods to fit NUM_PODS.
set -uo pipefail
N="${1:-150}"; R="${2:-6}"; SETTLE="${3:-25}"
NS="${NS:-bootrace-min}"
RESTART_CMD="${RESTART_CMD:-sudo systemctl restart kubelet}"
NODE="${NODE:-$(kubectl get nodes --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk '$2=="Ready"{print $1; exit}')}"
[ -z "$NODE" ] && { echo "ERROR: no Ready node; set NODE=<name>"; exit 1; }

kubectl create namespace "$NS" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: Secret\nmetadata: {name: s%d, namespace: %s}\nstringData: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: ConfigMap\nmetadata: {name: c%d, namespace: %s}\ndata: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do cat <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: p$i, namespace: $NS, labels: {app: bootrace-min}}
spec:
  nodeName: $NODE
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: sec, mountPath: /etc/sec, readOnly: true}
    - {name: cm,  mountPath: /etc/cm,  readOnly: true}
  volumes:
  - {name: sec, secret: {secretName: s$i}}
  - {name: cm,  configMap: {name: c$i}}
---
EOF
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null

for t in $(seq 1 120); do
  run=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$run" -ge "$N" ] && break; sleep 4
done
echo "Running: $run / $N"

total=0
for b in $(seq 1 "$R"); do
  kubectl -n "$NS" delete events --all >/dev/null 2>&1
  eval "$RESTART_CMD"
  sleep "$SETTLE"
  hits=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount \
           -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.message}{"\n"}{end}' 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'not registered')
  total=$((total + hits))
  printf 'restart %2d/%d | FailedMount "not registered": %d\n' "$b" "$R" "$hits"
done
echo "TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: $total"
echo "Cleanup: kubectl delete ns $NS"
```
</details>

### Sample output (single-node, 2 vCPU, 150 distinct-object pods)

```
restart  1/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 14
restart  2/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 4
restart  3/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 58
restart  4/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 46
restart  5/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 15
restart  6/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 6
TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: 143
```

Inspect: `kubectl -n bootrace-min get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount | grep 'not registered'`

## Related issues

- #105204 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.22–1.23)
- #119361 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.27)

title: kubelet /configz leaks --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys)
body:
kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

```go
config := kubeletServer.KubeletConfiguration.DeepCopy()
for k := range config.StaticPodURLHeader {
    config.StaticPodURLHeader[k] = []string{"<masked>"}
}
logger.V(5).Info("KubeletConfiguration", "configuration", klog.Format(config))
```

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

```go
func setConfigz(cz *configz.Config, kc *kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration) error {
    scheme, _, err := kubeletscheme.NewSchemeAndCodecs()
    ...
    versioned := &kubeletconfigv1beta1.KubeletConfiguration{}
    if err := scheme.Convert(kc, versioned, nil); err != nil { return err }   // raw headers flow through
    versioned.GetObjectKind().SetGroupVersionKind(...)
    return cz.Set(versioned)
}
```

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops an in-package Go test that calls the real `setConfigz` + `configz.InstallHandler`, hits the handler with `GET /configz`, and asserts the secret header is in the JSON response. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
DIR="$ROOT/cmd/kubelet/app"
F="$DIR/zz_poc_configz_leak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package app

import (
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"k8s.io/component-base/configz"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
)

func TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader(t *testing.T) {
	const name = "poc-configz-leak"
	const secret = "Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"
	cz, err := configz.New(name)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("register: %v", err)
	}
	t.Cleanup(func() { configz.Delete(name) })

	kc := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "https://manifests.example.invalid/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
	}
	if err := setConfigz(cz, kc); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("setConfigz: %v", err)
	}

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	configz.InstallHandler(mux)
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	mux.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/configz", nil))
	if rec.Code != http.StatusOK {
		t.Fatalf("status=%d body=%s", rec.Code, rec.Body.String())
	}
	if !strings.Contains(rec.Body.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in /configz body:\n%s", rec.Body.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: /configz body contains %q", secret)
	t.Logf("body: %s", rec.Body.String())
}
GOEOF
go test ./cmd/kubelet/app -run TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader -count=1 -v
```

Expected: test **passes**, and the `body:` line shows
`"staticPodURLHeader":{"Authorization":["Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"]}` — the header value in cleartext. (Against a real node: `curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <kubelet-token>" https://<node>:10250/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.staticPodURLHeader'`.)

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials via an authenticated kubelet endpoint. It is a credentials/config exposure issue — any caller already trusted to read `/configz` (ops, monitoring, support) gains the manifest-auth credentials, which they were not meant to receive.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` (file source) are not affected.

title: kubelet logs --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys) to runtime logs
body:
When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext.

At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393
manifestURLHeader := make(http.Header)
if len(kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader) > 0 {
    for k, v := range kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader {
        for i := range v {
            manifestURLHeader.Add(k, v[i])          // values copied into a plain http.Header
        }
    }
}
...
if kubeCfg.StaticPodURL != "" {
    logger.Info("Adding pod URL with HTTP header", "URL", kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, "header", manifestURLHeader)  // <-- sink
    config.NewSourceURL(logger, kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, manifestURLHeader, ...)
}
```

The codebase already knows this field is secret and masks it elsewhere:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the *config-dump* path redacts it before logging the full `KubeletConfiguration` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:287-290` masks the map to `<masked>`). But `makePodSourceConfig` logs the **runtime `http.Header` copy**, not the config map — so neither the `datapolicy:"token"` tag nor the logging-mask applies, and the header values ship out verbatim. (`datapolicy` only fires on a strongly-typed field argument; here the value has been flattened into an `http.Header` passed as a generic `"header"` argument.)

`makePodSourceConfig` should not log the header values. The `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the `server.go:287-290` config-mask both express the intent that `StaticPodURLHeader` is secret; this code path bypasses both by logging a runtime copy. The sink should mask/drop the `header` field (e.g. log only that headers are present, or redact like the config-dump path does). Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet` that calls the real `makePodSourceConfig` with a custom `logr` sink capturing klog output, sets `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret`, and asserts the secret appears in the captured logs. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/zz_poc_staticpodheader_logleak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package kubelet

import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-logr/logr"
	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
	kubeletutil "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/util"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSink struct{ buf *bytes.Buffer }

func (s *pocSink) Init(logr.RuntimeInfo)          {}
func (s *pocSink) Enabled(int) bool               { return true }
func (s *pocSink) Info(_ int, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) Error(err error, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg, err}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) WithValues(kv ...interface{}) logr.LogSink { return s }
func (s *pocSink) WithName(string) logr.LogSink              { return s }

func TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	ctx := klog.NewContext(context.Background(), logr.New(&pocSink{buf: &logs}))

	const secret = "Bearer static-pod-url-secret"
	kubeCfg := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
		HTTPCheckFrequency:  metav1.Duration{Duration: time.Hour},
	}
	deps := &Dependencies{PodStartupLatencyTracker: kubeletutil.NewPodStartupLatencyTracker()}

	if _, err := makePodSourceConfig(ctx, kubeCfg, deps, "node-a", func() bool { return true }); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("makePodSourceConfig: %v", err)
	}
	if !strings.Contains(logs.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in logs:\n%s", logs.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs\n%s", logs.String())
}
GOEOF
( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet -run TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 | grep -E 'VULNERABLE|Adding pod URL|PASS|FAIL|ok ' )
```

Expected: printed lines show the secret in the kubelet log output, then `PASS`:

```text
VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs
    Adding pod URL with HTTP header URL http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml header map[Authorization:[Bearer static-pod-url-secret]]
--- PASS: TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak (0.00s)
ok  	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet
```

i.e. the `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret` value is logged verbatim by `Adding pod URL with HTTP header`.

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials to kubelet logs, at default verbosity. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_staticpodurlheader_log_leak`.
- Distinct from `kubelet_configz_staticpodurlheader_leak` (the `/configz` JSON path, different sink and code path) — both leak the same `StaticPodURLHeader` field but via different endpoints; both capitalize on the fact that `makePodSourceConfig`/`setConfigz` bypass the `datapolicy`/config-mask that `server.go:287-290` applies.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` are not affected.

title: Excessive "Label not found" V(4) logs for optional container annotations flood kubelet logs and cause rapid disk space consumption
body:
When kubelet runs with `--v=4` (a common debug level), the log is continuously flooded with lines like:

```plaintext
I0627 08:10:30.787761    9911 labels.go:293] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.pod.deletionGracePeriod"
I0627 08:10:30.787766    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.preStopHandler"
I0627 08:10:30.787771    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.ports"
...
I0627 09:00:34.694549    9911 labels.go:293] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.pod.deletionGracePeriod"
I0627 09:00:34.695552    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.preStopHandler"
I0627 09:00:34.695745    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.ports"
```

In a kubemark cluster, this was observed to run continuously and consume disk space rapidly, with approximately 220 pods (2 containers per pod) running on each node.

Logging "Label not found" for optional annotations at V(4) might be too verbose, since these labels are typically absent for many containers. It would be better to raise the log level so it doesn't appear during typical debug verbosity, or perhaps consider removing the line entirely.

1. Run kubelet with --v=4.
2. Schedule a high density of pods on the node (e.g., ~200 pods), whose containers have no preStop handler, no ports, and whose pod has no deletionGracePeriodSeconds (i.e. almost every pod).
3. Observe the three "Label not found" lines being emitted continuously during pod syncs, consuming disk space rapidly.

> Commit [ab839c93](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/ab839c93ff85072b2cc289a5826f61ff409b937a)

In `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/labels.go`, the "Label not found" logs are emitted by `getInt64PointerFromLabel` and `getJSONObjectFromLabel` whenever a label is absent.

These labels are only written conditionally in `newContainerAnnotations`:

`podDeletionGracePeriodLabel` — only if `pod.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds != nil`
`containerPreStopHandlerLabel` — only if `container.Lifecycle.PreStop != nil`
`containerPortsLabel` — only if `len(container.Ports) > 0`
Since these conditions are not met for most containers, the labels are expected to be missing. However, `getContainerInfoFromAnnotations` is called on every status lookup, triggering the log on the normal path.

title: kubelet HTTP probe logs probe `httpHeaders` (Authorization / Cookie / API keys) at -v=4
body:
When kubelet runs an HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probe, it logs probe parameters at verbosity `-v=4` — and the logged fields include the raw `HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` values taken directly from the PodSpec:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:160-173
case p.HTTPGet != nil:
    req, err := httpprobe.NewRequestForHTTPGetAction(p.HTTPGet, &container, status.PodIP, "probe")
    if err != nil {
        logger.V(4).Info("HTTP-Probe failed to create request", "error", err)
        return probe.Unknown, "", err
    }
    if loggerV4 := logger.V(4); logger.Enabled() {
        port := req.URL.Port()
        host := req.URL.Hostname()
        path := req.URL.Path
        scheme := req.URL.Scheme
        headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders              // <-- raw PodSpec headers
        loggerV4.Info("HTTP-Probe", "scheme", scheme, "host", host, "port", port,
            "path", path, "timeout", timeout, "headers", headers, "probeType", probeType)  // <-- sink
    }
    return pb.http.Probe(req, timeout)
```

`headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` is the user-supplied header list with **no redaction**, emitted into the `"headers"` structured field.

The kubelet prober should not log raw probe `httpHeaders`. The `"headers"` field should be dropped or redacted (e.g. log only header names, or omit the value) in the `HTTP-Probe` line at `prober.go:173` — matching how other secret-bearing probe fields are handled. As written, attacker/operator-supplied credential headers are emitted verbatim into verbose logs.

copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet/prober`, sets `-v=4`, builds an HTTP liveness probe with `Authorization: Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token`, calls the real `(*prober).runProbe`, and the fake HTTP prober returns `Success` — proving the leak happens **before** the request executes and does not require probe failure. Cleans up after itself; no cluster needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/prober/zz_poc_probe_header_leak_test.go"
SECRET="Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package prober

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"net/http"
	"testing"
	"time"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"
	kubecontainer "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/container"
	"k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/probe"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSuccessHTTPProber struct{}

func (pocSuccessHTTPProber) Probe(_ *http.Request, _ time.Duration) (probe.Result, string, error) {
	return probe.Success, "ok", nil // probe SUCCEEDS — leak is pre-request, not failure-only
}

func TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	if flag.CommandLine.Lookup("v") == nil {
		klog.InitFlags(nil)
	}
	if err := flag.Set("v", "4"); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	pb := &prober{http: pocSuccessHTTPProber{}}
	_, _, err := pb.runProbe(
		context.Background(),
		liveness,
		&v1.Probe{ProbeHandler: v1.ProbeHandler{HTTPGet: &v1.HTTPGetAction{
			Path: "/healthz",
			Port: intstr.FromInt32(8080),
			HTTPHeaders: []v1.HTTPHeader{
				{Name: "Authorization", Value: "Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"},
			},
		}}},
		&v1.Pod{},
		v1.PodStatus{PodIP: "127.0.0.1"},
		v1.Container{Name: "app"},
		kubecontainer.ContainerID{Type: "test", ID: "container"},
	)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	klog.Flush()
}
GOEOF
OUT="$( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet/prober -run TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 )"
printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep 'HTTP-Probe' || true
if printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep -F "$SECRET"; then
  echo "VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs"
else
  echo "NOT VULNERABLE: secret header not observed in logs" >&2; exit 1
fi
```

Expected: a `prober.go` `HTTP-Probe` log line containing the secret in the `headers` field, followed by the `VULNERABLE` confirmation:

```text
I0702 11:32:34.631974 2674209 prober.go:173] "HTTP-Probe" scheme="http" host="127.0.0.1" port="8080" path="/healthz" timeout="0s" headers=[{"name":"Authorization","value":"Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"}] probeType="Liveness"
VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs
```

- This is secret disclosure of probe-configured credentials to kubelet verbose logs. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_prober_http_probe_header_log_leak`.
- It is **distinct** from the recorded `kubelet_http_probe_header_log_leak` (sink `pkg/probe/http/http.go:119`, failure-only). This report's sink is `pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:173` (pre-request), so successful probes leak too. Both are already separately recorded in the knowledge base.
- Affects HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probes; requires kubelet `-v>=4`. `TCP`/`Exec`/`GRPC` probes do not carry `httpHeaders` at this sink.

title: Evaluate node stability risks and support hybrid workload Memory QoS in KEP 2570
body:
### Problem: KEP-2570 `memory.min` Introduces Node Stability Risks & Bin-Packing Regressions

The current Memory QoS (KEP-2570) implementation brings vital cgroups v2 protections, but enforcing `memory.min` as the default, one-size-fits-all solution for Guaranteed pods creates severe operational risks for mixed workloads.

Mapping memory requests to the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is structurally necessary to satisfy node-local agents (NRI plugins, telemetry daemons) without injecting synchronous HTTP calls to the `kube-apiserver` during pod startup. However, the chosen cgroup primitive (`memory.min` for Guaranteed) fundamentally breaks node elasticity.

#### 1. The `memory.min` Bin-Packing Problem

The KEP assumes all Guaranteed pods require strict, kernel-level memory locking. In reality, users often set requests equal to limits solely to prevent Kubelet eviction (e.g., for ML inference or periodic batch jobs). These workloads might allocate a large heap but sit idle for long periods. When mapped to `memory.min`, the kernel is legally forbidden from reclaiming their idle page cache. Locking unused memory behind a hard wall destroys the node's ability to safely maximize resource utilization and share capacity with neighboring pods.

#### 2. Behavioral Shifts and Starvation

Because the Kubelet applies this logic universally by default via `TieredReservation`, existing cluster behavior will change drastically. When Guaranteed pods hoard idle cache behind a node-wide `memory.min` wall, the node exhausts shareable memory much faster. During memory pressure, instead of gracefully and proportionally reclaiming page cache, the kernel hits a hard wall and is forced to immediately OOM-kill BestEffort and Burstable pods.

#### 3. Node-Level Enforcement Breaks Mixed Workloads

Relying exclusively on node-level configurations forces a single profile onto all workloads. Administrators cannot safely run a latency-sensitive database (requiring strict `memory.min` protection) alongside an elastic web application on the exact same machine. Applying `memory.high` globally means a large workload might be aggressively throttled well before it consumes its physical free capacity. This node-level rigidity defeats the purpose of high-density Kubernetes colocation.

---

### Proposed Solution: The Tiered Protection Architecture

We propose modifying the Memory QoS architecture to establish `memory.low` as the global default baseline, while allowing opt-in escalation for hard protections via node-level flags or per-pod APIs (DRA).

#### 1. The Baseline: Map All Requests to `memory.low` (Soft Protection)

Instead of forcing Guaranteed pods to `memory.min`, the Kubelet should map all pod memory requests (Guaranteed and Burstable) to `memory.low` by default.

* **Maximum Elasticity & Bin-Packing:** This protects memory during normal operations, but during a catastrophic node-level emergency, the kernel retains the flexibility to reclaim idle cache rather than hitting a hard boundary that triggers artificial OOM kills.
* **Industry Validation:** This matches the `fbtax2` architecture utilized at scale by Meta, which explicitly favors `memory.low` because it is "work-conserving" and safely handles system memory overcommit without thrashing.
* **CRI Visibility:** Mapping to `memory.low` successfully populates the CRI payload, satisfying local node agents instantly without API server queries.

**Action Item:** Expand `memoryReservationPolicy` to include a `SoftReservation` mode (or update the default behavior of `TieredReservation`) where all requests are mapped to `memory.low`.

#### 2. Node-Level Hard Protection (Explicit Opt-In)

For specialized, dedicated hardware pools (e.g., dedicated database nodes), administrators should be able to explicitly toggle `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation` to universally map Guaranteed workloads to `memory.min`.

* **Action Item:** Ensure that even when `memory.min` is enforced, the Kubelet redundantly populates `memory.low` with the same value in the CRI payload so node daemons retain a uniform schema regardless of the enforcement mechanism.

#### 3. Long-Term Vision: Per-Pod Memory QoS via DRA

Because Kubelet-level enforcement is too blunt for hybrid clusters, fine-grained hard memory locks (`memory.min`) and custom proactive throttling thresholds (`memory.high`) should be managed via **Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)**.

* **Industry Validation:** Organizations like Alibaba Cloud already recognize the upstream limits of KEP-2570, resorting to external Koordinator agents and custom annotations to inject per-pod Memory QoS policies.
* **Action Item:** Transition application cgroup routing out of Kubelet defaults. The Kubelet should focus on protecting the node (`kube-reserved`), while users request strict memory isolation via DRA `ResourceClaims` that instruct the container runtime to append `memory.min` or `memory.high` on a per-pod basis.

---

### Discussion Request for SIG-Node (July 7, 2026)

We would love to get SIG-Node's feedback on:

1. Shifting the baseline cgroups v2 mapping strategy from `memory.min` to `memory.low` for Guaranteed & Burstable workloads to prevent aggressive OOM starvation.
2. The viability of expanding `memoryReservationPolicy` to give administrators explicit `SoftReservation` / `HardReservation` choices in the upcoming beta cycles.
3. The long-term roadmap for offloading specialized, per-pod Memory QoS configurations (like hard locking and custom throttling factors) to Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA).

title: Kubelet allocates system-reserved CPU to pod when cpu-topology is hybrid
body:
Following CPU topology (hybrid i.e. cores with id `0-28` are hyper-threaded and `32-43` are single-threaded) was given.
```
Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700
CPU(s):                28
On-line CPU(s) list:   0-27
Core(s) per socket:    20
Socket(s):             1
NUMA node(s):          1
```

For pod with 2 guaranteed CPUs, kubelet allocated `0-1` cpuset, despite `0` was explicitly reserved for system purposes. Kubelet was launched with following flags: `--kubelet-flags="--cpu-manager-policy=static --reserved-cpus=0`. 

Here are some kubelet logs:
```
I0710 16:32:08.192397  353056 policy_static.go:185] "Reserved CPUs not available for exclusive assignment" reservedSize=1 reserved="0" reservedPhysicalCPUs="0-1"
...
I0710 16:32:45.032352  353056 policy_static.go:556] "Allocate start" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1"
I0710 16:32:45.032419  353056 policy_static.go:675] "AllocateCPUs" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1" numCPUs=2 socket=null
I0710 16:32:45.035206  353056 policy_static.go:708] "AllocateCPUs" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1" result="0-1 aligned=<uncore:true>"
I0710 16:32:45.037033  353056 policy_static.go:621] "Allocate end" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1"
```

Then, kubelet was **restarted**, but it can't boot again due to invalid state:
```
I0713 16:37:04.270175  593834 state_mem.go:143] "Updated default CPUSet" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint.CPUManager state memory" cpuSet="2-27"
I0713 16:37:04.270195  593834 state_mem.go:161] "Updated CPUSet assignments" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint.CPUManager state memory" assignments="{\"35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb\":{\"testcnt1\":\"0-1\"}}"
I0713 15:37:04.270215  593834 state_checkpoint.go:182] "restored state from checkpoint" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint"
I0713 16:37:04.270227  593834 state_checkpoint.go:183] "defaultCPUSet" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint" defaultCpuSet="2-27"
E0713 16:37:04.270257  593834 policy_static.go:303] "invalid state, please drain node and remove policy state file" err="not all reserved cpus: \"0\" are present in defaultCpuSet: \"2-27\""
E0713 16:37:04.270266  593834 cpu_manager.go:263] "Policy start error" err="not all reserved cpus: \"0\" are present in defaultCpuSet: \"2-27\""
E0713 16:37:04.270277  593834 kubelet.go:1837] "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="start cpu manager error: not all reserved cpus: \"0\" are present in defaultCpuSet: \"2-27\""
```

Kubelet allocates 2 CPUs that do not interfere with reserved CPUs. After restart kubelet starts smoothly.

1. Start local cluster using `hack/local-up-cluster.sh` script with proper flags set.
```console
CPUMANAGER_POLICY="static" KUBELET_FLAGS="--reserved-cpus=0" hack/local-up-cluster.sh
```
2. Deploy the pod with guaranteed CPU resources
```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: '2'
    memory: "2Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: '2'
    memory: "2Gi"
```
3. Kill the cluster and try to start it again.

title: CPUManager distribute-cpus-across-cores relies on CPU numbering order instead of topology
body:
The `distribute-cpus-across-cores` CPU manager policy option (KEP-4176, alpha since v1.31) does not correctly spread CPUs across physical cores on systems where sibling thread CPU IDs are contiguous (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3).

The spread algorithm in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` sorts CPUs numerically within each socket:

```go
func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int {
    var result []int
    for _, socket := range a.sortAvailableSockets() {
        cpus := a.details.CPUsInSockets(socket).UnsortedList()
        sort.Ints(cpus)
        result = append(result, cpus...)
    }
    return result
}
```

This assumes that numerically-sorted CPU IDs naturally interleave across physical cores. That assumption holds on systems where the BIOS/firmware enumerates all first threads before second threads (e.g., core 0 thread 0 = CPU 0, core 1 thread 0 = CPU 1, ..., core 0 thread 1 = CPU 8, core 1 thread 1 = CPU 9), but fails when sibling threads have contiguous IDs (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3).

With contiguous siblings, `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` produces the same CPU order as `sortAvailableCPUsPacked()`, and the spreading has no effect — both allocate sibling threads together.

## How to reproduce

On any system with contiguous sibling CPU IDs (common in VMs/QEMU, and some bare-metal configurations):

```
$ lscpu | grep Thread
Thread(s) per core:  2

$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/topology/thread_siblings_list
0-1
$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu2/topology/thread_siblings_list
2-3
```

Enable the CPU manager with `distribute-cpus-across-cores`:
```
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--feature-gates=CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions=true
--cpu-manager-policy-options=distribute-cpus-across-cores=true
```

Create a Guaranteed pod requesting 4 CPUs. The allocated cpuset will be contiguous (e.g., `1-4`), hitting only 2-3 physical cores instead of spreading across 4 separate cores.

The kubelet logs confirm the option is active:
```
"created with configuration" options={"DistributeCPUsAcrossCores":true,...} cpuGroupSize=2
```

## Expected behavior

Requesting 4 CPUs on a system with 8 cores × 2 threads should allocate 1 thread from each of 4 different physical cores (e.g., CPUs 0, 2, 4, 6), regardless of whether sibling IDs are contiguous or non-contiguous.

## Root cause

The algorithm uses `sort.Ints()` on CPU IDs as a proxy for topology-aware spreading. It should instead use the core topology information already available in `cpuAccumulator.details` to explicitly round-robin across cores:

```go
func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int {
    var result []int
    coresCPUs := make(map[int][]int)
    maxThreads := 0
    for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() {
        cpus := a.details.CPUsInCores(core).SortedList()
        coresCPUs[core] = cpus
        if len(cpus) > maxThreads {
            maxThreads = len(cpus)
        }
    }
    // Round-robin: pick thread 0 from all cores, then thread 1, etc.
    for t := 0; t < maxThreads; t++ {
        for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() {
            if t < len(coresCPUs[core]) {
                result = append(result, coresCPUs[core][t])
            }
        }
    }
    return result
}
```

This approach works regardless of CPU numbering because it explicitly iterates cores and picks one thread per core before doubling up.

## Additional context

- The KEP-4176 example topology assumes non-contiguous siblings (CPUs 0 and 6 as siblings), which is common on many server BIOSes that enumerate all thread-0 CPUs before thread-1 CPUs, but is not guaranteed.
- QEMU/KVM always produces contiguous sibling IDs (thread ID in lowest APIC bits), making this feature untestable in virtual environments.
- The Linux kernel topology documentation notes the "alternative enumeration" (non-contiguous siblings) depends on BIOS MADT ordering and explicitly states "we do not trust BIOSes to enumerate packages in a consistent way."
- Tested on Kubernetes v1.35.6 with `DistributeCPUsAcrossCores: true` confirmed in kubelet logs.

title: `TestVolumeAttachLimitExceededCleanup` flakes on Windows CI with `context deadline exceeded`
body:
pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

TestVolumeAttachLimitExceededCleanup

Since commit `954ac21c6c8b2bc77666373d5c4f5b68603a8e50` (2025-09-03), which introduced the test in PR #133357.

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140657/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2079304403352817664

The test creates 500 pods and expects all of them to reach `PodFailed` state within a 30-second timeout. On Windows CI this is insufficient due to:

1. **Mutex contention** — `FakeRuntime.GetPod` and `FakeRuntime.GetPodStatus` are called via `fakeCache.GetNewerThan` for each pod, each acquiring the `FakeRuntime` mutex. With 500 pods this results in ~1000 serialized lock acquisitions.
2. **Status manager contention** — `SetPodStatus` is called twice per pod (once for `PodPending`, once for `PodFailed`), each acquiring the `statusManager` mutex (~1000 acquisitions).
3. **Disk I/O** — `makePodDataDirs` performs 3 `os.MkdirAll` calls per pod (1500 total mkdir operations), which is slower on Windows CI.

The 30s timeout is exceeded before all 500 pods can be processed through the `podWorkerLoop` → `SyncPod` → `rejectPod` → `SetPodStatus(PodFailed)` pipeline.

title: [Failing Test] Windows e2e node CPUManager specs failing since 2026-07-17 (windows-e2e-node-master)
body:
- `ci-kubernetes-e2enode-windows-master` (every run since 2026-07-17T23:50 UTC; last green 2026-07-17T15:49 UTC)
- `pull-kubernetes-e2enode-windows` (every PR run since 2026-07-19, regardless of PR content)

All 12 `[sig-windows] [Feature:CPUManager] [Feature:Windows]` specs in `test/e2e_node_windows`, e.g.:

- `should not set CPU affinity on a burstable container` — fails with `burstable container must not receive exclusive CPU affinity: got 0 CPUs (host has 8)`
- `should set CPU affinity with exactly 1 CPU for a single-container pod` (and the 2/3-CPU, multi-container, init-container, and strict-cpu-reservation variants) — all `Timed out after 30.000s` waiting for affinity to appear.

`getWindowsContainerCPUAffinity` reads `ContainerStatus().Status.Resources.Windows.AffinityCpus` via CRI and gets an empty set for every container, i.e. the kubelet is no longer applying any Windows CPU group affinity (`WindowsCPUAndMemoryAffinity` / static CPU manager path via `PreCreateContainer` → `AffinityCpus`).

Because the failing specs each burn 30–77s and the suite is run as plain `go test` (10m default timeout), cmd/go kills the process (`*** Test killed: ran too long (11m0s)`), so junit/ginkgo reports are lost and the job surface just shows a timeout. Fix for that masking: kubernetes-sigs/windows-testing PR adding an explicit `--timeout`.

Onset between periodic runs 2078145122851098624 (green, started 2026-07-17T15:49:43Z) and 2078266162692493312 (first red, started 2026-07-17T23:50:41Z).

### Reason for failure (regression window analysis)

kubernetes/kubernetes merges in the window (green clone ~16:04 UTC → red clone ~23:55 UTC):

- #140682 (job controller dead-code removal), #140667 (scheduler unit test), #140150 (docs), #138833 / #138831 (kube-proxy ipvs/ipset prealloc, linux-only), #140497 (coredns manifest bump)

None touch kubelet, CRI, winstats, or the Windows tests → the k/k commit window is effectively empty.

Everything else pinned/unchanged across the boundary:

- kubernetes-sigs/windows-testing: no commits since 2026-07-09
- containerd: pinned 1.7.16
- Go on the VM: 1.26.4 on both sides of the boundary
- test images (busybox 1.37.0-2, pause 3.8): pinned digests

The one moving part is the Azure VM image: `MicrosoftWindowsServer:WindowsServer:2022-datacenter-core-smalldisk-g2:latest`. The first red run's node reports `KernelVersion: 10.0.20348.5386` (July 2026 WS2022 cumulative update; July Patch Tuesday was 2026-07-14, and marketplace image rollout lands ~that week). Green runs never dump Node Info so the prior build isn't in the logs, but the timing matches the image rollout window exactly.

Working hypothesis: the WS2022 July 2026 CU (OS build 20348.5386) changes behavior under the kubelet's Windows CPU affinity path — either winstats CPU topology discovery (`GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx`) returning something the CPU manager can't use, or HCS/job-object group affinity application/reporting — so no `AffinityCpus` ever reach the container.

### Suggested next steps

1. Repro on an Azure VM with the current image; collect kubelet.log (job currently only scps `c:/Logs/*.xml`).
2. Pin the job image to the previous exact version (`az vm image list --all` for the sku, use `:<previous-version>` instead of `:latest`) to confirm/unblock CI.
3. Compare winstats topology output between 20348 builds.

title: EvictionRequest: fix first sync race
body:
As mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137050#discussion_r3615804000 by @jpbetz, we should fix a race where a different controller can race the main controller to do illegal state initialization during the first sync.

> I think the first sync can bypass the anti-spoofing machinery. This gate only applies when oldStatus != nil, and none of the time checks below require state == Active, so the initializing write can pre-populate startTime and completionTime on Inactive entries too. With completionTime already set, the heartbeat deadline check is skipped on each later flip, so a single actor with status write can walk the whole responder chain to Completed in seconds without any responder acting, then set the final conditions.

Should the first sync require non-Active entries to be name and priority only instead of setting the whole struct? A test would be valuable.

title: Memory Manager pod scope drops hugepage requests used only by regular init containers
body:
With the static Memory Manager and pod-level Topology Manager scope, `getPodRequestedResources` drops a memory resource type when that resource is requested by a regular init container but by no app container.
﻿
A minimal example is:
﻿
- a regular init container requests `memory: 1Gi` and `hugepages-1Gi: 2Gi`;
- the app container requests `memory: 1Gi`, but does not request `hugepages-1Gi`.
﻿
The calculated pod request is:
﻿
```text
map[memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The expected result is:
﻿
```text
map[hugepages-1Gi:2147483648 memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The init container still receives an individual hugepage memory block because its resources are processed separately, but the pod allocation and global NUMA capacity do not account for that block. This can produce incorrect topology hints and leave the Memory Manager machine state with more available hugepage capacity than actually assigned.

getPodRequestedResources` should calculate each managed resource independently across the union of resource names requested by:
﻿
- app containers;
- restartable init containers;
- regular init containers.
﻿
For every resource name, the existing init-container and long-running-container maximum semantics should then be applied. A resource must not be omitted merely because no app container requests that resource type.
﻿
In the example above, both `memory` and `hugepages-1Gi` must be included in topology hint generation, pod memory blocks, and NUMA machine-state accounting.

Add the following case to `Test_getPodRequestedResources` in `pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager/policy_static_test.go`:

`{
	description: "resource requested only by a regular init container",
	pod: getPodWithInitContainers(
		"",
		[]v1.Container{
			{
				Name: "app-container",
				Resources: v1.ResourceRequirements{
					Requests: v1.ResourceList{
						v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("1Gi"),
					},
				},
			},
		},
		[]v1.Container{
			{
				Name: "init-container",
				Resources: v1.ResourceRequirements{
					Requests: v1.ResourceList{
						v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("1Gi"),
						hugepages1Gi:      resource.MustParse("2Gi"),
					},
				},
			},
		},
	),
	expected: map[v1.ResourceName]uint64{
		v1.ResourceMemory: 1 * gb,
		hugepages1Gi:      2 * gb,
	},
},
`

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager -run Test_getPodRequestedResources -count=1

title: Memory Manager AllocatePod re-applies restored pod allocations after kubelet restart
body:
With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, the static Memory Manager restores pod-level assignments from its checkpoint when kubelet starts. The existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod` with `AddOperation`.
﻿
`AllocatePod` does not check whether the Pod already has a restored allocation. It calculates the request again and applies it to a machine state which already includes that Pod's reservation.
﻿
Depending on the remaining capacity, this can:
﻿
- reject an existing Pod during post-restart admission because its own allocation is no longer considered free;
- extend or change the previously selected NUMA affinity;
- reserve the same memory a second time, reducing `Free` and increasing `Reserved` and `NumberOfAssignments` again.
﻿
The Pod and container block entries are overwritten, but the additional machine-state accounting remains and is checkpointed.
﻿
﻿

Pod-level Memory Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

When a complete allocation for the Pod has been restored from the checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the existing pod allocation, container assignments, NUMA affinity, and machine state. It should not consume capacity again or reject the Pod because of its own reservation.

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestMemoryManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static Memory Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory requests and limits and one container.
4. Start Memory Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Save the pod blocks, container blocks, and machine state.
6. Recreate Memory Manager with the same checkpoint directory to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Start the new manager and verify that the state was restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod` again with `AddOperation`, as post-restart admission does.
9. Verify that the call succeeds and all restored state remains unchanged.

With the current implementation, step 8 either accounts the Pod again or fails when there is not enough unreserved capacity to satisfy the same request a second time.

Using a single-container Pod keeps this reproducer separate from pod-scope hint regeneration behavior for multi-container Pods.

title: Ensure Credential Pulled Images tests still flaking with "pulled record ... never appeared" after #138527/#138642 (kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial)
body:
Title
Ensure Credential Pulled Images tests still flaking with "pulled record ... never appeared" after 
#138527/
#138642

Body

Hitting this on kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial - pretty sure this is the same flake as 
#136546/
#138527, just came back.

Testgrid: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-kubelet#kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial

A few sub-tests under Ensure Credential Pulled Images ... [FeatureGate:KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages] are failing, all through the same shared BeforeEach helper (tempRemoveImagePulledRecord in test/e2e_node/util_kubeletconfig.go):

util_kubeletconfig.go:133] Unexpected error: the file with the pulled record for the image ID never appeared:
<context.deadlineExceededError>: context deadline exceeded
Quick rundown of what that helper does: it polls every 1s for up to 5s waiting for kubelet to write an ImagePulledRecord at /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-<hash>, then moves it aside so a later step can check kubelet's behavior when the record's missing. If nothing shows up in 5s, it just fails.

#138527 got closed by 
#138642, but looking at that PR, it only added debug logging to this wait loop - didn't touch the 5s timeout or actually figure out why the record's sometimes missing. So this was never really fixed, just made easier to see happening.

And that's actually how I found something new - the extra logging from 
#138642 caught this in a recent run (2026-07-25, ~12:40 UTC) that wasn't visible back when 
#138527 was filed:

util_kubeletconfig.go:116] failed to stat file ".../pulled/sha256-c0a25c4ccec43320c35febdf68a46e03b3f9323eada881535d78d91aa9962741": ... no such file or directory
util_kubeletconfig.go:128] contents of "/var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled": map[
  .../pulled/sha256-fbeb66043fabeed6f125049e44aef32e0b8f9e657a240b5a2091b292bab530f2:
    {"kind":"ImagePulledRecord", ..., "lastUpdatedTime":"2026-07-25T14:26:20Z", ...}
]
So at the moment it fails, the pulled/ directory isn't actually empty - there's a record in there, just for a different image, written ~23 minutes earlier by (presumably) an earlier sub-test in the same run. The record this specific check is waiting for just never shows up in the 5s window.

That makes me think this isn't pure slowness - more likely kubelet just doesn't write a new ImagePulledRecord at all when the image's already cached from an earlier sub-test in the same run, and the poll is timing out waiting for something that was never coming. Would be good to get sig-node's take on whether that's expected - if so, the fix is probably on the test's assumptions, not the timeout.

Checked the last 10 Testgrid columns for this job (~07-24 to 07-26) - failed 3/10 times, 6/20 over a longer window, so it's a real recurring thing, not a one-off. One specific run if useful: prow job 2080994746846679040 (2026-07-25, ~12:40-14:49 UTC), 2 sub-tests failed with this exact error.

#136546, 
#138527, 
#138642

title: kubelet: stopping a probe worker does not cancel an in-flight exec probe
body:
Stopping a probe worker does not cancel a probe that is already executing. `worker.stop()` does a non-blocking send on `stopCh`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L204-L211

and `run()` only selects on `stopCh` between probes, after `doProbe` returns:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L186-L201

So when `RemovePod` / `CleanupPods` / `StopLivenessAndStartup` stops a worker, an exec probe that is mid-flight keeps running against a container that is being killed. It ends only when its own `TimeoutSeconds` elapses, and `runProbeWithRetries` will retry up to `maxProbeRetries` (3) if the attempt errors, so the worst case is roughly `3 * TimeoutSeconds` after `stop()`. `TimeoutSeconds` is user-controlled, so that can be minutes. The worker also records the result of that last probe after it was told to stop.

Between #130487 (v1.35.0) and #140882 this happened to be papered over: workers inherited the pod worker's sync context, which the pod worker cancels at teardown, so in-flight execs died promptly. That was not a fix, it was the cause of #140881. The same cancellation also killed every readiness probe for the entire grace period, which is the much worse bug. #140882 detaches the worker context with `context.WithoutCancel` and restores the pre-1.35 behavior, which reinstates this gap.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659050743.

`stop()` cancels the probe that is currently executing, and the worker goroutine exits promptly instead of waiting out `TimeoutSeconds`.

Pod with an exec readiness probe whose command blocks (`sleep 300`) and `timeoutSeconds: 60`, plus `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1`. Delete the pod while a probe is in flight and watch `--v=4` kubelet logs: the `Exec-Probe runProbe` for that worker has no matching completion until the timeout fires, well after the container is gone.

Suggested fix: give each worker its own context derived from the (detached) manager context and cancel it from `stop()`, roughly:

1. In `newWorker`, `w.ctx, w.cancel = context.WithCancel(ctx)`.
2. `run()` uses `w.ctx` for `doProbe` and adds `<-w.ctx.Done()` to the select.
3. `stop()` calls `w.cancel()` in addition to signalling `stopCh`, so an in-flight `ExecSync` is cancelled.

That keeps the worker lifecycle owned by the prober manager instead of the pod worker, which is what #140882 is after, while still bounding shutdown.

Worth checking as part of this whether cancelling mid-probe can record a spurious result. `doProbe` throws away errored results today, which is what made #140881 invisible, so a cancelled probe should not flip readiness either way. A test for "stop() during an in-flight probe records no result" would be good to have alongside.

title: No e2e coverage for readiness probes during graceful pod termination
body:
#140881 was a total loss of exec readiness probing during the entire graceful termination window, shipped in v1.35.0 and caught by a user, not by CI. Nothing in the e2e suite asserts anything about probes after a pod's `deletionTimestamp` is set.

`test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go` covers startup, ordering, timeouts, restart counts, and readiness before delete, but every readiness assertion happens while the pod is running normally. `test/e2e/node/pod_termination*.go` and the graceful-shutdown tests cover termination but assert on lifecycle, not readiness. So the probe path and the termination path are each well covered and the intersection is not covered at all.

The unit regression test added in #140882 (`TestProbeWorkersSurviveSyncContextCancellation`) pins the specific context plumbing, but it fakes the pod worker's cancellation. It would not catch a different regression that breaks probing during termination somewhere else in the stack, e.g. in `pod_workers.go` or in the CRI call path.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659065740, per @SergeyKanzhelev's request to keep the e2e work out of the backport-able patch.

An e2e test that deletes a pod whose readiness probe starts failing on SIGTERM and asserts the pod's `Ready` condition flips to `False` well before the grace period ends.

N/A, this is a coverage gap. To confirm it: revert #140882 on master and run `test/e2e/common/node` plus the node e2e probe suites. Everything passes.

Sketch of the test, matching the manual repro in #140881:

- busybox container that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps `TERM` with `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, then idles.
- exec readiness probe `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
- Wait for `Ready=True`, delete the pod, then assert `Ready=False` within ~10s, with the pod still in `Terminating`.

Two traps worth writing into the test as comments so the next person does not re-learn them:

1. Assert on the pod's `Ready` condition, not on EndpointSlice membership. The `deletionTimestamp` withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug completely.
2. The grace period has to be long enough that the container is still alive when the assertion runs, otherwise the test passes for the wrong reason.

Coverage worth adding beyond the base case, in rough priority order:

1. exec readiness probe during termination (the actual regression).
2. HTTP readiness probe during termination. Not affected by #140881 because the HTTP prober does not take the probe context, but it is the same contract and nothing pins it.
3. Readiness recorded during termination is reflected in the pod status, so a preStop hook that intentionally fails readiness behaves as documented.

Home is probably `test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go`. It should not be a `ConformanceIt` initially, since it asserts kubelet timing behavior rather than an API guarantee, but it is a reasonable promotion candidate later.

Happy to take this one. PR to follow once #140882 merges, so the test lands against the fixed behavior rather than a known-red baseline.
