title: CPU Manager AllocatePod re-allocates restored pod CPUs after kubelet restart
body:
With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, static CPU Manager is not idempotent across kubelet restart.

After restart, pod-level CPU assignments are restored from the checkpoint. Existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod(AddOperation)`. In `allocatePodForAdd`, the pod-scope path does not check whether a complete pod-level allocation was already restored. It allocates again from the default CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment.

This causes two deterministic failure modes:

- If the remaining default CPU set cannot satisfy the same request again, kubelet rejects an existing Pod after restart.
- If enough CPUs remain, CPU Manager assigns a second CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment, while the original CPUs stay removed from the default set, effectively leaking exclusive CPUs.

Examples with 1 reserved CPU and a Pod requesting 2 CPUs:

```text
4 CPUs:
restored pod cpuset:     1-2
restored default cpuset: 0,3
readmission error:       not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1

6 CPUs:
pod cpuset:              1-2 -> 3-4
default cpuset:          0,3-5 -> 0,5
readmission error:       <nil>
```

The current path is here: [`allocatePodForAdd`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L397-L440). It calls `allocateCPUs` and `SetPodCPUSet` without consulting the restored pod allocation.

Pod-level CPU Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

If a complete pod-level allocation was restored from checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the restored pod CPU set, container assignments, and default CPU set. It should not allocate a second CPU set or reject the existing Pod because of its own restored reservation.

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestCPUManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static CPU Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager, 1 reserved CPU, and either 4 or 6 single-threaded CPUs.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level request/limit of 2 CPUs and 1 container.
4. Start CPU Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Add the container so the pod/container assignments are checkpointed.
6. Recreate CPU Manager with the same checkpoint dir to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Verify the pod CPU set, container assignment, and default CPU set were restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod(AddOperation)` again.
9. Verify the restored state is unchanged.

Observed results:

- On 4 CPUs: `not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1`
- On 6 CPUs: the restored pod CPU set changes from `1-2` to `3-4`, and the default CPU set changes from `0,3-5` to `0,5`

This is the CPU Manager counterpart of #140906.

This is separate from #129078 / #129079. Those concern the older container-level `full-pcpus-only` SMT validation path. This reproducer does not enable `full-pcpus-only`; it exercises the pod-level allocation path introduced by #134768.

`PodLevelResourceManagers` was promoted to Beta and enabled by default for Kubernetes 1.37 in #140573.

`master` commit `5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35`

title: Memory Manager pod-scope restore compares container blocks with the pod request
body:
With pod-scope Topology Manager, after a kubelet restart, Memory Manager finds a restored container allocation and calls `regenerateHints` with that container's blocks and the whole Pod memory request.

For a multi-container Pod, those values differ, so `regenerateHints` returns no hint instead of restoring the Pod's previous NUMA hint. This can cause an existing Pod to fail admission under `restricted` or `single-numa-node`.

Pod-scope hint restoration should use the restored pod-level allocation and preserve the previous NUMA hint.

### How can we reproduce it?

Use a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory resources and two containers, allocate it with static Memory Manager, restart from the checkpoint, then call `GetPodTopologyHints`. The current code returns no regenerated hint because it compares one container's blocks with the Pod request.

title: Liveness probe failure container restart leads to container starting up with started=true and liveness probes starting before startup probes have run
body:
The full details of the repro can be seen in the Bash script below, but roughly:

1. Start a container with startup and liveness probe.
2. Wait for both to succeed. All normal so far.
3. Flip liveness probe to fail.
4. Container restarts.
5. New container sees liveness probe before startup probe.

I would expect the new container to first need to pass its startup probes before liveness probes begin, as per the docs here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/#startup-probe.

Reproduction bash script:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

CLUSTER="probe-repro-$$"
K3S_IMAGE="rancher/k3s:v1.36.2-k3s1"
KIND_IMAGE="kindest/node:v1.36.1@sha256:3489c7674813ba5d8b1a9977baea8a6e553784dab7b84759d1014dbd78f7ebd5"
MINIKUBE_KUBERNETES_VERSION="v1.36.2"
POD="probe-repro"
ENVIRONMENT="k3s"
KIND_KUBECONFIG=""

usage() {
  echo "usage: $0 [--k3s | --minikube | --kind]" >&2
}

if (($# > 1)); then
  usage
  exit 2
fi

case "${1:---k3s}" in
  --k3s) ENVIRONMENT="k3s" ;;
  --minikube) ENVIRONMENT="minikube" ;;
  --kind) ENVIRONMENT="kind" ;;
  --help)
    usage
    exit
    ;;
  *)
    usage
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

if [[ "$ENVIRONMENT" == "kind" ]]; then
  KIND_KUBECONFIG=$(mktemp)
fi

cleanup() {
  case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
    k3s) docker rm --force "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
    minikube) minikube delete --profile "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
    kind) kind delete cluster --name "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
  esac
  if [[ -n "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" ]]; then
    rm -f "$KIND_KUBECONFIG"
  fi
}
trap cleanup EXIT

k() {
  case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
    k3s) docker exec --interactive "$CLUSTER" /bin/kubectl "$@" ;;
    minikube) minikube --profile "$CLUSTER" kubectl -- --context="$CLUSTER" "$@" ;;
    kind) kubectl --kubeconfig "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" "$@" ;;
  esac
}

c() {
  k exec "$POD" -- "$@"
}

echo "Booting $ENVIRONMENT..."

case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
  k3s)
    command -v docker >/dev/null
    docker run --detach --privileged --name "$CLUSTER" "$K3S_IMAGE" \
      server --disable=traefik --disable=servicelb >/dev/null
    ;;
  minikube)
    command -v minikube >/dev/null
    minikube start \
      --profile "$CLUSTER" \
      --driver=docker \
      --container-runtime=containerd \
      --kubernetes-version="$MINIKUBE_KUBERNETES_VERSION" \
      --keep-context
    ;;
  kind)
    command -v kind >/dev/null
    command -v kubectl >/dev/null
    kind create cluster \
      --name "$CLUSTER" \
      --image "$KIND_IMAGE" \
      --kubeconfig "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" \
      --wait 120s
    ;;
esac

until k get serviceaccount default >/dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 0.2
done

echo "Applying manifest..."

k apply -f - >/dev/null <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: probe-repro
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 2
  volumes:
    - name: state
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: [sh, -c]
      args:
        - |
          instance=initial
          if test -f /state/container-seen; then
            instance=replacement
          else
            touch /state/container-seen
          fi
          echo "$instance" > /state/instance
          printf '%s  %-11s  container started\n' \
            "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" >> /state/events
          on_term() {
            printf '%s  %-11s  received SIGTERM\n' \
              "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" >> /state/events
            exit 0
          }
          trap on_term TERM
          sleep 3600 &
          wait $!
      volumeMounts:
        - name: state
          mountPath: /state
      startupProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              instance=$(cat /state/instance)
              result=failure
              test "$instance" = initial && result=success
              printf '%s  %-11s  startup probe: %s\n' \
                "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" "$result" >> /state/events
              test "$result" = success
        periodSeconds: 1
        failureThreshold: 100
      livenessProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              instance=$(cat /state/instance)
              result=success
              if test "$instance" = initial && test -f /state/fail-liveness; then
                result=failure
              fi
              printf '%s  %-11s  liveness probe: %s\n' \
                "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" "$result" >> /state/events
              test "$result" = success
        periodSeconds: 1
        failureThreshold: 1
EOF

k wait "pod/$POD" \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'=true \
  --timeout=120s >/dev/null

FIRST_ID=$(k get pod "$POD" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID}')

echo "First container ID: $FIRST_ID"
echo "Waiting 2 seconds to allow some probe successes..."

sleep 2

echo "Failing liveness probe..."
c touch /state/fail-liveness

echo "Waiting for container to restart..."

SECOND_ID="$FIRST_ID"
for _ in {1..600}; do
  SECOND_ID=$(k get pod "$POD" \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID}')
  [[ -n "$SECOND_ID" && "$SECOND_ID" != "$FIRST_ID" ]] && break
  sleep 0.1
done

[[ "$SECOND_ID" != "$FIRST_ID" ]]

echo "Second container ID: $SECOND_ID"

STARTED=$(k get pod "$POD" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}')
c sh -c \
  'printf "%s  %-11s  Kubernetes status started=%s\n" "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" replacement "$1" >> /state/events' \
  sh "$STARTED"

echo "Waiting 3 seconds for some probes to happen..."

sleep 3

echo "Event log:"

c cat /state/events
```

title: CPU Manager strict reservation can leave an empty default CPUSet
body:
With the static CPU Manager policy and `strict-cpu-reservation`, exclusive allocations can consume every non-reserved CPU and leave `defaultCPUSet` empty.

KEP-4540 discusses shared workloads starving when the shared pool reaches zero. The current implementation has different side effects:

- reconcile skips shared containers when their resolved CPUSet is empty, so an existing container can keep its previous affinity and overlap newly exclusive CPUs;
- a new shared container gets no `CpusetCpus` value because `PreCreateContainer` treats the empty set as unset;
- after a kubelet restart, CPU Manager rejects a checkpoint that has assignments and an empty default CPUSet with `default cpuset cannot be empty`.

The allocator removes assigned CPUs from the default set without checking whether the result is empty:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L727-L729

The empty-set handling is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go#L511-L519
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/internal_container_lifecycle_linux.go#L31-L36
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L215-L223

An empty shared pool should have defined behavior that does not silently drop CPU affinity, overlap exclusive CPUs, or prevent kubelet from restarting.

The fix might reject the final exclusive allocation, reject configurations that can produce an empty shared pool, or use another policy. This issue does not assume which behavior is preferred.

On a four-CPU Linux node, configure the static policy with CPU 0 reserved:

```yaml
cpuManagerPolicy: static
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  strict-cpu-reservation: "true"
reservedSystemCPUs: "0"
systemReserved:
  cpu: "1"
```

1. Remove the old CPU Manager state and start kubelet. The initial default CPUSet is `1-3`.
2. Start a BestEffort Pod so it uses the shared pool.
3. Start a Guaranteed Pod whose CPU and memory requests equal its limits and whose CPU request is `3`.
4. Check `/var/lib/kubelet/cpu_manager_state`. The Guaranteed Pod owns CPUs `1-3` and `defaultCpuSet` is empty.
5. Wait for reconciliation. The BestEffort container cannot be updated to an empty CPUSet and may keep its previous `1-3` affinity.
6. Restart kubelet. CPU Manager state validation fails with `default cpuset cannot be empty`.

A BestEffort Pod created after step 4 also receives no explicit `CpusetCpus` from CPU Manager.

KEP-4540 intentionally archived minimum-shared-CPU proposals and added a shared-pool-size metric:
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4540-strict-cpu-reservation

The KEP describes starvation as the zero-pool outcome. It does not describe dropping cpuset enforcement or rejecting the checkpoint after restart.

Related work:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127483
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127506
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134388

`master` at `ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674`

Not cloud-provider specific.

Linux.

Not install-tool specific.

Not runtime specific.

None.

title: Non deterministic pod ordering with PodsByCreationTime
body:
`PodsByCreationTime` sorts pods by creation time.
However when pods have same creation time (which can occur during batch creation or on systems with coarse clock resolution) the order is undefined.

This is particularly important during kubelet restart when pods are re-admitted through `HandlePodAdditions`, as it requires predictable ordering for resource allocation decisions.

Sorting pods by `PodsByCreationTime` be stable and always return same predictable ordering.

I didn't reproduce the issue. The bug is reported based on code analysis.

The issue appeared in github discussion: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141041#discussion_r3725040877

title: DRA: allocator should fail closed (per-node) on a malformed ResourceSlice nodeSelector term count
body:
Follow-up to #141212 and #141213. The validation fix in #141213 stops a new or modified ResourceSlice from carrying a per-device `nodeSelector` whose term count is not exactly one. It ratchets the new constraint, so a slice with a multi-term selector that was stored before the fix, or accepted by an older API server during a version-skewed rolling upgrade, is still admitted on an unchanged update.

Those already-stored multi-term slices can still reach the structured allocator. `createNodeSelector` handles the term count like this:

- `len == 0`: no-op. This is not reachable through a normal allocation. `ValidateNodeSelector` already rejects a zero-term selector ("must have at least one node selector term"), and even a stored one matches no node, because `nodeaffinity`'s `Match` returns false when there are no terms, so `isSelectable` filters the device through `NodeMatches` before `createNodeSelector` runs. Rejecting zero terms here would be defense in depth, not a fix for a demonstrated available-everywhere allocation.
- `len == 1`: merged.
- `len > 1`: returns `fmt.Errorf("unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with %d terms", ...)`.

The `> 1` error is not wrapped with `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so the DynamicResources Filter plugin treats it as a framework error rather than an `Unschedulable` result for that node. A framework error from Filter cancels the remaining node search and aborts the scheduling cycle, and it recurs on retry while the malformed slice stays in place. #141212 has a v1.36.2 reproducer.

There is also an ordering edge. `createNodeSelector` returns as soon as it sees a result with a `nodeName`, so a multi-term selector on a device that appears after a `nodeName` device is never inspected, while the same selector before it returns the hard error. Whether a malformed slice aborts the cycle therefore depends on result order.

Admission-time validation cannot retroactively fix a slice that was already stored, and version skew lets an older API server accept one during an upgrade, so the allocator should degrade gracefully instead of aborting the scheduling cycle for the whole Pod.

Proposed change, in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants (or their shared source):

- Treat a term count greater than one as a classified per-node failure: return an error wrapped with `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so Filter reports `Unschedulable` for that node and keeps searching the rest.
- Check the term count for every selected result before the `nodeName` early return, so result order does not decide whether a malformed slice is caught.
- Optionally reject zero terms in the same place as defense in depth, even though the normal path filters it earlier.

Tests would assert that a more-than-one-term selector returns an error satisfying `errors.Is(err, ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)` with the malformed selector both before and after a `nodeName` device, and that a single term keeps its current behavior.

This is intentionally kept out of #141213 to keep that admission fix small and reviewable during the v1.37 freeze. Linking here so the allocator gap is not lost when #141212 is closed by #141213.

title: DRA: a negative device consumesCounters value is accepted and over-commits a shared counter set
body:
A device's `consumesCounters` value may be negative. ResourceSlice validation accepts it, and the
structured allocator subtracts it from the counter set, so a negative consumption inflates the set's
available capacity and admits an allocation that over-commits the set.

`validateDeviceCounter` (`pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`) returns nil for any parsed
quantity, with no sign check:

```go
func validateDeviceCounter(counter resource.Counter, fldPath *field.Path) field.ErrorList {
	// Any parsed quantity is valid.
	return nil
}
```

The allocator subtracts each allocated device's consumption from the set (`existingCounter.Value.Sub(c.Value)`
in `checkAvailableCounters`); a negative `c.Value` raises the available value instead of lowering it, so a
device consuming a large positive amount then fits against the inflated available.

The sibling consumable-capacity path already guards exactly this class. `CmpRequestOverCapacity`
(`.../structured/internal/experimental/consumable_capacity.go`) rejects a negative resolved capacity with
`errNegativeCapacity` (`if consumedCapacity.Sign() < 0`), and its comment notes a negative "can reach the
allocator from a stored ResourceSlice ... which admission does not re-check." The counter path has no such
guard — that asymmetry is the bug.

Either ResourceSlice validation should reject a negative counter value (mirroring the capacity path's
stance that a negative is invalid input), or the allocator should fail closed on a negative consumption
rather than subtracting it into a larger available.

Publish a CounterSet of 8Gi, a phantom device consuming `-100Gi`, and a real device consuming `100Gi`:

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata: {name: nc-counters}
spec:
  driver: nc.example
  pool: {name: nc-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 2}
  allNodes: true
  sharedCounters:
  - name: mem
    counters: {memory: {value: 8Gi}}
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata: {name: nc-devices}
spec:
  driver: nc.example
  pool: {name: nc-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 2}
  allNodes: true
  devices:
  - name: phantom
    consumesCounters: [{counterSet: mem, counters: {memory: {value: -100Gi}}}]   # negative, accepted
  - name: real
    consumesCounters: [{counterSet: mem, counters: {memory: {value: 100Gi}}}]
```

The slice is accepted (`resourceslice ... created`; the `-100Gi` is stored). A ResourceClaim requesting
`count: 2` from `nc-pool` allocates **both** devices (Pod `Scheduled`), because the aggregate consumption is
`-100Gi + 100Gi = 0 ≤ 8Gi` — even though the `real` device alone consumes `100Gi` from an `8Gi` set. Without
the phantom device, a `count: 1` claim for the `100Gi` device is refused (`100Gi > 8Gi`). Observed on a real
v1.36.2 cluster.

The straightforward fix is a sign check on counter values in `validateDeviceCounter` (fail closed on a
negative), matching `errNegativeCapacity` in the consumable-capacity path; an allocator-side guard on a
negative consumption is a defensive complement. Threat model: a negative reaches the allocator from a DRA
driver's ResourceSlice, or from a slice stored before stricter validation — the same model the capacity
path's guard already accepts.

`DRAPartitionableDevices` (shared counters) is Beta and enabled by default since v1.36.

title: CPU Manager incorrectly spans sockets with distribute-cpus-across-cores and align-by-socket enabled
body:
When using CPU Manager with `static` policy and both of the following options enabled:
- `distribute-cpus-across-cores=true` (distributes CPUs evenly across NUMA nodes)
- `align-by-socket=true` (prefers NUMA nodes within the same socket)

CPUs may be allocated across multiple sockets instead of staying within a single socket. This violates the socket affinity guarantee that `align-by-socket=true` is supposed to provide.

For example:
- Socket 0: NUMA 0-3 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 0: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 1: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 2: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 3: (30 CPUs available)

- Socket 1: NUMA 4-7 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 4: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 5: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 6: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 7: (30 CPUs available)

Result: CPUs are allocated from NUMA 0,1,3,6 across both sockets.

With `align-by-socket=true`, the 120 CPUs should be allocated entirely from Socket 0 (NUMA 0,1,2,3) (which has 126 available CPUs).

Configure kubelet with:
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--cpu-manager-policy-options="distribute-cpus-across-cores=true,align-by-socket=true"

Set the available CPUs as above example, and create a pod with 120 CPUs.

title: DRA converting watch does not stop on Stop(): `break` inside `select` never leaves the loop
body:
In `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/client/generic.go`, `watchSomething.run` uses a
naked `break` in the `<-w.stopChan` case of a `select`:

```go
for {
	e, ok := <-resultChan
	if !ok {
		break
	}
	... convert e ...
	// This must not get blocked when the consumer stops reading,
	// hence the stopChan.
	select {
	case w.resultChan <- e:
	case <-w.stopChan:
		break        // exits the select, NOT the for loop
	}
}
```

In Go a naked `break` inside a `select` terminates the `select`, not the enclosing `for`. The
surrounding comment makes the intent clear, but after `Stop()` the goroutine loops back, keeps
pulling from the upstream watch, converts each event via `scheme.Convert` and discards it, and
never reaches the deferred `close(w.resultChan)`.

`watch.Interface` consumers expect `ResultChan()` to be closed after `Stop()`; here that only
happens if the upstream happens to close its own channel.

`run` should return when `stopChan` is closed, running both deferred calls
(`utilruntime.HandleCrash` and `close(w.resultChan)`), and should stop consuming upstream events.

Needs an upstream whose channel stays open after `Stop()`. Add to the `client` package:

```go
type stalledWatch struct{ ch chan watch.Event }

func (s *stalledWatch) Stop()                          {}
func (s *stalledWatch) ResultChan() <-chan watch.Event { return s.ch }

func TestRepro(t *testing.T) {
	up := &stalledWatch{ch: make(chan watch.Event, 8)}
	for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
		up.ch <- watch.Event{Type: watch.Added, Object: &resourcev1.ResourceSlice{}}
	}
	w := &watchSomething[*resourcev1.ResourceSlice, resourcev1.ResourceSlice, *resourcev1beta1.ResourceSlice]{
		upstream: up, resultChan: make(chan watch.Event), stopChan: make(chan struct{}),
	}
	done := make(chan struct{})
	go func() { defer close(done); w.run() }()

	time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
	w.Stop()

	select {
	case <-done:
	case <-time.After(5 * time.Second):
		t.Fatal("run did not return after Stop")   // this fires
	}
}
```

Observed: `run` never returns; the wrapper also drains the queued upstream events
(`upstream queue before Stop()=4, after Stop()=0`).
Expected: `run` returns promptly and the queued events are left untouched.

**This is usually masked in production.** `Stop()` calls `w.upstream.Stop()` first, and a
well-behaved `watch.Interface` closes its result channel in response, which ends the loop via the
`!ok` branch instead. I was not able to demonstrate a hang with a real client-go watch. It shows
up when the upstream is slow to close or does not close, and the wrapper should not depend on
upstream behaviour for its own termination in any case.

Grading this as a latent defect rather than an active outage. A repo-wide scan for `break` inside
a `select` inside a `for` found this as the only occurrence in `pkg/`, `cmd/`, `plugin/` and
`staging/`.

title: LimitRange maximum can be exceeded by declaring hugepages at the pod level
body:
A `LimitRange` of type `Pod` with a `max` for `hugepages-*` does not constrain a Pod that
declares its hugepages through pod-level resources (`spec.resources`). Such a Pod is admitted
even when its effective hugepages consumption exceeds the configured maximum.

The LimitRanger admission plugin keeps a private copy of the "is this a pod-level resource?"
predicate that lists only cpu and memory:

```go
// plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger/admission.go
var supportedPodLevelResources = sets.New(api.ResourceCPU, api.ResourceMemory)

func isSupportedPodLevelResource(name api.ResourceName) bool {
	return supportedPodLevelResources.Has(name)
}
```

The canonical predicate in component-helpers also matches the `hugepages-` prefix. Because of the
drift, `podRequests`/`podLimits` skip the pod-level override for hugepages and evaluate the
aggregated **container** values instead.

API validation explicitly permits the pod-level value to exceed the container aggregate (it only
rejects the reverse: "pod level limit for %s is insufficient to cover the aggregated container
and node-allocatable DRA limits"), so the two numbers can legitimately differ.

The Pod-scoped `LimitRange` maximum should be enforced against the effective pod-level hugepages
value, the same way it is enforced when the value is written at container level.

Requires the `PodLevelResources` feature gate (Beta, on by default since 1.34).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: hugepages-max
  namespace: demo
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Pod
      max:
        hugepages-2Mi: 4Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: over-the-limit
  namespace: demo
spec:
  resources:                 # pod-level: 8Gi, twice the LimitRange max
    requests:
      hugepages-2Mi: 8Gi
    limits:
      hugepages-2Mi: 8Gi
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
      resources:             # container aggregate stays within the max
        requests:
          hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
        limits:
          hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
```

Observed: the Pod is admitted.
Expected: rejected, as with `maximum hugepages-2Mi usage per Pod is 4Gi, but limit is 8Gi` -
which is exactly what happens if the same `8Gi` is written on the container instead.

Equivalent unit-level reproduction in `plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger`:

```go
err := PodValidateLimitFunc(&limitRange, &pod)  // returns nil; expected an error
```

The duplicated helper carries a `TODO(ndixita): Find alternatives to avoid duplicating the code`
and a comment saying it exists "to avoid conversion of v1.Pod to api.Pod". That rationale does not
apply to this function - it takes only a resource name - so it can simply delegate to
`resourcehelper.IsSupportedPodLevelResource`.

The neighbouring duplicated helpers (`podRequests`, `podLimits`, `addResourceList`,
`maxResourceList`) carry the same TODO and are worth auditing for similar drift.

title: CPU manager exclusive allocation metrics drifts
body:
The static policy in CPU Manager maintains the `CPUManagerExclusiveCPUsAllocationCount` and `CPUManagerSharedPoolSizeMilliCores` gauges by applying per-event deltas, and updates `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` only for the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation. This drifts away from the actual allocation state in several scenarios:

1. Init container CPU reuse is double counted (container scope). When an app container reuses the CPUs of a non-restartable init container, `allocateCPUs` returns the full allocation including the reused CPUs, which stay assigned to the init container too. The allocation path adds the full size of both allocations, counting the reused CPUs twice. The release path correctly subtracts the sibling-adjusted sets, so after the pod is removed the gauge keeps a permanent positive residue equal to the number of reused CPUs. The shared pool gauge has the mirrored problem: the allocation delta subtracts CPUs which have never been taken out of the default CPU set.

2. Fresh allocations and restarts disagree. During a kubelet run the exclusive allocation gauge accumulates deltas with the duplicates described above, while after a restart `initializeMetrics` recomputes it as the union of the checkpointed assignments (no duplicates). The same node state can therefore report two different values before and after a kubelet restart.

3. Pod-level (pod scope) allocations can leak on partial failure. `allocatePodForAdd` updates the metrics and stores the pod-level CPU set, but a failure while partitioning the bubble among the containers (takeByTopology) returns an error without releasing anything: the bubble stays out of the default CPU set, the gauge stays inflated, and nothing can ever clean it up, because `RemoveContainer` returns early for a pod with no container assignments and `removeStaleState` only iterates over container assignments.

4. Pod-level releases can drift the gauge below the real value. `RemoveContainer` subtracts the whole pod-level CPU set when the last container assignment is removed, but after a kubelet restart `initializeMetrics` only accounts the union of the remaining container assignments, which is smaller than the bubble if some containers have already been removed before the restart. Releasing a pod which died while the kubelet was down then over-subtracts the difference.

5. `initializeMetrics` ignores the pod-level CPU sets. After a restart the gauge is seeded only from the container assignments, so the part of a pod-level bubble not covered by any container assignment is not counted, even though it is excluded from the default CPU set.

6. `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` never drops back to zero. The update loop only writes the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation, so once the last exclusively allocated CPU of a node is released, the node keeps reporting its last non-zero value forever. The metric is also fed only with the container assignments, making a pod-level bubble invisible at allocation time, because the container assignments are stored later than the pod-level CPU set.

Metrics always present valid current state of exclusive CPUs allocations.

The scenarios are described in issue.
They are also fully covered by unit tests.
Running unit tests without changes to the code will reveal the problems.

title: [Bug] Device taint NoExecute eviction does not evict pods using DRA-backed extended-resource claims (pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus)
body:
**TL;DR:** the device-taint eviction controller (`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction`) only discovers which
claims a pod is using by reading `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. A pod that got its device through the newer
Extended Resource Backed by DRA path (KEP-5004, `DRAExtendedResource`) has its claim reference in
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus` instead — a field this controller never looks at. Both
`DRADeviceTaints` and `DRAExtendedResource` are Beta and **default-on since v1.36**, so this affects any
cluster running a stock 1.36+ apiserver/controller-manager with a DRA driver installed — no unusual
configuration required.

Live-reproduced on a `kind` cluster (full steps and output below): two pods, each holding one device from the
same driver, then a single `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` applied against that driver:

| Pod | Requests its device via | Claim reference lives in | Result after `NoExecute` taint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pod-to-be-evicted` | `ResourceClaimTemplate` | `pod.spec.resourceClaims` | Evicted within ~10s (correct) |
| `pod0` | plain `resources.limits` extended-resource request | `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus` | **Still `Running`, untouched** — the bug |

The `DeviceTaintRule`'s own status confirms only one pod was ever considered:
`"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace"` → `"1 pod evicted since starting the controller"`.

**Scope note, to save a maintainer the round-trip:** this is specifically about the *post-allocation eviction*
path. Allocation-time taint enforcement (a **new** pod being blocked from a `NoSchedule`/`NoExecute`-tainted
device it doesn't tolerate) is unaffected and works correctly for both request styles. The bug is
narrowly in the separate, already-allocated-pod eviction controller.

**Couple of affected use cases**
- GPU health-triggered auto-remediation. A node-health/GPU-health controller (e.g. something reacting to Xid/ECC errors, similar in spirit to NVIDIA GPU Operator's health checks) detects a failing GPU and applies a NoExecute DeviceTaintRule to force workloads off it before quarantining or repairing the device. Any pod still using the classic nvidia.com/gpu: 1-style request — which is the majority of existing GPU workloads, since KEP-5004's entire purpose is letting them keep working unmodified under DRA — is never evicted, and keeps running on a known-bad GPU instead of being cleanly rescheduled. Worst case: silently corrupted training/inference output rather than a clean failure.
- Targeted single-device maintenance on a multi-GPU node. An admin wants to service or replace one GPU on a node without draining the whole node (disruptive to the node's other GPUs/workloads), so they taint just that device NoExecute instead of cordoning the node. Any pod holding that device via an extended-resource request keeps running through the "drain," so the device can't actually be safely pulled for maintenance without an admin separately hunting down and manually killing those pods — defeating the point of device-level (vs. node-level) maintenance tooling.
- Clusters mid-migration from device plugins to DRA. KEP-5004 exists specifically so clusters can adopt DRA drivers without immediately rewriting every pod spec — meaning a long transitional period where legacy extended-resource-requesting Deployments/Jobs and newer ResourceClaim-based workloads coexist on the same devices. During that period, any device-taint-based enforcement (decommissioning a device, isolating a suspect one) only works for the already-migrated minority of workloads, silently failing for everyone else — undermining the mechanism cluster-wide for as long as the migration takes, which for large fleets could be months.

A `NoExecute` device taint should evict every pod actually consuming the tainted device, independent of which
API surface the pod used to request it. An admin tainting a failing/draining GPU for maintenance has no way to
know (and shouldn't need to know) whether a given consumer pod requested it via a `ResourceClaim` or via a
classic `resources.limits` extended-resource request — both end up running on the same physical device via
the same DRA driver and the same underlying `ResourceClaim` object. Today only one of the two is actually
evicted.

Reproducible deterministically on a `kind` cluster with no real GPU hardware, using
[kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) (a maintained,
public example DRA driver that simulates GPUs). All manifests below are the driver's own unmodified example
manifests (`demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/` and
`demo/examples/extended-resource-request/`), just applied side by side.

**Prerequisites:** Docker, `kind` v0.20+, `helm` v3.7+, `kubectl`.

```bash
# 1. Create a kind cluster with the required feature gates and API version.
#    (DynamicResourceAllocation and DRAAdminAccess are already GA/locked-on by v1.36 and are
#    omitted; DRADeviceTaints/DRAExtendedResource are Beta+default-on in 1.36 but included
#    explicitly for clarity; DRADeviceTaintRules is Beta+default-OFF in 1.36 and must be set.)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  DRADeviceTaints: true
  DRAExtendedResource: true
  DRADeviceTaintRules: true
runtimeConfig:
  resource.k8s.io/v1beta2: "true"
containerdConfigPatches:
- |-
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
    enable_cdi = true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name dra-repro --image kindest/node:v1.36.1 --config kind-config.yaml --wait 3m

# 2. Install the example DRA driver (8 simulated GPUs, no real hardware, default values).
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.4.0 https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver.git
helm upgrade -i --create-namespace --namespace dra-example-driver dra-example-driver \
  dra-example-driver/deployments/helm/dra-example-driver
kubectl -n dra-example-driver wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=kubeletplugin --timeout=90s

# 3. Control pod: requests a GPU via a ResourceClaimTemplate (pod.spec.resourceClaims).
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/1-basic-resourceclaimtemplate.yaml
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/2-pod-to-be-evicted.yaml
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod-to-be-evicted --timeout=60s

# 4. Treatment pod: requests a GPU via the classic extended-resource field. The scheduler
#    satisfies it via DRA and records the claim in pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus instead
#    of pod.spec.resourceClaims (confirmed with the jsonpath check below).
kubectl create namespace extended-resource-request
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: extended-resource-request
  name: pod0
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ctr0
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: ["bash", "-c"]
    args: ["export; trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
    resources:
      limits:
        deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com: 1
EOF
kubectl -n extended-resource-request wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod0 --timeout=60s
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}{"\n"}'

# 5. Taint the whole driver's devices NoExecute — both pods' devices are in scope.
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1beta2
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    driver: gpu.example.com
  taint:
    key: gpu.example.com/unhealthy
    value: "true"
    effect: NoExecute
EOF

# 6. Observe.
sleep 15
kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to

title: DRA structured allocator overflows the native-int device-count sum in the per-claim limit check
body:
The structured allocator adds device counts in native `int` before comparing to `resourceapi.AllocationResultsMaxSize`. `allocateOne` forms `len(results) + requestData.numDevices - r.deviceIndex`, and the pre-flight `Allocate` loop accumulates `minDevicesPerClaim += numDevices`. `DeviceRequest.Count` is validated only as `> 0`, never against the result limit, so several large-but-valid counts sum past the limit and wrap. Two counts of `math.MaxInt/2 + 1` wrap to a negative total, so `total > MaxSize` is false and the check is skipped; four wrap back near zero. A `FirstAvailable` request whose first alternative carries a huge count, sitting behind a device already allocated for the claim, drives the overflowing subtraction and misdirects the backtracking rather than pruning the oversized alternative.

### What you expected to happen

Each request is refused against the remaining capacity before the sum is formed, so no addition overflows and an oversized count is rejected with `number of requested devices exceeds the claim limit`.

### How to reproduce it

A single claim with two `ExactCount` requests of `math.MaxInt/2 + 1` each: the total overflows negative and is admitted today. A `FirstAvailable` request with a first subrequest of `math.MaxInt` behind one already-allocated device: the oversized alternative should be pruned and the small one taken. Both are covered by the tests in #141307, and the fix is applied identically across the stable, incubating, and experimental tiers.

`math.MaxInt` makes the counts overflow on 32-bit builds as well. This is worth a backport decision for the release branches that already carry the per-claim result-limit check.

### Related

This is the concrete in-tree instance behind #140424, which asks for an upper bound or overflow-safety contract on `DeviceRequest.Count`. #140424 observes that the structured allocator guards the single-count path; the gap here is the multi-count sum on that same path, one large count plus the devices already allocated for the claim, which was not guarded until #141307.

/wg device-management

_This issue was written in part with the assistance of generative AI. I checked the allocator paths and the overflow cases against the code and the tests myself._

title: A pod using a Dynamic Resource Allocation claim got permanently stuck in CreateContainerError after its node rebooted, with no automatic recovery.
body:
A pod using a Dynamic Resource Allocation claim got permanently stuck in `CreateContainerError` after its
node rebooted, with no automatic recovery.

Setup: a pod with a `ResourceClaimTemplate`-based claim, already `Running` with its device allocated and
prepared. I rebooted the node (a full reboot — kubelet and the container runtime both restart, along with
every workload container on that node, including the DRA driver's own pod).

After the node came back:
- The driver re-registered and kubelet re-prepared the same already-allocated claim (confirmed via the
  driver's own logs — it logged a fresh "prepare" call for the exact same claim UID and returned success).
- Despite that, the pod's container repeatedly failed to start:
  ```
  Warning  Failed  Error: failed to create containerd container: CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices k8s.gpu.example.com/gpu=<uid>-gpu-0
  ```
- This did not resolve on its own. I watched it for 5+ minutes: kubelet kept retrying the identical
  container creation with the identical (still-unresolvable) device reference, backing off further each
  time. It never attempted to re-prepare the claim again.
- The only way I found to recover was deleting and recreating the pod, which allocates a fresh claim and
  works immediately.

Note: a plain `systemctl restart kubelet` alone (container runtime left untouched, containers kept running)
does **not** reproduce this — I tried that first and saw no re-prepare attempt at all over several minutes.
The container runtime itself needs to also restart (i.e. an actual node reboot, or restarting kubelet and
the container runtime together) for this to trigger.

Either the pod should recover cleanly after the node comes back, or if the replayed prepare produces a
result that doesn't actually work, there should be some way to detect that and retry — an Event, a condition,
or another re-prepare attempt — rather than an indefinite retry loop with a generic container-runtime error
that gives no indication anything DRA-related happened.

1. Set up a DRA driver and create a pod with a `ResourceClaimTemplate`-based claim (used
   [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) v0.4.0 for
   this repro). Confirm it reaches `Running` with the claim allocated.
2. Fully reboot the node the pod is running on (in a `kind` cluster: `docker restart <node-container>`; on a
   real cluster: an actual node reboot, or restarting the container runtime and kubelet together).
3. Wait for the node to report `Ready` again and the driver's pod to come back up and re-register.
4. Observe: `kubectl describe pod` shows repeated `CreateContainerError` / `CDI device injection failed:
   unresolvable CDI devices ...` events, with a growing `BackOff`. This does not resolve on its own.
5. Delete and recreate the pod — it comes up fine immediately with a fresh claim.

I reproduced this the same way on a second, real (non-kind) cluster — same sequence of events, same
`CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices` error, same lack of self-recovery. A comparison pod
on a node that wasn't rebooted kept running the whole time, so this is specifically tied to the reboot, not
something intermittent.

Two things worth separating here, since I've only tested with one driver:

- Kubelet does not appear to remember, across a restart, that a claim was already successfully prepared —
  every claim gets treated as unprepared again after a reboot, and gets a fresh `NodePrepareResources` call
  regardless of which driver is behind it. This part reproduced identically on both clusters.
- Once that replayed call happens, kubelet accepts whatever the driver responds with and never re-checks or
  retries even after the resulting container creation keeps failing — it just repeats the identical failing
  attempt indefinitely. This also isn't specific to any one driver's behavior; it's what kubelet does with
  the response once it gets it, and I did not see it change over the retries.
- What I can't say for certain is whether every DRA driver would produce an unusable result the way this one
  did on replay. I tested only [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver).
  A driver with more robust logic may not have any visible symptom. But it seems that kubelet
  gives a driver no way to tell "this is a replay of something you already told me was ready" versus a fresh
  request, and never verifies or retries regardless. So any driver whose restart-recovery isn't airtight may hit
 this type of problem. This happened on the very first attempt, with the reference driver
  meant to demonstrate best practices, using nothing more unusual than a node reboot.

title: [Failing-test]: ci-kind-dra-1-34 times out before DRA suite can finish
body:
> **Status 2026-09-14.** The comments below carry `[UPDATED]` notes and strike-through where they were wrong.
>
> - The failures are memory pressure at the 6Gi limit, not the CPU quota. Prow reports `Job pod was OOM killed by the cluster.` for both builds listed below (test container `OOMKilled`, exit 127 in the first) and for 22 of the 40 `ci-kind-dra-1-34` runs from 08-03 to 09-11, 21 of them after running into the 90 minute timeout. The kind node journals cannot see that kill, so I missed it at first.
> - The runner CPU quota problem was real but separate. kubernetes/test-infra#37733 (merged 08-21, in the job image since 09-07) copies the pod's `cpu.max` into the runner's `init` leaf. The release-1.34 binaries have `containermaxprocs=0` (`godebug default=go1.24`) and ignore it; with `GOMAXPROCS=2` in the runner env (kubernetes/test-infra#37731) my replica of the job still ran into the 6Gi limit (one run each way). Neither explains the OOM kills.
> - The apiserver leak claim is withdrawn. The memory comes from `ResourceSlice Controller creates slices`, which on release-1.34 and release-1.35 publishes 100 max-size ResourceSlices; master cut it to 10 in #136156 (1847d5b1a, "created too much load for an E2E test"). Same branch, count as the only change: about 2 GiB less non-reclaimable memory for the suite on both branches, 3.0 to 3.4 GiB in the 1.34 random seed runs that hit the scheduler log mode below.
> - Why 1.34 is worse than 1.35, and why the seed matters: the scheduler's experimental structured allocator logs the full ResourceSlice list at V(5) once per node it evaluates, per scheduling attempt (`structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`, "Gathering pools"), about 74 MB per line while the 100 slices exist, and the jobs run kube-scheduler at `--v=5`. release-1.34 picks that allocator with the default gates (`DRAResourceClaimDeviceStatus`, beta); release-1.35 only when an alpha gate selects it (`DRADeviceBindingConditions` together with device status, or `DRAConsumableCapacity`), which the all-gates presubmit `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all` does. Master dropped the statement in #136588. In uncapped replays with random seeds the scheduler wrote 0.2 to 5.9 GB of log within about 30 s of that test; in job replicas at 2 CPUs, 0.2 to 4.3 GB, within about a minute at 12Gi and spread over 8 to 28 minutes in the 6Gi runs that thrashed; kube-scheduler at 1.0 to 1.7 GiB where it was sampled. With the statement deleted, the 100 slice presubmit replicas completed at 6Gi on both branches, still at 93 to 95% of the limit non-reclaimable.
> - Outcome (09-14): the remedy is the job memory, not branch code. #142082 (delete the log statement on release-1.35) and #142083 (the 100 to 10 change from #136156, release-1.35) were closed, they do not meet the cherry-pick guidelines; kubernetes/test-infra#37865 (6Gi to 12Gi for the 1.34 and 1.35 kind DRA jobs) merged on 09-14 06:25 UTC; the periodics run on a 24h interval and pick it up on their next runs, due around 14:20 UTC for `ci-kind-dra-1-34` and 20:17 UTC for `ci-kind-dra-1-35`. kubernetes/test-infra#37731 is closed. Whether the jobs stay green at 12Gi is what the next runs will show. First prow runs on the two PRs before they were closed (09-14): #142083 passed all three kind-dra presubmits; #142082 on its own passed the plain and `-all-slow` jobs; its `-all` job failed twice without an OOM kill (the first time with the apiserver stalling while the 100 slices were created and deleted, the second time on a different spec, a pod the kubelet rejected at device-plugin admission with the control plane quiet) and passed on the third run, so the log deletion alone leaves that job on the edge at 6Gi. The numbers are summarized in those PRs; I have the raw samples if anyone wants them.
>
> The original report follows, unchanged apart from the `[UPDATED]` notes, the strike-through and two heading remarks. The canary matrix and the three run rule were my own proposal at the time, superseded by the above.

- https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation#ci-kind-dra-1-34

I confirmed these failed runs:

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kind-dra-1-34/2088993552422932480
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kind-dra-1-34/2082106833379528704

It is not only one test. The DRA suite starts but cannot finish.

One confirmed run says:

```text
Will run 66 of 7144 specs
Running in parallel across 8 processes

5 specs pass, then:

[FAILED] [847.336 seconds] [BeforeEach]
test/e2e/dra/utils/deploy.go:287

wait for service account "default" in namespace "dra-9418":
timed out waiting for the condition

Process did not finish before 1h30m0s timeout
```

There is no final `Ran N of M Specs` summary.

I confirmed the two runs above.

I did not confirm the exact first bad run yet, so I do not want to give a wrong regression date. [UPDATED: the first run prow labeled as OOM-killed was on 07-14, the first run on the 07-13 kubekins image that moved dind under the pod cgroup (kubernetes/test-infra#37440).]

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation#ci-kind-dra-1-34

The primary failure is the Prow 1h30m timeout.

The job already started the tests, but namespace setup and control plane operation became very slow. One `BeforeEach` spent about 847 seconds and two namespaces could not get the default ServiceAccount in time.

The cleanup later also hit OOM or command failures around `kind export logs` and `kind delete cluster`. ~~I think this is secondary because the test process was already terminated by the Prow timeout.~~ [UPDATED: not secondary; prow reports the job pod itself as OOM-killed for this build, see the status at the top.]

Current job runs all these in one Prow container:

- Docker-in-Docker
- four kind nodes
- eight Ginkgo processes
- Kubernetes control plane
- 2 CPU
- 6Gi memory

Possible reasons (as listed at the time):

1. Eight Ginkgo processes and four kind nodes saturate the 2 CPU limit.
2. Memory reclaim makes apiserver, controller-manager or etcd very slow before OOM.
3. etcd or container storage has high I/O wait.
4. release-1.34 has a control plane or DRA regression.
5. The job downloads latest kind, and latest kind may interact badly with old release branch.
6. One DRA test or cleanup leaks cluster resources.
7. The floating latest 1.34 CI package introduced the regression.

I do not think increasing only the timeout is a good first fix.

Proposed canary matrix (superseded, see the status at the top):

| Ginkgo nodes | CPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 2 | 6Gi |
| 4 | 2 | 6Gi |
| 8 | 4 | 6Gi |
| 4 | 4 | 6Gi |

~~Add 8Gi memory only when `memory.events`, `memory.peak` or container metrics show memory pressure before the timeout.~~

For each run, collect:

- `cpu.stat`
- `memory.current`
- `memory.peak`
- `memory.events`
- `docker stats`
- kube-apiserver logs
- kube-controller-manager logs
- etcd logs
- time from namespace creation to default ServiceAccount creation
- final Ginkgo summary
- cleanup exit status

~~A resource or parallelism change should have at least three successful runs before merge.~~

This is different from #140701.

In #140701, the Ubuntu node jobs were OOM killed before tests and before guest VM creation. In this job, the kind cluster and tests already run, then the control plane becomes too slow.

Related test-infra history:

- kubernetes/test-infra#34343 moved etcd data to `/tmp` and reduced this job memory from 9Gi to 6Gi after a canary.
- kubernetes/test-infra#37491 changed DRA node-e2e jobs from 1Gi to 2Gi. That is another job type and another failure shape.

Cleanup error handling should be a separate PR. It should preserve the primary test exit code, always try both log export and cluster deletion, and not replace the first failure with a cleanup failure.

title: Kubelet restart preserves stale readiness for a replaced container when the API server status is outdated
body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141155#issuecomment-5272111983 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141155#issuecomment-5274991536.

#141342 stops a replacement container from inheriting the previous container's `Started` by comparing container IDs in `convertToAPIContainerStatuses`. The same identity problem exists on the readiness side of the kubelet restart preservation logic (`ChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart=false`, the default since 1.35):

1. `worker.go` decides `isRestart` purely from the container start time being older than the kubelet start plus the 10s grace period, and in that case does not seed the initial `Failure` result for the new container ID: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/94ece9779a9b1a07efd6cc986fa81ebb8947db28/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L257-L283
2. `setReadyStateOnKubeletRestart` sets `ready=true` when there is no readiness result yet and the container predates the grace period, and only backs off if the `PodReady` condition in `pod.Status` is not True: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/94ece9779a9b1a07efd6cc986fa81ebb8947db28/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go#L312-L341

Neither checks whether the container the API server knew about is the same container the runtime is reporting. If container A is replaced by B while the kubelet cannot reach the API server, and the kubelet then restarts, B is treated as a container that survived the restart and inherits A's `Ready=true`. B is reported Ready before its own readiness probe has ever run, until the first real probe result lands, which is delayed by `initialDelaySeconds`.

Reproduced on kind v1.36.1 (readiness-only pod, `initialDelaySeconds: 60`, probe `test -f /tmp/ready` that only the original container satisfied):

```
15:01:03 worker->apiserver blocked (iptables), liveness failure triggered
15:01:06 runtime creates replacement B (8bb688...), A exited
15:01:12 API still shows A: ready=true restarts=0
15:01:12 kubelet stopped, wait 12s so B is older than the grace period
15:01:24 API unblocked, kubelet started
15:01:27 API shows B: ready=true started=true restarts=1 podReady=True
         ... B stays Ready for ~43s, its readiness probe never passed ...
15:02:10 first probe result after initialDelay: ready=false podReady=False
```

Containers with a startup probe are covered by #141342 because B stays `Started=false` until its startup probe passes and readiness is gated behind that. Containers with only a readiness probe are not.

A replacement container should not inherit the previous container's `Ready` state. Readiness preservation across kubelet restart should only apply when the container ID in the API status matches the container ID reported by the runtime, consistent with the `Started` handling in #141342.

Two-node kind cluster (`kindest/node:v1.36.1`), pod pinned to the worker:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: q2
spec:
  nodeName: <worker>
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    readinessProbe:
      exec: {command: ["test","-f","/tmp/ready"]}
      initialDelaySeconds: 60
      periodSeconds: 2
    livenessProbe:
      exec: {command: ["test","!","-f","/tmp/die"]}
      periodSeconds: 1
      failureThreshold: 1
```

1. `kubectl exec q2 -- touch /tmp/ready`, wait for the pod to be Ready.
2. On the worker: `iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -j DROP` (and `ip6tables`), `ss -K dport = :6443`.
3. `kubectl exec q2 -- touch /tmp/die` so the kubelet replaces the container while the API is unreachable. Confirm with `crictl ps -a` that a new container is running.
4. `systemctl stop kubelet`, sleep 12s (keep the whole blocked window under the 40s node monitor grace period so the node lifecycle controller does not set PodReady=False for you).
5. Remove the iptables rules, `systemctl start kubelet`.
6. `kubectl get pod q2 -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID} {.status.containerStatuses[0].ready}'` shows the new container ID with `ready=true` until `initialDelaySeconds` elapses.

Proposed fix: apply the same container identity rule in both places above. `w.pod.Status.ContainerStatuses` / `InitContainerStatuses` (snapshot taken at `AddPod`) and `pod.Status` in `UpdatePodStatus` carry the pre-restart API view, so the old ID can be looked up by container name. If the known ID is non-empty and differs from the runtime ID, seed the initial readiness result and skip `setReadyStateOnKubeletRestart`.

One interaction to keep in mind: in a multi-container pod where X is unchanged and Y is replaced, correctly marking Y NotReady flips `PodReady=False`, and on the next sync `setReadyStateOnKubeletRestart` will also drop X to NotReady if X's first probe result has not landed yet. That is an existing property of the preservation design, but worth covering in unit tests.

Unit tests in `worker_test.go` (`TestChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart` already has isRestart fixtures) and `prober_manager_test.go` should be enough; an e2e is likely not practical.

Reproduced on v1.36.1; affects master and every release since v1.35 where `ChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart` defaulted to false.

title: Kubelet misses memory request cgroup reconstruction during cgroup config recovery (breaks InPlacePodVerticalScaling and MemoryQoS on restart)
body:
In `pkg/kubelet/cm/cgroup_manager_linux.go`, the helper function `readCgroupMemoryConfig` is used to parse the configured memory limits of a cgroup from the underlying cgroupfs (e.g. during Kubelet recovery on startup or when verifying existing container resource values for resizing).

However, `readCgroupMemoryConfig` only reads the memory limits (`memory.max` or `memory.limit_in_bytes`) and completely ignores memory requests/guarantees:

```go
func readCgroupMemoryConfig(cgroupPath string, memLimitFile string) (*ResourceConfig, error) {
	memLimit, err := fscommon.GetCgroupParamUint(cgroupPath, memLimitFile)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to read %s for cgroup %v: %v", memLimitFile, cgroupPath, err)
	}
	mLim := int64(memLimit)
	//TODO(vinaykul,InPlacePodVerticalScaling): Add memory request support
	return &ResourceConfig{Memory: &mLim}, nil
}
```

As highlighted in the codebase TODO comment, memory request support is missing. Under cgroups v2, Kubelet configures memory request/soft reservation limits using `memory.min` (for Guaranteed pods) or `memory.low` (for Burstable pods) when the `MemoryQoS` feature is enabled.

When Kubelet restarts, or when pod resource configurations are read for validation during `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` operations (in `pcm.GetPodCgroupConfig`), this missing support results in the Kubelet retrieving a `ResourceConfig` where the `Unified` settings containing `memory.min` or `memory.low` are absent. The validation logic (e.g., in `validatePodResizeAction`) is thus forced to operate with incomplete state, believing the current memory requests are zero or unset, which leads to incorrect validation, reconciliation discrepancies, or potential starvation issues on restart.

Kubelet should retrieve both the memory limits and the configured memory request guarantees (`memory.min` / `memory.low` when running on cgroups v2) when reading a cgroup's memory configuration. The returned `ResourceConfig` should accurately reflect the active QoS memory reservation parameters on the host.

1. Enable the `MemoryQoS` and `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` feature gates.
2. Create a Burstable pod that has a memory request (e.g., `requests: { memory: "128Mi" }`, `limits: { memory: "256Mi" }`).
3. Verify that the Kubelet correctly writes soft guarantees to the cgroups v2 hierarchy path (check `memory.low` value for the pod's cgroup).
4. Invoke `GetPodCgroupConfig` for `v1.ResourceMemory` (or trigger an in-place vertical scaling memory requests adjustment).
5. Inspect the returned `ResourceConfig`: the `Unified` map does not contain `memory.low` or `memory.min` settings, showing that Kubelet failed to reconstruct/read the current cgroup memory requests.

This is a highly valuable issue for Kubelet state reconciliation correctness and for the stability of `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` and `MemoryQoS` integrations.

**Proposed Solution Direction:**
1. Update `readCgroupMemoryConfig` to detect if running in cgroups v2 unified mode.
2. If cgroups v2 is active, read the `memory.min` and `memory.low` parameters from the cgroup path.
3. If they are set and greater than 0, populate them in the `Unified` map of the returned `ResourceConfig` struct.
4. Add unit test assertions in `pkg/kubelet/cm/node_container_manager_linux_test.go` or equivalent test suite to ensure that reconstructed memory configuration contains the expected memory requests.

title: DeviceTaintRule with deviceSelector omitted blocks device allocation cluster-wide, including adminAccess claims, contradicting documented behavior
body:
A `DeviceTaintRule` with the `deviceSelector` field entirely omitted (not an empty `{}` object
-- the field itself absent) makes every device on every node, across every driver and pool,
untolerated and therefore unschedulable -- not just whatever devices the taint was meant to
target.

Live-verified on a freshly-created kind cluster running v1.37.0 GA with **no non-default
feature gates set at all** (`DynamicResourceAllocation`/`DRADeviceTaints`/`DRADeviceTaintRules`
are all GA and enabled by default at this release):

1. An ordinary `ResourceClaim` targeting one device (`gpu-0`) allocates and its Pod runs, with
   zero `DeviceTaintRule`s present.
2. Apply a `DeviceTaintRule` with `taint.effect: NoSchedule` and `deviceSelector` omitted:
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
   kind: DeviceTaintRule
   metadata:
     name: taint-no-selector
   spec:
     taint:
       key: example.com/no-selector-test
       value: "true"
       effect: NoSchedule
   ```
3. The exact same claim/Pod from step 1, recreated, now fails to schedule (`FailedScheduling`,
   `cannot allocate all claims`).
4. Also confirmed on a 4-device pool: every device becomes unschedulable, not just one --
   including a claim declaring `adminAccess: true`, which is otherwise documented to bypass
   ordinary device exclusivity but is not exempted from `DeviceTaintRule` enforcement.
5. Deleting only the `DeviceTaintRule` (no other change) immediately restores every
   previously-blocked claim to allocate successfully.

According to the field's own documentation (`kubectl explain devicetaintrule.spec.deviceSelector`):

> The empty selector matches all devices. Without a selector, no devices are matches [sic].

A `DeviceTaintRule` with `deviceSelector` omitted should match **zero** devices and have no
scheduling effect -- the opposite of what actually happens.

1. Create a cluster running v1.37.0 (no special feature gates required).
2. Install any DRA driver advertising at least one device (repro used
   `kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver` v0.4.0).
3. Create an ordinary `ResourceClaim` + Pod referencing one device; confirm it runs.
4. Apply a `DeviceTaintRule` with any `taint` and `deviceSelector` omitted entirely.
5. Observe: any *new* claim against *any* device in the cluster -- including unrelated
   drivers/pools, and `adminAccess: true` claims -- fails to schedule.
6. Delete the `DeviceTaintRule`; confirm previously-blocked claims immediately allocate.

- This appears specific to the `NoSchedule` enforcement path. Tested `NoExecute` separately: a
  `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` with `deviceSelector` omitted does **not** evict an already-running
  pod on an unrelated device (its `EvictionInProgress` condition stays `reason: NotStarted`
  indefinitely) -- confirmed the eviction mechanism itself works correctly in the same environment
  via a positive control (a `NoExecute` taint with a matching selector evicted the target pod
  within 5 seconds). So the nil-selector matching bug looks confined to whatever code path
  `NoSchedule` uses to block new allocation, not the separate eviction controller.
- Distinct from #141422 / the pending fix in #141425: that issue concerns a selector that is
  *present but empty* (`deviceSelector: {}`). This report is about the field being *absent*
  entirely -- confirmed by reading #141425's diff that its new validation only rejects the
  empty-but-present case and returns immediately with no error when the selector is nil, so it
  does not cover this scenario.
- Creating a `DeviceTaintRule` is a cluster-scoped permission not granted by any built-in
  `view`/`edit`/`admin` ClusterRole -- but this bug means anyone holding that permission can
  silently take down DRA scheduling cluster-wide with one missing field, when the documented
  default behavior should be a no-op.

title: e2e_node image configs use a negated character class instead of excluding the -cgroupsv1 suffix
body:
The GCE node-e2e image selection filters candidate images with `image_regex` from the image config. `pickNewestImage` in `test/e2e_node/remote/gce/gce_runner.go` compiles it and keeps only images whose name matches:

```go
imageRe := regexp.MustCompile(imageRegex)
...
if imageRegex != "" && !imageRe.MatchString(instance.Name) {
    continue
}
```

The Ubuntu configs, and about nineteen image-config files in total, set:

```yaml
image_regex: ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$"
```

The intent, from kubernetes/test-infra#35723, is to drop the `-cgroupsv1` suffix and force cgroup v2. The problem is that `[^-cgroupsv1]` is a negated character class. It constrains the final character to be none of `-`, `c`, `g`, `r`, `o`, `u`, `p`, `s`, `v`, `1`, so it does drop `-cgroupsv1`, but it also drops any image whose name ends in one of those characters. A build tagged `...v20260801` ends in `1` and gets filtered out.

An image should be excluded only when its name ends in `-cgroupsv1`. A normal newest image that happens to end in one of those characters should still be selectable. As written, the filter can silently skip the real newest image and fall back to an older one whose name ends in an allowed character.

### How to reproduce it

Point a config's `image_regex` at `.*[^-cgroupsv1]$` and give the family a newest image whose name ends in `1`, such as a `v2026...01` build. `pickNewestImage` skips it and returns an older image.

### Proposed fix

RE2 has no negative lookahead, so `^(?!.*-cgroupsv1$).*` is not available. A separate exclude field matches the suffix directly and reads clearly:

```go
ImageExcludeRegex string `json:"image_exclude_regex,omitempty"`
```

```go
includeRe, err := regexp.Compile(imageRegex)
excludeRe, err := regexp.Compile(imageExcludeRegex)
...
if includeRe != nil && !includeRe.MatchString(instance.Name) {
    continue
}
if excludeRe != nil && excludeRe.MatchString(instance.Name) {
    continue
}
```

A config then reads:

```yaml
image_exclude_regex: "-cgroupsv1$"
```

This also gives a reason to switch the current `regexp.MustCompile` to `regexp.Compile`, so a bad config regex reports a clear error instead of panicking.

The `[^-cgroupsv1]$` pattern appears in about nineteen image-config files, so the config change spans several jobs once the field exists. This is separate from the image-resolution memory work in #141590 and #141434.

title: DRA: AllocationMode All errors for incomplete or invalid pools are not per-node failures
body:
An `AllocationMode: All` request returns a plain error when a pool gathered for the candidate node is incomplete or invalid. In `validateDeviceRequest`, same code in the stable, incubating and experimental variants:

```go
if pool.IsIncomplete {
	return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently being updated", klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID)
}
if pool.IsInvalid {
	return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently invalid", klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID)
}
```

Neither wraps `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`. `DynamicResources.Filter` maps only that sentinel to an `Unschedulable` result for the node; anything else becomes a framework `Error`, and `checkNode` in `findNodesThatPassFilters` cancels the remaining node checks when one shows up.

The other failing cases in the same suite do wrap it. Probe on master `a818af18fe2`, logging `errors.Is(err, ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)` for every case that errors:

```
all-devices-of-the-incomplete-pool                                                false | claim claim-0, request req-0: asks for all devices, but resource pool driver-a/pool-1 is currently being updated
invalid-pool-is-error-if-no-other-device-can-be-allocated                          true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
duplicate-slice                                                                   true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-validation-error-on-non-targeting-slice                     true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-device-counter-consumption-references-unknown-counter-set    true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-same-counter-set-name-in-different-resource-slices           true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
```

Same in all three variants.

`IsIncomplete` does not need a malformed object. `GatherPools` sets it when the generation resolved for the node holds fewer slices than its declared `resourceSliceCount`, which is what a pool looks like while a driver is publishing a new generation.

The check itself looks right and I would leave it alone: a slice that has not arrived may hold another device matching the request, so the allocator cannot know the full set yet.

The classification is the part that looks wrong. Wrapping the sentinel keeps the visible message, since it has no text of its own, and keeps the failure on one node:

```go
return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently being updated%w",
	klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID, internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)
```

Other nodes then keep being evaluated, and if all of them fail the Pod is `Unschedulable`. `EventsToRegister` already lists `ResourceSlice` `Add` and `Update`, so the slice update that finishes the rollout requeues it. The invalid branch wants the same treatment.

`all-devices-of-the-incomplete-pool` in `allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` already reaches the incomplete branch. Adding this next to the existing `expectError` assertion produces the output above:

```go
if err != nil {
	t.Logf("PROBE %s errors.Is=%v", name, errors.Is(err, internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode))
}
```

No case covers the invalid branch today.

Same classification shape as #141214 and #141338, different trigger. Those need a malformed stored per-device `nodeSelector`; this one fires during an ordinary generation rollout. Filing separately so the accepted scope of #141214 stays as it is.

@trungminhdo4-glitch offered on #141214 to fold this into #141338 if the maintainers would rather keep the per-node classification changes together. I am not opening a competing PR either way.

Read and probed on master `a818af18fe2`. The code path is unchanged on current master.
