title: kubelet can fail to start when the user namespace ID pool changes while pods with user namespaces exist on the node
body:
If the subordinate ID pool kubelet uses for user namespaces changes between restarts, and a pod on disk holds a mapping that falls outside the new pool, the kubelet does not start:

```
create user namespace manager: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 7340032 is out of range
```

[`record()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L252-L255) rejects a persisted mapping outside the current pool, and [the replay loop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L185-L189) returns on the first such pod, so `MakeUserNsManager()` fails and `NewMainKubelet()` with it. As far as I can tell the only ways out are to restore the previous pool or to delete the pod directory by hand, and the message points at neither.

Several ordinary things change the pool. Editing `/etc/subuid` to move kubelet's range does it. So does installing `getsubids` on a node that did not have it, or creating the `kubelet` account on a node where it did not exist, since both move the node from the built-in default range to whatever `getsubids` then reports. None of these involve cgo or #135870; that PR just adds one more way to get here, which is where I ran into it.

Whether a given node survives is luck. Blocks come from `allocator.NewAllocationMap`, which picks at random, so it depends on where the running pod happens to sit relative to the new pool. Going from the default pool to a delegated one is close to a certainty: the default holds 65535 blocks against a typical delegated pool of ~128.

`UserNamespacesSupport` has been GA with `LockToDefault` since 1.36, so the path is active on every Linux kubelet, but only nodes running pods with `hostUsers: false` are affected, since pods without a user namespace write no mapping file and are skipped on replay.

Something recoverable. Failing the whole kubelet over one pod whose persisted mapping no longer fits seems heavy next to, say, refusing that pod and saying why, and either way the error could name the pod directory an operator would have to clear.

I do not know which is right, and it overlaps with #140190, which is looking at persisted-mapping replay from the terminal-ID angle and deliberately kept its guard on the allocation side so that older on-disk mappings stay replayable.

Drop this in `pkg/kubelet/userns/` and run `go test ./pkg/kubelet/userns/ -run TestPoolChangeReplay -v`. No cgo, no NSS, no changes to the host.

```go
package userns

import (
	"testing"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/types"
	utilfeature "k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/feature"
	featuregatetesting "k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/testing"
	pkgfeatures "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/features"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2/ktesting"
)

func TestPoolChangeReplay(t *testing.T) {
	logger, _ := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
	featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate, pkgfeatures.UserNamespacesSupport, true)

	hostUsers := false
	try := func(label string, fromFirst, fromLen, toFirst, toLen uint32) {
		dir, uid := t.TempDir(), types.UID("p")
		m, err := MakeUserNsManager(logger, &testUserNsPodsManager{podDir: dir, userns: true,
			maxPods: 110, mappingFirstID: fromFirst, mappingLen: fromLen}, nil)
		if err != nil {
			t.Fatalf("%s: %v", label, err)
		}
		pod := &v1.Pod{Spec: v1.PodSpec{HostUsers: &hostUsers}}
		pod.UID = uid
		uns, err := m.GetOrCreateUserNamespaceMappings(logger, pod, "")
		if err != nil {
			t.Fatalf("%s alloc: %v", label, err)
		}
		_, err = MakeUserNsManager(logger, &testUserNsPodsManager{podDir: dir, userns: true,
			maxPods: 110, mappingFirstID: toFirst, mappingLen: toLen,
			podList: []types.UID{uid}}, nil)
		res := "restarts OK"
		if err != nil {
			res = "FAILS: " + err.Error()
		}
		t.Logf("%-42s block %-6d %s", label, uns.GetUids()[0].GetHostId()/65536, res)
	}

	try("subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608", 1048576, 8388608, 8388608, 8388608)
	try("subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks", 1048576, 8388608, 1048576, 7208960)
	try("default pool -> delegated pool", 65536, 4294901760, 1048576, 8388608)
}
```

One run:

```
subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608      block 112    FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 7340032 is out of range
subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks      block 131    FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 8585216 is out of range
default pool -> delegated pool             block 15363  FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 1006829568 is out of range
```

All three depend on where the pod happened to land, so one run understates it. Over 20 runs:

```
subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608   19 fail,  1 restarts OK   [16..143] -> [128..255], survives on 16 of 128 blocks
subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks    2 fail, 18 restart OK    [16..143] -> [16..125],  survives on 110 of 128
default pool -> delegated pool          20 fail,  0 restart OK    [1..65535] -> [16..143], survives on 128 of 65535
```

which matches the geometry in each case. The third row is the one that matters in practice: a node coming from the default pool has roughly a 0.2% chance per userns pod of sitting somewhere a delegated pool can still replay.

This is a unit-level reproduction in a checkout rather than something I have watched a real node do. It came out of #135870, where I raised it before @dims suggested splitting it into separate issues, but the PR is a trigger rather than the cause, so it stands on its own.

title: kubelet ignores the configured subordinate ID range for a local kubelet account when getent is not on PATH
body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870, which replaced `user.Lookup("kubelet")` with a `getent passwd` shell-out.

[`getentUserExists`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L188-L191) returns early when `LookPath` fails:

```go
getent, err := exec.LookPath("getent")
if err != nil {
	return false, nil // no getent: same as "not configured"
}
```

[The caller](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L151-L158) reads that as "no kubelet account", skips `getsubids` and returns the built-in default range. The account itself is never examined, so a local `/etc/passwd` entry is affected the same way, which is wider than the directory-service case the PR body describes.

Same node, with `getent` on PATH and then off it:

```
getent on PATH   firstID=1048576 rangeLen=8388608
getent off PATH  firstID=65536   rangeLen=4294901760
```

Before 6bb4235 the cgo `user.Lookup` resolved a local account without `getent`, so a node in this state used to get its configured range. I ran the two versions of that branch side by side against a real local account with `getent` off PATH: `user.Lookup` reports the account, `getentUserExists` reports it missing.

The configured subordinate IDs to still be used when the account is in `/etc/passwd`, or something in the log saying they were skipped. Today it is a `V(5)` line and no error.

@kginonredhat suggested a fallback during review: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870#discussion_r3966541751

That shape looks right to me with one adjustment. I would gate it on `exec.ErrNotFound` only, since `LookPath` also returns `ErrDot` alongside a usable path, and swallowing that turns a resolvable `getent` into a missing account.

Run from anywhere inside a checkout of master. No root, cleans up after itself.

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
W=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$W" pkg/kubelet/zz_getent_repro_test.go' EXIT
mkdir -p "$W/with" "$W/without"

# stand-ins for a node whose /etc/passwd has a kubelet account and whose
# /etc/subuid delegates 1048576/8388608 to it
cat > "$W/with/getent" <<'G'
#!/bin/sh
[ "$1" = passwd ] && [ "$2" = kubelet ] && { echo "kubelet:x:999:999::/var/lib/kubelet:/sbin/nologin"; exit 0; }
exit 2
G
cat > "$W/with/getsubids" <<'G'
#!/bin/sh
[ "$1" = -g ] && shift
[ "$1" = kubelet ] && { echo "0: kubelet 1048576 8388608"; exit 0; }
exit 1
G
chmod +x "$W/with/getent" "$W/with/getsubids"
cp "$W/with/getsubids" "$W/without/"   # same node, only getent is off PATH

cat > pkg/kubelet/zz_getent_repro_test.go <<'T'
package kubelet

import (
	"os"

	"k8s.io/klog/v2/ktesting"

func TestGetentRepro(t *testing.T) {
	logger, _ := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
	t.Setenv("PATH", os.Getenv("REPRO_PATH"))
	first, length, err := (&Kubelet{}).getKubeletMappings(logger, 65536)
	t.Logf("firstID=%d rangeLen=%d err=%v", first, length, err)
}
T
```

title: Memory Manager accepts an incomplete pod-level checkpoint as a restored allocation after kubelet restart
body:
With the static Memory Manager, pod-scope Topology Manager, and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, pod-level allocation is persisted through independent checkpoint updates: `PodMemoryAssignments` first, then per-container assignments, then `MachineState`. If kubelet stops after the real `SetPodMemoryBlocks` write completes but before the first `SetMemoryBlocks`, the resulting checkpoint is structurally valid but contains a PodEntry for UID `podUID`, no container assignments for that pod, and the pre-allocation machine state.

On restart, `validateState` reconstructs expected accounting by iterating `ContainerMemoryAssignments`. Because this pod has no container entries, the orphan pod assignment is not inspected and startup succeeds. `GetPodTopologyHints` then regenerates a hint from the PodEntry, and pod-scope admission calls `AllocatePod`. `AllocatePod` sees `GetPodMemoryBlocks(podUID) != nil` and returns success as though allocation were complete. The container `MemoryBlocks` and machine reservation remain absent.

This is an ordinary functional-correctness issue. No security impact is being claimed.

An incomplete pod-level allocation must not be treated as a completely restored allocation. Restart handling should reject the inconsistent checkpoint, repair it, or safely reconstruct/reallocate the missing state before successful admission is reported.

A deterministic unit reproducer, `TestMemoryManagerRestorePartialPodCheckpoint`, uses pod name `pod1` and UID `podUID`. It:

1. enables `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`;
2. creates the real static Memory Manager with the real checkpoint backend and a real best-effort, pod-scope Topology Manager;
3. wraps the state so `SetPodMemoryBlocks` first invokes the real setter and only then simulates process interruption;
4. verifies that the PodEntry is durable, container assignments are empty, and `MachineState` is unchanged;
5. creates new managers against the same checkpoint directory; and
6. performs normal pod-scope Topology Manager admission.

With the proposed validation guard removed on current master, the restored manager starts and admission succeeds, followed by these invariant failures:

```text
successful restored pod allocation left container "container1" without memory blocks
successful restored pod allocation left machine state without the pod reservation
```

This constructs the precise checkpoint through production state APIs; it does not claim that a live production node was intentionally crashed.

Related but distinct work:

- #140906 / #141077 preserve a fully completed restored pod allocation; this issue concerns a PodEntry-only partial checkpoint.
- #141070 restores pod topology hints from the pod-level allocation, which is why the orphan PodEntry can supply the post-restart hint.
- #141261 addresses a sibling CPU Manager partial-state cleanup problem.
- kubernetes/enhancements#5526 is the Pod Level Resource Managers design context.

A deterministic regression test and minimal startup-validation fix are prepared, and I intend to open a PR shortly.

Current upstream `master` at `654c2de7b8cabdb8353ec891122ee433deeb4457` (fetched and verified on 2026-09-10).

Not provider-specific.

The deterministic unit reproducer ran on macOS 26.6.2 (Build 25G83), arm64, against the platform-independent Memory Manager and Topology Manager code. The affected production static Memory Manager policy is Linux-specific. I did not intentionally crash a live production node.

Not installer-specific.

Not runtime-specific for reproduction.

None.

title: DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate overlong rolling-update service socket paths
body:
On current Kubernetes master, the DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate an unusable automatic service socket endpoint when rolling updates are enabled with a valid long driver name.

With normal defaults:

```text
plugin directory:
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/<driver name>

rolling service socket:
dra-<Pod UID>.sock
```

With a normal 36-byte Pod UID:

```text
full endpoint length = 71 + len(driverName)
```

A valid 37-byte driver name:

```text
abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io
```

produces exactly a 108-byte endpoint under the affected implementation. Kubernetes requires AF_UNIX pathname-based endpoints to remain shorter than 108 bytes. A valid 63-byte driver name produces a 134-byte old-style endpoint.

Valid DRA drivers using `RollingUpdate` with the normal automatic/default directory and socket naming should receive an AF_UNIX-compatible endpoint. Rolling instances must remain distinguishable.

This expectation does not extend to arbitrary custom `PluginDataDirectoryPath` values.

Use:

```go
DriverName("abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io")
RollingUpdate("11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555")
// no PluginDataDirectoryPath override
// no PluginSocket override
```

An injected `PluginListener` can observe the real automatically generated endpoint without relying on the local macOS Unix-socket behavior.

The affected implementation produces:

```text
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io/dra-11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555.sock
```

and its length is exactly 108 bytes. The valid 36-byte control driver produces 107 bytes.

### Root cause

Rolling-update service socket naming includes the complete Pod UID. The default containing directory independently contains the complete driver name. The service socket did not check the combined full-path budget or fall back to a shorter basename.

### Relationship to existing work

- #139166 / #139623 addressed the rolling **registration socket** under `plugins_registry`.
- #139623 explicitly left `dra-<uid>.sock` service sockets unchanged.
- #141815 corrected the registration fallback's exact-108 boundary.
- #140837 added kubelet-side endpoint and driver validation but does not prevent this helper from generating an invalid automatic service endpoint.

### Affected scope

Reproduced on Kubernetes master at `3af569e862d19a046cdfd63cda837f9bb29da6fa`. Older releases were not verified.

No production incident was observed.

title: kubelet: cut PLEG relist memory with CRI field projection + delta listing
body:
Two additive, opt-in changes to the CRI container/pod list calls so the kubelet's PLEG can stop decoding data it doesn't use:

1. **Field projection** Let the client request only the fields it needs (container id, state, and the `io.kubernetes.*` identity labels). The runtime omits everything else; older runtimes ignore the request field and behave as today.
2. **Delta listing** Let the client receive only the containers that changed since the last relist, instead of the full set every cycle.

This came out of a hallway conversation at gRPCConf after my talk on CRI list streaming: a few gRPC maintainers and I got into why server-streaming a big response doesn't actually cut memory and the receiver still decodes the whole object graph. That pointed back at the kubelet's own CRI list path, so I went and measured it.

PLEG relists every container on the node about once a second and the kubelet decodes the entire
result each time. On dense or high-churn nodes this is large, mostly-redundant memory and CPU:

- Measured on master: ~18k containers with realistic annotations ≈ **1.57M allocations / ~79 MB
  held per relist**, re-paid every second.
- A full "fat" response can cross the 16 MiB CRI client cap (`maxMsgSize`), so `ListContainers`
  fails → PLEG stalls → node NotReady → and container GC can't run because it needs the same list
  (the "PLEG is not healthy" failure on high-churn nodes).
- The list is dominated by accumulated terminated containers that never change, re-decoded every
  second for nothing.

Existing work doesn't cover this axis: KEP-5825 (CRIListStreaming) fixes the per-message size cap but, in its own words, "does not reduce kubelet memory usage"; KEP-3386 / PLEGOnDemandRelist change relist *frequency*, not per-object payload.

I have a small benchmark harness (happy to push it) that measures decode + hold cost for full vs projected vs changed-only responses on representative payloads:

- **Projection** (measured): −45% memory, −65% wire, −34% allocations.
- **Changed-only** reduces it much further, since the list is mostly static terminated containers, the mechanism is measured and linear, and the exact factor depends on per-relist churn, which isn't instrumented upstream today (I model it at ≤1% for the accumulated-dead-container case, giving ≥99%; grounding that number would be step one of an alpha).
- **Correctness:** projection is client-declared per call, so it can't remove a field a consumer is reading and safe by construction. For the PLEG path specifically, the needed set is small and verified in code (event generation uses only id + state; container→pod mapping uses only `pod.uid`; the restart hash comes from `ContainerStatus`, not the list).

I'd like to bring this to sig-node as a KEP; opening this to track the problem and gather input.

title: kubelet: containers that fail before ever running don't get exponential CrashLoopBackOff treatment
body:
When `startContainer` fails before the container ever reaches a running state — e.g. `CreateContainer` is rejected by the CRI because a resource limit (such as memory) is below the runtime's floor, or a pre-create/pre-start hook fails , no container status is ever recorded for that attempt.

`kubeGenericRuntimeManager.doBackOff` decides whether to apply `CrashLoopBackOff` by looking for an *exited* container status in `podStatus.ContainerStatuses`. Since these pre-run failures never produce a container status, `doBackOff` never finds one to back off against.

The pod is still retried (the pod-worker's flat ~10s backoff on `SyncPod` errors still applies , see `backOffPeriod` in `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go`), but these container-start failures never get the *exponential* backoff or the `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event that other persistently-failing containers get once they've run and exited at least once. This is inconsistent: two containers that both fail forever are treated differently depending on whether the failure happened before or after the container briefly started.

Containers that repeatedly fail to start , even before ever reaching a running state — should get the same exponential backoff escalation (up to the standard cap) and `CrashLoopBackOff` status/event reporting as containers that repeatedly exit after starting.

1. Create a Pod with a container whose resource request/limit is set below what the container runtime enforces as a floor (e.g. a memory limit below the runtime's minimum).
2. Observe that `CreateContainer` is rejected on every retry.
3. Observe that kubelet retries at a flat ~10s cadence indefinitely, without back-off escalating over time, and without a `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event ever appearing ,unlike a container that starts and then repeatedly exits

title: Kubelet omits volume stats after all pod container cgroups are removed
body:
The kubelet's cAdvisor stats provider can omit a Running pod's mounted volume stats after cAdvisor has removed every pod-managed container record.

PR #142249 preserves volume stats when all container samples are filtered as terminated, but `ListPodStats` still builds its pod map from cAdvisor records carrying pod labels. If every container cgroup has already been garbage-collected and cAdvisor reports only the unlabeled pod-level cgroup, the provider cannot build a `PodReference`. The pod and its cached volume stats are therefore absent from the Summary API and from `kubelet_volume_stats_*`.

A Running pod should retain cached stats for its mounted volumes while the kubelet still knows the pod and the resource analyzer still has volume data, even when no pod-managed container cgroup remains.

### How can we reproduce it?

At the unit-test level:

1. Have the pod manager return a Running pod with a valid start time.
2. Have the resource analyzer return cached persistent volume stats for that pod.
3. Have cAdvisor return the root cgroup and the pod-level cgroup, with no labeled container records.
4. Call the cAdvisor provider's `ListPodStats`.

The current provider returns an empty pod list. A focused regression test fails with:

```
"[]" should have 1 item(s), but has 0
```

### Proposed fix

Use the kubelet pod manager as the fallback source of pod identity when cAdvisor has no labeled container record. Only seed a missing pod when cached volume stats exist, then apply the existing start-time and Running-phase validation before returning it.

This is a follow-up to #141350 and #142249.

title: [Flaking Test] [sig-testing] ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master kubetest.Timeout [gce-cos-alphafeatures-master, gce-cos-alphafeatures-1.37]
body:
sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master (`ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master`)
sig-release-1.37-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-1.37 (`ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta`, the fork of the same job)

Triage: https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?job=%5Eci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master%24&test=%5ETimeout%24

Status 2026-09-23: tracked as FLAKY on the CI Signal board per the Release Signal lead. Triage accepted by SIG Node (harche); priority/critical-urgent as set at triage. I hold the Release Signal follow-up. Next step per upodroid is a test-side improvement by SIG Node; no test owner confirmed yet. The blocking or non-blocking call for v1.38.0-alpha.1 (2026-09-23) is with SIG Node and pending; no mitigation is agreed. Master count from the 2026-09-16 00:57 UTC run through the 2026-09-23 18:44 UTC run is 23 of 93 completed runs timed out (25%), 2 of the last 13; 1.37 is 1 of its last 4. The three recent failures are the same pattern: suite passed, teardown interrupted by the timer. The numbers below are the 2026-09-21 06:00 UTC snapshot.

`kubetest.Timeout`. The e2e suite passes in all but one of the timed-out runs; in that one the timeout interrupted the suite.

Snapshot 2026-09-21 06:00 UTC. On master, 15 of the 61 runs since 2026-09-16 00:57 UTC hit the timeout: the first at 2026-09-17 13:04 UTC, the last two at 2026-09-21 00:16 UTC and 02:19 UTC, with passing runs in between. On the 1.37 fork, 7 of the 21 runs since 2026-09-16 01:00 UTC, the latest at 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC.

Examples:
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101858636748820480 (2026-09-21 02:19 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101736329489420288 (2026-09-20 18:13 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008 (2026-09-19 12:07 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta/2101658314709405696 (1.37, 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC)

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master

The job runs out of its kubetest budget, not out of tests. It passes `--timeout=120m` to kubetest, which covers cluster up, the tests and teardown. Up and teardown are steady at about 15 minutes together, which leaves roughly 105 minutes for the suite. In 14 of the 15 timed-out master runs the suite finished with `91 Passed | 0 Failed` after 105 to 112 minutes and the budget ran out in the teardown steps; in the other run ginkgo was interrupted at 113 minutes with one spec still running (`90 Passed | 1 Failed`).

The suite's runtime is not fixed. The same 91 specs took 76 minutes in a passing run on 2026-09-19 at 14:08 UTC (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101312282582585344) and 106 minutes in the timed-out run two hours earlier (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008), on the same Kubernetes commit (`v1.38.0-alpha.0.948+96b5e4e3ae3f8d`) and the same COS image. So a code or image change alone does not explain the timeouts; whether something makes the resize path slower under some conditions is open. Across the 59 runs since 2026-09-16 the test phase ranged from 76 to 113 minutes; the 45 passing runs took 76 to 103 minutes with a median of 87, and passing and timed-out runs occur on the same commits.

Almost all of that variance sits in one feature. `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` is 63 of the 91 specs and took 57 minutes in the fast run and 86 in the slow one; the other 28 specs took 19 minutes in both. 62 of the 63 resize specs are slower in the slow run, by 20 seconds at the median and up to 83 seconds, with no single spec standing out, so the extra time is inside the resize specs themselves. What inside them is slower I have not established; the kubelet logs of both runs show no deferred or infeasible resizes.

This is the same shape as #141186 on `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-alpha-features`, which runs almost the same focus. That was resolved by kubernetes/test-infra#37724: kubetest to `--timeout=180m`, the prow timeout to 3h20m, and the job moved to release-informing, on the basis that alpha-feature lanes do not fit the two-hour release-blocking budget. The note on that issue that the 1.37 blocking board shows the same thing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141186#issuecomment-5316283473) was not followed up for the sig-release jobs, which still have `--timeout=120m` and a 2h20m prow timeout in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-release/gce-cos-e2e-master.yaml` and `release-branch-jobs/1.37.yaml`.

Update after upodroid's comment (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142262#issuecomment-5759352510): the next step is on the test side. SIG Node is asked to look at reducing the resize specs' execution time or their run-to-run variance while keeping the coverage. Skipping the resize tests is not on the table, and a timeout increase or dashboard change is not agreed; it would come after that attempt, if at all. A test-side owner is not confirmed yet.

Background for whoever picks it up: InPlacePodVerticalScaling is Stable since 1.35, and this lane is the only blocking coverage the 63 resize specs have. The sig-node node-e2e lanes skip `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` explicitly or do not focus on it; the node alpha-features lane (`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features`) ran 3 memory-backed-volume resize specs in its latest build, none of the 63. The job runs ginkgo with `--nodes=1`, and the presubmit alpha-features job sets `--ginkgo-parallel=1` explicitly, so I have not assumed parallelism is safe for these specs. The sibling job's uncensored timing distribution is in the comments.

SIG Node's call on whether this blocks v1.38.0-alpha.1 on 2026-09-23 is still needed, with the reason and any conditions; I will relay it to the Release Signal lead and the release-cut representative. FLAKY on the CI Signal board is a tracking category and says nothing about the cut.

This is not #142205. That one is a single spec (the allocated pods endpoint test) failing on the kind alpha-beta lane. Here the specs pass, apart from the one interrupted run, and the job runs out of its time budget.

title: [Feature][scheduler] Asynchronously or concurrently update (Composite)PodGroup status conditions to avoid scheduling cycle head-of-line blocking
body:
### Description
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140670, status condition updates for `PodGroup` and `CompositePodGroup` were integrated into the scheduler pipeline.
Currently, in `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go`), status updates for every group within a hierarchy are performed sequentially and synchronously on the main scheduling goroutine:
```go
for _, podGroupResult := range podGroupResults {
    pgi := podGroupResult.podGroupInfo
    if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil {
        sched.submitCompositePodGroupResult(ctx, podGroupResult)
        continue
    }
    queuedPodInfos := rootPodGroupInfo.QueuedPodInfos[pgi.GetKey()]
    sched.submitPodGroupResult(ctx, schedFwk, podGroupState, queuedPodInfos, podGroupResult)
}
```
Each call to `submitCompositePodGroupResult` / `submitPodGroupResult` issues an individual, synchronous status patch request to the API server (`util.PatchPodGroupStatus` / `util.PatchCompositePodGroupStatus`).
### Why this is a problem
For larger or deeper hierarchies containing multiple intermediate composite groups and leaf pod groups, issuing sequential synchronous HTTP patch calls directly on the scheduling thread:
- Multiplies scheduling cycle latency linearly by the number of groups in the subtree.
- Contributes to head-of-line (HoL) blocking in the active scheduling queue, as the scheduler cannot pick up the next queued workload until all status updates complete.
### Potential Mitigations to Discuss
- **Asynchronous dispatch**: Offload status patching to background goroutines (similar to `sched.runBindingCycle`) or a dedicated worker queue so the main scheduling goroutine can immediately proceed to the next cycle.
- **Concurrent patching**: If status updates must be bounded or completed within the cycle, patch group statuses concurrently (e.g., using an `errgroup` or bounded worker pool) rather than strictly sequentially.

title: Kubelet emits spurious Pod status updates due to nondeterministic allocated resource health ordering
body:
With `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled, kubelet can change the order of entries in `status.containerStatuses[*].allocatedResourcesStatus` even when device and claim health have not changed.

There are two nondeterministic paths in kubelet v1.36.3:

1. The device manager constructs each `ResourceStatus.Resources` slice by iterating a map of device IDs. The same resource IDs can therefore be emitted in a different order on later syncs.
2. The DRA manager rebuilds `AllocatedResourcesStatus` by iterating `resourceStatusMap`. This can reorder device-plugin and claim statuses, for example:

```text
[nvidia.com/gpu, claim:channel]
[claim:channel, nvidia.com/gpu]
```

The resulting Pod status is semantically unchanged but serialized differently. Kubelet treats it as a status change and sends a Pod status update. The API server then stores a new resource version and broadcasts a full `MODIFIED` watch event. This can create continuous status and watch churn for otherwise unchanged Pods.

Kubelet should produce a stable `AllocatedResourcesStatus` representation when resource health is unchanged. Both the outer `[]ResourceStatus` and each inner `[]ResourceHealth` should have deterministic ordering, so repeated syncs do not cause unnecessary Pod status updates.

1. Run kubelet v1.36.3 with `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled.
2. Start a Pod whose container has at least two device-plugin devices and a DRA resource claim with health reporting. Generic test device-plugin and DRA drivers are sufficient.
3. Keep all reported health values unchanged.
4. Trigger or wait for repeated Pod status syncs and watch:

```console
kubectl get pod <pod> -w -o json
```

5. Observe that either:
   - entries in a `ResourceStatus.Resources` slice change order, or
   - entries in `AllocatedResourcesStatus` change order.

The Pod `resourceVersion` advances and a `MODIFIED` watch event is emitted despite no health change.

This can also be reproduced in unit tests by calling the two `UpdateAllocatedResourcesStatus` implementations repeatedly with multiple map entries and asserting that their output is canonical.

The relevant v1.36.3 code paths are:

- Device ID map iteration while constructing `ResourceStatus.Resources`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L1162-L1177
- DRA map iteration while rebuilding `AllocatedResourcesStatus`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L936-L943
- The device-manager-then-DRA call order: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L1135-L1145

A minimal fix is to canonicalize the final status by `ResourceStatus.Name` and each resource list by `ResourceHealth.ResourceID`, with regression tests covering stable output across repeated calls.

